SU(2) Yang–Mills:
Spectral Bounds, Vacuum Concentration,
and Criteria for the Continuum Limit
Aleksandar Mihajlovic
Technical Faculty, Singidunum University, Belgrade, Serbia
Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
aleksandar.mihajlovic.10.dls@singimail.rs
ORCID: 0009-0009-0623-8080
5 November 2026 Version 5
Abstract
A continuum mass-gap argument must preserve nonzero renormalized states and a positive
spectral estimate while the spatial cutoff is removed and physical volume grows. We develop
quantitative results that separate these requirements. Gauge reduction, reflection positivity
and attributed strong-coupling estimates give physical-transfer bounds with nontrivial local
sectors. At fixed spatial cutoff and positive coupling, we construct subsequential infinite-
volume physical-time dynamics from local history correlations, with nonconstant gauge-
invariant observables. For finite spatial boxes, explicit bounds apply to the entire physical
vacuum complement; finite-matrix criteria include all omitted representations. Vacuum
concentration gives extensive entropy bounds, quantitative fidelity obstructions for hard
electric cutoffs, and necessary growth of retained representation spaces. A sharper local
comparison yields complete bounds on fixed discarded-link sectors, while collective projection
and Schur estimates isolate the additional input needed for a volume-uniform gap. The work
also certifies a finite three-link conditioning functional through Wilson coupling 0.354, with its
physical interpretation conditional on the stated block-comparison hypotheses. Exact blocking,
corrected effective-potential theorems and a representation-by-representation two-dimensional
benchmark clarify which approximations preserve the relevant observables. Published glueball
measurements retain their original attribution; the new analysis of those data and the recorded
replica experiment have explicitly statistical scope. Complete derivations and reproducible
calculations support a set of certified benchmarks and continuum transfer criteria. A nontrivial
four-dimensional spatial-cutoff construction and a positive spectral bound along it are not
established; no exact continuum mass is asserted.
Keywords: lattice Yang–Mills theory; physical transfer operator; mass gap; vacuum concen-
tration; representation truncation; reflection positivity; infinite-volume dynamics; continuum
limits.

1 The research question and the sequence of results
The motivating question is quantitative: what can be proved about the lowest physical excitation
of four-dimensional pure SU(2) Yang–Mills theory, and which finite-cutoff estimates can survive
the construction of a continuum theory? Positivity at one regulator is the beginning of this
question. Its endpoint requires compatible nonzero physical states, local observables and time
correlations as the regulator and volume change. The mathematical development below follows
that progression.
The physical object is a gauge-invariant transfer operator, or the Hamiltonian obtained in its
continuous-time limit. The vacuum is removed using its actual ground state. The gap is measured
on the whole remaining physical space, unless a smaller subspace is explicitly specified. Markov
chains used to sample a lattice measure, auxiliary Wilson flow, and physical time are distinguished
throughout.
1.1 Models, normalization and units
For Euclidean Wilson theory on a finite four-dimensional lattice, write
Fp(U) = 1 2 TrUp, W (U) = ∑ p (1−Fp(U)), dµβW =Z−1e−βWW (U) ∏ e dUe.
Haar measure is normalized, the links take values in SU(2), and βW = 4/g2 0 is the conventional
isotropic Wilson normalization [1, 2]. The strong-coupling direction is small βW. The asymp-
totically free continuum direction is weak bare coupling, with increasing βW; a theorem on a
bounded strong-coupling interval does not control that direction.
On a periodic cubic spatial lattice with spacing as, the Hamiltonian convention used in the
spectral sections is
Has,L,s = s 2as ∑ e Ce + 4 sas ∑ p (1−Fp), s =g2 > 0, (1.1)
on Hphys = L2(SU(2)Es,dµ)G. Here Ce has eigenvalues j(j +1) and the second sum is over spatial
plaquettes. The normalization is the temporal Wilson limit of the Kogut–Susskind construction
[3, 4]. At fixed as,s, the anisotropic parameters obey βt = 4as/(sϵ) and βs = 4ϵ/(sas) as the
temporal step ϵ↓ 0. This limit removes the temporal discretization while leaving the spatial
cutoff in place.
Symbol Meaning and convention
as, ϵ Spatial spacing and physical temporal step; a means the relevant spacing where locally specified.
L, asL Number of spatial sites per direction and physical side length.
βW, s Isotropic Euclidean inverse coupling and Hamiltonian coupling g2; their limiting trajectories
are not silently identified.
T, λ0 Positive physical transfer operator and its leading eigenvalue.
δ, ∆ Dimensionless transfer gap− log(λ1/λ0) and a Hamiltonian or physical energy gap.
h, ν Positive normalized finite-volume ground state and its probability measure dν =h2dµ.
J Highest retained electric representation spin, when a cutoff is imposed.
t, tflow Physical time and auxiliary smoothing time, respectively. Monte Carlo sweeps are a third,
algorithmic parameter.
Local sections define additional notation. Distinct settings such as two-dimensional gauge theory
and scalar effective models are identified before any theorem is applied to them.

1.2 What is established
The first step is exact gauge reduction and construction of the physical transfer space. Com-
pactness, positivity and the treatment of the vacuum give genuine finite-spatial-volume gaps.
Strong-coupling comparison then supplies estimates independent of the number of lattice sites.
The sharp single-link quarter transport estimate and the perfect-forest βW < 1/3 framework are
attributed to Bhattacharjee and Bhattacharya [5]; their arguments are included with the gauge
and physical-sector details needed here. They are not claimed as a new historical discovery of
this work. Classical transfer and reconstruction results are due to Lüscher, Osterwalder–Seiler
and Osterwalder–Schrader [6, 7, 8, 9]. The relation to other strong-coupling approaches is made
explicit [10, 11].
The development then addresses quantities that these strong-coupling theorems leave uncontrolled:
the spatial Hamiltonian sequence, its ground states, discarded representation sectors and collective
spectral effects. For every fixed spatial spacing and positive coupling, local history correlations
have subsequential thermodynamic limits. They reconstruct strongly continuous physical-
time dynamics with nonconstant local gauge-invariant correlations. This is an infinite-volume
construction with a spatial lattice, not a simultaneous four-dimensional continuum construction.

The vacuum-fidelity results make a complementary requirement quantitative. For the specified
hard cutoff, g↓ 0 and gJ→ 0 force the best vacuum fidelity in the retained subspace to vanish.

in norm. Exact spectral tails and renormalized state maps must be treated together.

tion, with outward rational error bounds, and the exact fixed-representation blocking coefficient
in Proposition 80.14. For the adjoint representation its value is 25/16. They are quantitative
additions to the research programme; no claim of priority over all prior literature is made.

1.3 The continuum conclusion and its remaining premises
Let Ak = Tk/λ0,k, let at,k ↓ 0 be the physical temporal step and let P0,k = |Ωk⟩⟨Ωk| project onto
the normalized actual vacuum. A sufficient lattice spectral statement is
0≤Ak
⏐⏐
Ran(I−P0,k) ≤e−δkI, lim inf k δk at,k ≥M > 0. (1.3)
It must accompany a nontrivial continuum construction: renormalized physical states and local
observables must have compatible limiting norms, adjoints and physical-time correlations, and
the limiting probe family must be dense in the full physical vacuum complement. The spatial
cutoff must tend to zero and physical spatial volume must grow with these controls intact.
Under these hypotheses, the correlation inequality passes to ⟨ψ,e−tHψ⟩≤ e−Mt∥ψ∥2. The
spectral theorem then excludes spectrum in (0,M) and any additional zero-energy vector in that
complement. The detailed versions below specify the embeddings, norm control, time rounding
and density requirements. They also exhibit counterexamples when those hypotheses are omitted.
The conclusion concerns a limiting theory only after its construction and identification have been
justified.
Lower-dimensional stochastic constructions and ultraviolet gauge-field estimates provide relevant
context, with their dimensions and conclusions retained [12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. They are not inputs
that establish the missing four-dimensional spatial-cutoff limit. Likewise, the empirical mass
ratio in Section 82 is evidence about the measured scalar channel; it is not a theorem excluding
every possible low-energy physical state.
1.4 Organization and reproducibility
Parts I–II establish the gauge-invariant finite-cutoff setting and strong-coupling consequences.
Part III develops finite conditioning and its complete certificate. Parts IV–V construct and
analyse the spatial Hamiltonian sequence, with the fixed-cutoff thermodynamic theory placed
before the collective gap and cutoff-obstruction results. Part VI states the continuum transfer
criteria and their missing hypotheses. Part VII tests confinement and approximation methods
in explicit comparison settings. Part VIII presents attributable numerical evidence and the
resulting research targets.
Mathematical error bounds appear beside the calculations they certify. Detailed executable
programs, exact fractions, interval boxes, frozen stochastic inputs and numerical records accom-
pany the manuscript. Hashes identify those records; arithmetic checks certify the quantities they
actually enclose. Neither is a replacement for an analytic proof of the model assumptions. Proof
assumptions are stated at the point of use; build and reproduction instructions accompany the
source and data.

Part I
Gauge reduction and the physical lattice

2 Exactgaugereduction, planarsolutions, andthefirstcurvature
constraint
This section develops a finite-cutoff calculation far enough that its successful steps and its
obstruction in higher dimension can both be inspected exactly. The calculation begins with the
compact-group integral defining the Wilson model. It removes a spanning tree without changing
any gauge-invariant expectation, solves the free-boundary rectangular model in two dimensions,
evaluates the resulting single-plaquette integrals for SU(2), and then calculates the first failure of
independent plaquettes on a cube. No continuum field integral is used as a formal intermediate
object.
These constructions belong to established lattice gauge theory. Wilson introduced the compact
lattice regulator [1]; the rigorous two-dimensional theory and its continuum holonomy construction
are developed in Lévy’s work [17]. The purpose of the proofs here is to make the exact algebra
and its limitations available in the present research programme. In particular, the independent-
plaquette calculation is not presented as a newly discovered four-dimensional reduction. The
one-cube calculation gives an explicit reason why that proposed reduction would be false.
2.1 Finite graphs and normalized Haar integration
Let G be a compact Lie group and let h be its Haar probability measure. Thus h(G) = 1,
left and right multiplication preserve h, and inversion preserves h. Let Γ = (V,E) be a finite
connected graph. For each geometric edge choose one orientation. A configuration is a tuple
U = (Ue)e∈E ∈ GE. Reversing an edge means using U¯e = U−1 e ; it does not introduce another
integration variable.
If a path c traverses oriented edges e1,...,ek, its holonomy is the ordered product
U(c) =Ue1 ···Uek.
An immediately retraced edge cancels. Reversing the path inverts the product. These are
algebraic identities, independent of a probability law. If c is a closed path, changing its starting
vertex conjugates its holonomy by the holonomy of the intervening segment. A central function
of the loop holonomy is consequently independent of the choice of starting vertex.
The vertex gauge group isGV =GV. We use the convention
Ug xy =gxUxyg−1 y .
For a path from x to y, cancellation of the intermediate factors gives
Ug(c) =gxU(c)g−1 y .
For a closed path based at x, a trace in any finite-dimensional representation is therefore
unchanged. Let ρ :G→U(N) be a continuous unitary representation, and set

This elementary estimate establishes the finite integral, but it is not a useful volume-uniform
estimate: its exponent grows with the number of faces. A proof that silently carries this constant
into an infinite-volume limit has not controlled that limit.
Product Haar measure is gauge invariant. To verify this, fix g∈GV and change one edge variable
at a time by Uxy ↦→gxUxyg−1 y . Bi-invariance of h preserves every factor. The Wilson density is
also unchanged because each face holonomy is conjugated. Hence µβ is gauge invariant. This
argument does not require choosing a gauge or dividing by a gauge-group volume; the latter is
already one in the normalized convention.
The face family may contain repeated or composite loops if these are explicitly part of the model.
In the rectangular and cubical examples below it consists of elementary squares, each included
once. All statements use finite open graphs. Periodic boundary conditions introduce global cycles
and are not covered by the independent-plaquette conclusion without additional variables and
constraints.
2.2 Spanning-tree reduction with its measure identity
Choose a root vertex o and a spanning tree T⊂E. For each vertex v, let cv be the unique tree
path from o to v, and define
to = 1, tv =U(cv).
For every edge e = (x,y) outside the tree, define
Xe =txUet−1 y .
For a tree edge this expression equals the identity, with the same conclusion if its chosen orientation
is opposite to its orientation away from the root. Thus the gauge transformation gv = tv sets all
tree links equal to one. The gauge transformation is a function of the configuration, so measure
preservation should not be asserted merely from invariance under fixed transformations. The
required stronger assertion is the next change-of-variables theorem.
Theorem G1 (exact spanning-tree factorization). The map

Proof. On an edge of the rooted tree joining a parent x to a child y, the formula ty = txUxy

equation uses the inverse link. Conversely, Uxy = t−1 x ty reconstructs every tree link. For a
non-tree edge the displayed inverse reconstructs its link once t and X are given. These formulas
prove bijectivity and continuity in both directions.
Order the non-root vertices so that parents precede children. Under independent Haar tree links,
condition on the transport variables already generated. The next variable is a fixed left translate
of an independent Haar variable, or of its inverse. Its conditional law is again h and does not
depend on the preceding transports. Induction shows that all tv, v̸= o, are independent Haar
variables.
Conditional on all tree links, the non-tree links remain independent Haar variables. Each change
Uxy ↦→txUxyt−1 y preserves Haar measure. Consequently the conditional law of the whole tuple
X is hE\T, independent of t. This proves the measure identity first for rectangles in the target
product sigma-field and then for bounded Borel functions by the monotone-class theorem. □

The reduced variables are not automatically plaquettes. What remains to be proved in each
geometry is whether the chosen face holonomies give independent coordinates on these variables.
There is still a global conjugation symmetry. To see it directly, apply an arbitrary gauge
transformation g before tree reduction. The new tree transport is
t′ v =gotvg−1 v ,
and hence
X′ e =goXeg−1 o .
Thus the gauge-orbit space of the original graph is naturally identified with the simultaneous-
conjugation orbit space of the reduced tuple. The tree has removed vertex-dependent redundancy
but has not selected a preferred representative of a conjugacy orbit. No Faddeev–Popov deter-
minant is missing: the full identity is a finite product-Haar change of variables, not a formal
differential gauge-fixing calculation.

2.3 A dense class of finite-cutoff gauge observables
The phrase “a dense class of observables” needs a specified norm and measure. On a fixed finite
graph those questions have a precise elementary answer. They should not be conflated with
density of renormalized physical states after removing the cutoff.
Assume that G is represented faithfully as a compact matrix group. Let P be the algebra of finite
complex polynomials in all matrix entries of the edge variables and their complex conjugates. It
contains constants, is closed under complex conjugation, and separates points of the compact
space GE. The complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem implies that P is uniformly dense in C(GE).
For a continuous function define gauge averaging by
PF (U) =
∫
GV
F (Ug)dhV (g).
Proposition G2 (finite-cutoff gauge projection and density). For any gauge-invariant
Borel probability measure µ on GE, the operator P extends to an orthogonal projection in L2(µ)
onto the gauge-invariant subspace. The averaged polynomial functions PP are uniformly dense
in the continuous invariant functions and dense in the invariant subspace of L2(µ).
Proof. Jensen’s inequality and invariance of µ give
∥PF∥2 L2(µ) ≤
∫ ∫
|F (Ug)|2 dhV (g)dµ(U) =∥F∥2 L2(µ).
Haar invariance gives P2 = P. For continuous F,H, change variables U ↦→ Ug−1 and then
g↦→g−1 to obtain
⟨F, PH⟩L2(µ) =⟨PF,H⟩L2(µ).
Thus the bounded extension is a self-adjoint idempotent and is an orthogonal projection. Its range
consists exactly of the vectors fixed by all unitary gauge transformations: averaging produces
fixed vectors, and a fixed vector is unchanged by the average.
If F is continuous and invariant, choose pn ∈P with ∥pn −F∥∞ → 0. Gauge averaging is a
contraction in the supremum norm, so ∥Ppn −F∥∞ → 0. Averaging a finite polynomial still
produces a finite polynomial in the edge entries: its finitely many coefficient functions in the
gauge variables are simply integrated. This proves the uniform assertion.
Finally, continuous functions are dense in L2 of a finite regular Borel measure on a compact
metric space. Given an invariant vector, approximate it by continuous functions and apply
the L2 contraction P. Approximate each resulting continuous invariant function by averaged
polynomials. The triangle inequality proves the L2 assertion. □
This construction is a direct route to spin-network-type observables without claiming that traces
in one chosen representation suffice for every compact group. Completeness results specifically
for Wilson-loop algebras require their own group hypotheses; Lévy’s work proves such results for
the stated families of classical compact groups [18]. The averaged-polynomial argument above is
enough for the finite-cutoff statement used here.
Two additional steps would be needed to use this density in a continuum mass-gap proof. First,
these observables must be renormalized with limits in the appropriate reflected inner product.
Second, their limiting classes must remain total. Neither follows from uniform approximation
at one fixed cutoff. Ordinary variance and reflected physical norm are also different quantities.
For independent identically distributed variables X+,X− exchanged by reflection, a centered

function f(X+) can have positive ordinary variance but reflected norm E[f(X−)f(X+)] = 0. The
finite-cutoff projection theorem does not rule out that loss of physical states.
2.4 The free-boundary rectangular model is exactly factorized
Take the square graph with vertices (i,j), 0 ≤ i≤ L, 0 ≤ j≤ H, and all nearest-neighbor
edges inside it. Orient horizontal edges to the right and vertical edges upward. There are LH
elementary plaquettes. Use as spanning tree every vertical edge together with the L horizontal
edges on the bottom row. This set is connected and has
H(L + 1) +L = (L + 1)(H + 1)− 1
edges, so it is indeed a tree.
After tree reduction, every vertical link and bottom horizontal link is one. Denote the remaining

2.5 Rectangular Wilson loops and central convolution
We now prove the loop law without discarding the noncommutative conjugations. Let C bound

conditional law and preserves independence. The resulting loop holonomy therefore has law

diverges.

continuum shortcut: a single plaquette becomes almost trivial at precisely the scale at which a
macroscopic loop contains many plaquettes. The limiting observable is neither forced to zero nor
forced to one. In four dimensions, proving the analogous balance must also handle interactions
between the plaquettes, which are already visible on the smallest cube.
2.10 Six cube faces are constrained by five cycle variables
Consider the graph formed by the twelve edges of the unit cube with vertices (x,y,z) ∈{0, 1}3.
Orient each edge in its positive coordinate direction. Choose as a tree all four vertical z-edges,
the two bottom x-edges, and the bottom y-edge at x = 0. The tree has seven edges. After setting
its variables to one, write the five remaining links as follows:
• a: the bottom y-edge at x = 1;
• b,c: the top x-edges at y = 0, 1, respectively;
• d,e: the top y-edges at x = 0, 1, respectively.
For a face in the xy plane orient its path by positive x then positive y, followed by the negative
directions. Use the corresponding increasing-coordinate convention for xz and yz faces. In the
tree gauge, direct multiplication gives
Pz0 =a, Pz1 =bec−1d−1,
Py0 =b−1, Py1 =c−1,
Px0 =d−1, Px1 =ae−1.
22
=== PAGE 23 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Before gauge fixing, interpret these as holonomies transported to the root along the chosen
tree. This is essential in the nonabelian case: face holonomies at different basepoints cannot be
multiplied as though they already lived in a common gauge frame.
Theorem G8 (explicit one-cube curvature relation). The six based face holonomies satisfy
Pz1 =P−1 y0 P−1 x1 Pz0Py1Px0.
The five variables on the right are independent Haar variables under the original product Haar
law. The sixth is determined by them and cannot be an additional independent nondegenerate
Haar variable.
Proof. The first five displayed face formulas can be inverted as
a =Pz0, b =P−1 y0 , c =P−1 y1 , d =P−1 x0 , e =P−1 x1 Pz0.
Insert these into bec−1d−1 to obtain the relation. Theorem G1 makes a,b,c,d,e independent
Haar variables. Inversion preserves Haar measure, while conditional on a, the variable ae−1
is Haar and independent of a,b,c,d. Thus the five face coordinates in the theorem are also
independent Haar variables. The sixth is their displayed deterministic function. □
This is an exact finite-dimensional obstruction to treating all plaquettes as independent. It does
not arise from a divergent perturbation series or an uncertain continuum limit. A four-dimensional
hypercubic lattice contains such three-dimensional cubes. Any construction replacing every
based plaquette by an independent group variable has already changed the model on those
subcomplexes unless it imposes the associated constraints and their interactions.
The dimension count provides a compatible check. The cube has cycle rank 12 − 8 + 1 = 5 but
six faces. For a positive-dimensional compact Lie group the map from its five reduced variables
to six based face holonomies has image of Haar measure zero in G6. Indeed, a smooth map
from a compact manifold of dimension 5 dimG into one of dimension 6 dimG has image of zero
full-dimensional volume: cover the domain by finitely many Lipschitz coordinate charts and
subdivide into cubes of side δ; the image can be covered by O(δ−5 dimG) balls of radius O(δ),
whose total 6 dimG-volume tends to zero. A sixfold product law with a strictly positive density
cannot be supported on that image.
For an abelian group the same relation reduces to the familiar signed product constraint around
a cube. For a nonabelian group, the order and the transporting paths are part of the statement.
Merely retaining the abelian product relation loses information. Conversely, the existence of a
cube constraint is not a proof that no useful plaquette representation can be built: it specifies
what such a representation must encode.

2.12 Exact blocking generates more than one Wilson coupling
The planar solution also permits a precise test of a common renormalization shortcut. A block
containing B elementary faces has holonomy law ν∗B β . It is tempting to replace this law by a
Wilson density νβ′ with a changed coupling chosen to reproduce its fundamental trace. Matching
that one expectation is possible. Matching the entire probability law is a stronger assertion, and
it fails already in this exactly solvable model.
Theorem G10 (failure of one-parameter Wilson closure). Fix an integer B≥ 2. There is
δB > 0 such that for every 0<β <δB, no β′≥ 0 satisfies

strictly between zero and one is achieved exactly once, proving existence and uniqueness of the
fundamental-mean match.
Write a1 for the normalized spin-one coefficient. If the probability laws were equal, their
fundamental and spin-one coefficients would both agree:

This theorem does not say that one-coupling approximations are useless. It says that they
are approximations requiring a controlled remainder. Even when plaquettes are independent,
integrating them into a larger face generally creates an action with more character coefficients.
In higher dimensions there are additionally interactions linking several coarse faces. A proposed
exact renormalization recursion must specify these generated terms and estimate them, rather
than declare closure after fitting one number.
It is particularly useful as a unit test for a proposed blocking argument: the argument should
reproduce the different fundamental and adjoint transformations in this solvable setting before
being applied to a coupled four-dimensional measure.
2.13 Nonuniform planar couplings and an explicit accumulated-error bound
The continuum-area calculation need not assume that every fine plaquette has the same coupling.
This extension illustrates how a local asymptotic estimate must be summed over an increasing
number of cells. An error small on one cell is useful only when its accumulated value stays
controlled.

2.14 What these exact calculations contribute to the continuum programme
The section supplies three kinds of information that can be used without conjectural premises.
The spanning-tree theorem gives exact finite-dimensional coordinates and a verified integration
formula. The planar theorem gives an all-coupling solution and a nontrivial physical-area
scaling limit for a specified family of loop expectations. The cube theorem identifies an exact
higher-dimensional curvature interaction and evaluates its first contribution.
These results also sharpen the next research question. A proposed four-dimensional plaquette
description must retain the transported cube relations. A proposed blocking transformation must
calculate how those relations and the associated effective interactions change under integration.
A proposed continuum observable family must control its reflected norm after the normalization
and limit, rather than appeal only to finite-cutoff polynomial density. These are concrete
mathematical requirements exposed by exact calculations, not generic objections to trying a
different method.
The planar scaling proof demonstrates that an increasing coupling can balance a growing number
of plaquettes without making a loop expectation vanish. It does not show that the same balance
survives the coupled four-dimensional measure. The cube calculation shows that the discarded
interaction is nonzero even in the first cell where it can occur. The task in the full theory is
therefore to estimate and organize such interactions, including their long-distance effects, with
constants suitable for both the continuum and infinite-volume limits.
The displayed finite and two-dimensional results provide exact normalization and dependence
checks. Their application to four-dimensional cutoff removal requires estimates for the interacting
measure with its cube constraints intact.
3 Reflectionpositivity, exacttransferoperators, andacontinuum
comparison
Reflection positivity is the mechanism that turns suitable Euclidean correlations into nonnegative
physical norms. It is an algebraic inequality with analytical consequences, not an estimate of
the rate at which correlations decay. This section proves the inequality for precisely specified
finite Wilson systems, constructs their finite-spatial-volume transfer Hamiltonians, and then
gives an explicit continuum Gaussian model in which every part of the same construction can be
calculated. The two constructions make it possible to identify the additional estimate needed in
an interacting continuum limit without concealing it inside the word “reconstruction.”
The Wilson transfer construction and the Osterwalder–Schrader framework are established
mathematics [6, 7, 8, 9]. The proofs here are self-contained for the statements actually used.
They are not a claim that these methods, or their consequences at finite spatial volume, were
first discovered in this manuscript. The construction below includes no fermions, no gauge-fixing
determinants, and no formal continuum functional integral.
28
=== PAGE 29 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
3.1 Reflected forms and their null spaces
Let (X,F,µ) be a probability space with a measurable involution ϑ : X→X preserving µ. An
involution means ϑ2 is the identity. Let A+ be a complex vector space of bounded measurable
functions interpreted as positive-time observables. Define the antilinear operation
ΘF =F◦ϑ
and the reflected sesquilinear form
Q(F,G) =
∫
X
(ΘF )Gdµ.
The convention is that inner products are antilinear in the first argument. Reflection invariance
gives Q(F,G) =Q(G,F ): conjugate the integral defining Q(G,F ) and then change variables by
ϑ. Reflection positivity is the additional statement
Q(F,F )≥ 0 (F∈A+).
Ordinary positivity of the probability density does not imply this inequality. The integrand need
not be a squared absolute value at the same configuration. It couples a function of the positive
half of the configuration to a function of the negative half.
Lemma R1 (quotient norm and ordinary L2 control). If the reflected form is positive,
then
|Q(F,G)|2 ≤Q(F,F )Q(G,G), 0≤Q(F,F )≤∥F∥2 L2(µ).
Consequently the set N = {F : Q(F,F ) = 0} is a vector subspace, every element of N is
orthogonal to every element ofA+, and Q induces an inner product onA+/N.
Proof. For any complex z, positivity of Q(F + zG,F + zG) gives the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
by minimizing the resulting quadratic polynomial. If Q(G,G) = 0, varying the magnitude and
phase of z first forces Q(F,G) = 0, so the same conclusion covers the degenerate case. The
ordinary integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives
|Q(F,F )|≤∥F◦ϑ∥2∥F∥2 =∥F∥2 2.
The equality of norms uses reflection invariance. The claims about the null space now follow
from the first inequality and sesquilinearity. Completing the quotient gives a Hilbert space. □
The constant function has reflected norm one. Its class is the candidate vacuum vector Ω = [1].
For any F, the centered vector is
[F−µ(F )], ∥[F−µ(F )]∥2 =Q(F,F )−|µ(F )|2.
The second identity follows by expanding the square and using µ(F◦ϑ) = µ(F ). It makes clear
that a nonzero ordinary variance need not give a nonzero physical state: the ordinary variance
uses µ(|F|2), whereas the physical squared norm uses a reflected correlation.
No Hamiltonian has been constructed by this quotient alone. One also needs an action of
positive-time translations, its compatibility with the null space, and continuity and contraction
properties. Those hypotheses are handled abstractly in the spectral-bridge section and concretely
for the transfer operator below.

3.2 A gluing lemma with an explicit positive kernel
Suppose Y is a probability space with measure ν. Let a : Y → [0,∞) be bounded, and suppose
a kernel K can be written as
K(x,y) =⟨Ψ(y), Ψ(x)⟩K,
where Ψ : Y →K is strongly measurable, K is a separable Hilbert space, and supx∥Ψ(x)∥<∞.
Assume K is real and nonnegative pointwise, and that
Z =
∫

These conditions define a probability law on two copies of Y. The reflection exchanges the copies.
For F depending on the first copy, the unnormalized reflected expectation is
∫
F (y)F (x)a(x)a(y)K(x,y)dν(x)dν(y).
Lemma R2 (positive-kernel gluing). This expectation is nonnegative for every bounded
complex F.
Proof. The Bochner integral vF =
∫
F (x)a(x)Ψ(x) dν(x) exists because its integrand has
integrable norm. Expanding ∥vF∥2 gives exactly the displayed double integral. Fubini is justified
by boundedness. Division by Z preserves the sign. □
The same proof applies to a finite product of kernels: replace the feature map by its tensor
product. It also applies to a kernel depending on shared boundary variables z. If each conditional
reflected integral is a squared norm for fixed z, integrating it against a positive boundary measure
preserves nonnegativity. The boundary measure need not be a product measure.
This lemma separates two tasks. The first is geometric: identify which factors of the action
belong to each half and which factors cross the reflection plane. The second is algebraic: express
each crossing factor as a positive kernel. A character identity alone does not accomplish the
geometric task.

Reflect time by ϑ(t,x) = (−t,x). Under reflection, a positively oriented temporal link is

Reflection-compatible boundaries are also essential. For a simple warning, take independent

supply a positive reflected form. Arbitrary-boundary covariance estimates and reflection-positive
boundary constructions have different hypotheses.

form is a sum of squared absolute values with nonnegative coefficients. Uniform convergence
passes that inequality to the full kernel. □
No irreducible-character decomposition is needed for positivity. The tensor representation may
be reducible. If it is decomposed into irreducibles, the multiplicities are nonnegative integers and
the resulting coefficients remain nonnegative. The direct tensor proof has the advantage that
every coefficient and every convergence bound is visible.
For β > 0 and a faithful representation, these features detect every nonzero L2(G,h) function.
Indeed, the algebra generated by matrix coefficients of ρ andρ contains constants, is closed under
conjugation, and separates group elements. The complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem makes it
uniformly dense in C(G), which is dense in L2(G,h). Every such product is a matrix coefficient
of one of the tensor representations occurring with strictly positive weight. Thus a function
orthogonal to all features is zero. This injectivity statement will be important for defining the
logarithm of the transfer operator.

The displayed integral kernel of T is strictly positive at every pair (x,y): all of its factors are
positive real exponentials, and W > 0. The compact self-adjoint spectral theorem supplies an
eigenvector at its norm λ0 > 0. The norm is a positive eigenvalue because T is a nonzero positive
operator. Replacing an eigenfunction by its absolute value cannot decrease its Rayleigh quotient,
since the kernel is positive. Consequently a normalized maximizing eigenfunction can be chosen
nonnegative. The eigenvalue equation then makes it continuous and strictly positive everywhere;
call it ψ0.
If the top eigenspace had dimension greater than one, there would be a nonzero real top
eigenfunction f orthogonal to ψ0. Its positive and negative parts would both be nonzero on sets
of positive measure. Strict positivity of the kernel would give

contradicting maximality. Complex eigenfunctions reduce to real and imaginary parts because
the kernel is real. Thus the top eigenvalue is simple.
The assumed nonconstant invariant function implies dimHphys ≥ 2. Its vacuum orthocomplement
is a nonzero invariant subspace. The restriction of T there remains compact, positive and
injective; its norm λ1 is therefore a positive attained eigenvalue. Simplicity and isolation of the
top eigenvalue give λ1 <λ0.
Finally, injectivity means the spectral measure of T has no atom at zero on any nonzero vector.
The spectral function −a−1 log(λ/λ0) therefore defines a densely defined self-adjoint operator:
spectral cutoffs to λ≥ε give a dense core as ε↓ 0. It is nonnegative, has kernel precisely Cψ0,
and its spectrum on the orthocomplement begins at the displayed positive finite number. □
A spatial box containing a plaquette satisfies the nonconstant-function assumption whenever w
is nonconstant. Vary one link of that plaquette while keeping the others equal to the identity;
its trace changes. A tree graph is different: all link variables can be removed by vertex gauge
transformations, and the physical space may consist only of constants. The theorem deliberately
excludes that vacuous case.
The result is a genuine Hamiltonian statement, rather than the gap of an auxiliary sampling
algorithm. Its operator was derived from the Euclidean-time slab of the Wilson action, and

answer.

in the formula and in the dependence of ma,E on its two regulators.

the regulators are removed. The small-coupling volume-independent correlation theorem and
this all-positive-coupling finite-volume spectral theorem have complementary ranges of strength;
neither estimate is silently extended beyond its proved quantifiers.
3.8 Infinite-volume passage of reflection positivity
For countably many lattice links, GE is a compact metrizable space. A sequence of finite-box laws
can be extended to GE by assigning independent Haar variables outside each box. Compactness
of the space of probability measures gives weakly convergent subsequences. The extension is a
device for taking a common-space limit; it does not insert missing plaquette interactions into a
finite box.
Fix a reflection plane and choose boxes symmetric about it. If F is a continuous cylinder
observable supported in the positive half, then for all sufficiently large boxes the finite reflected
inequality applies. The function (ΘF )F is continuous and depends on finitely many links, so weak
convergence passes the inequality to the limit. This proves reflected positivity for continuous
cylinder observables of the relevant class. For link reflection that class remains gauge invariant.
Continuous functions are dense in the L2 space of each finite marginal, and the ordinary integral
Cauchy–Schwarz bound makes the reflected form continuous in L2. Consequently the inequality
extends to bounded cylinder observables by approximation; gauge averaging preserves the needed
invariant subspace.
For completeness, a subsequential free-boundary limit satisfies the ordinary infinite-volume
Wilson conditional equations. Fix a finite link set A. Once a box contains every plaquette
38
=== PAGE 39 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
meeting A, conditioning on all other links gives exactly the full Wilson conditional kernel on
A. For continuous local test functions, this kernel is a continuous function of finitely many
exterior links: its numerator and denominator are integrals of continuous bounded functions
over a compact product, and its denominator is strictly positive. Pass the finite conditioning
identity to the weak limit. A monotone-class argument extends from continuous local functions
to bounded measurable cylinder functions and then to the exterior sigma algebra. Thus the limit
is a Gibbs measure.
At a coupling for which the infinite-volume Gibbs measure is known to be unique, all such
subsequences have the same limit. In particular, the strong-coupling uniqueness theorem
established elsewhere in this manuscript identifies the site-reflection and link-reflection limits
with the same measure. Without uniqueness, a symmetric approximating sequence still gives
a reflection-positive limit for its chosen plane, but one must not silently identify different
subsequential limits.
Lemma R7 (positivity under correlation limits). Let F1,...,Fn be proposed limiting
positive-time observables, with cutoff representatives Fi,j. Suppose each cutoff reflected Gram
matrix
G(j) ik =µj[(ΘFi,j)Fk,j]
is positive semidefinite, and every entry converges to a finite number Gik. Then G is positive
semidefinite.
Proof. For each fixed coefficient vector c∈ Cn, entrywise convergence implies c∗G(j)c→c∗Gc.
The left side is nonnegative. □
The finite dimension in this argument is important. There is no exchange of an uncontrolled
infinite sum with the cutoff limit. To obtain a positive form on an infinite algebra, apply the
lemma separately to every finite list. Further growth and continuity conditions are needed before
these values define the distributions required by a full field-theoretic reconstruction.
There is a useful quantitative nontriviality check. Suppose for one observable the approximated
mean and reflected second moment are mj,Aj, with proved errors
|m−mj|≤δj, |A−Aj|≤ηj, |mj|≤B.
Then
⏐⏐⏐(A−|m|2)− (Aj −|mj|2) ⏐⏐⏐≤ηj + (2B +δj)δj.
Indeed, ||m|2 −|mj|2|≤|m−mj|(|m| + |mj|) and |m|≤B + δj. A strictly positive lower bound
for Aj −|mj|2 exceeding this error proves that the limiting centered physical state is nonzero.
This is the correct reflected quantity to certify. A lower bound on an unreflected lattice variance
cannot replace it.
3.9 Cylinder density and the meaning of a total family
Let µ be a reflection-invariant probability measure on a countable product of compact metric link
spaces. Let F+ be the sigma algebra generated by positive-half links, including plane links when
the reflection convention permits them. Bounded cylinder functions are dense in L2(F+,µ).
One proof begins with an increasing sequence of finite link sets generating F+. Conditional
expectations onto their sigma algebras are orthogonal projections onto increasing closed subspaces.
39
=== PAGE 40 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
The union of these subspaces is dense: indicators of cylinder sets generate the full sigma algebra,
and the class of sets whose indicators lie in the closure is closed under complements and increasing
countable unions. Truncating an L2 function first and then taking conditional expectations yields
bounded cylinder approximants converging in L2.
Assume additionally that µ is gauge invariant. If the target function is gauge invariant, its
approximants can be made gauge invariant. Average each finite-cylinder approximant over the
compact group of gauge transformations at the finitely many incident vertices. This preserves its
support and boundedness. Jensen’s inequality and gauge invariance of µ show that this averaging
is an L2 contraction. Since the target is invariant, averaging cannot increase its distance from the
target. The resulting gauge-invariant cylinder functions are dense in the invariant positive-time
subspace.
Lemma R1 now implies convergence in the reflected seminorm as well. Thus the OS completion
of this cutoff algebra can be generated by bounded gauge-invariant cylinder observables. This is
a valid totality statement at a fixed measure and a fixed set of variables.
A continuum totality assertion is different. A chosen renormalized family may consist only
of selected Wilson loops, smeared curvature traces, or polynomials at prescribed scales. The
density argument above does not prove that its limiting classes exhaust the physical Hilbert
space. To make that conclusion, one must either define the limiting algebra through that family
and establish all required field properties there, or prove approximation of every relevant state
by the family in the limiting reflected norm.
A simple Hilbert-space example illustrates the issue. Suppose H = CΩ ⊕K1 ⊕K2 and every
selected observable creates states only in K1. Bounds for all of those observables say nothing
about the spectrum on K2. The issue remains even if the selected family is countably infinite.
Its cardinality is not a substitute for a density proof.

continuum model by calculation. The positive parameter m was supplied in that model’s
covariance. No argument here derives such a parameter dynamically from the pure Yang–Mills
action.
3.12 What the free comparison proves about the remaining task
The same formulas with m = 0 give a reflection-positive massless Gaussian field in four dimensions.
The covariance integral remains finite for Schwartz functions because |p|−2 is locally integrable in
four dimensions. For the one-particle reflected map, functions with momentum support away from
zero give the preceding density proof, and these functions are dense in L2(R3). The Hamiltonian
is dΓ(|p|). It has a unique vacuum because a nonzero L2 wavefunction cannot be supported only
at the measure-zero point p = 0, but it has no positive gap because one-particle wavefunctions
can be supported in arbitrarily small nonzero momentum balls.
As m↓ 0, the massive covariances converge to the massless covariance by dominated convergence:
0≤ 1 p2 +m2 ≤ 1 p2 ,
and the Schwartz factors make the right side integrable. All Wick moments converge as well.
Reflection positivity survives this limit, while the mass gap tends to zero. This example proves
that positivity and convergence of all these Gaussian correlations do not by themselves preserve
a positive spectral threshold.
The comparison also identifies what would count as a completed interacting argument. One
needs a limiting positive-time algebra with controlled correlations, a nonzero centered reflected
norm, a total family of physical states, and a common exponential decay rate in physical time.
The Wilson finite-volume construction proves all these features at each fixed spatial regulator,
with a regulator-dependent rate. The spectral-bridge results describe how a uniform rate would
pass to a constructed limit. The missing interacting estimate is the uniformity and the nontrivial
limit together; it is not the elementary positivity of each regulated Wilson measure.
The section’s exact results can therefore be used as checkpoints for future proposals. A candidate
effective action must preserve the required reflected form or bound its defects. A proposed
observable normalization must preserve a centered reflected norm, not just a coincident variance.
A proposed transfer construction must identify the physical time step and the full gauge-invariant
state space. A proposed continuum gap must control the ratios λ1/λ0 or the equivalent dense-
state time correlations along removal of both regulators. These requirements are mathematical
43
=== PAGE 44 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
conditions already visible in the explicit constructions, rather than an appeal to numerical
evidence or external approval.

is distinct from the Hamiltonian one-plaquette model considered later.

bounded real f.
For a nonvacuum eigenfunction Tψ = λψ, the function f = ψ/h is continuous, bounded and
nonconstant, and Pf = (λ/λ0)f. Applying the oscillation estimate gives |λ|/λ0 ≤ tanhB.
All eigenvalues are positive, proving (4.11). This is an elementary form of the Birkhoff–Hopf
positive-operator contraction argument [20].
The best bound supplied by these two comparisons is the maximum of the right-hand sides of
(4.10) and (4.11). Neither is uniform along the required infinite-volume continuum limit.

4.4.1 Center sectors
The three independent center flips Ui ↦→−Ui commute with both C and W. Let Hϵ be the sector
with flip signs (−1)ϵi, ϵ∈{0, 1}3. In the spin-network decomposition, it consists of precisely
those labels for which 2ji ≡ϵi (mod 2). The positive, unique ground state lies in the neutral
sectorH000.
Lemma 4.8 (Sector kinetic norms). The kinetic norm above the constant in the neutral sector
is s. In a sector with k = 1, 2, 3 odd entries, the kinetic norm is rk. In H100, the top kinetic
eigenvalue r is simple, with normalized eigenvector f = trU1, and the norm on its orthogonal
complement is
τ = max{t,rs}. (4.14)
Proof. Neutral parity forces every ji to be an integer. Apart from the constant, at least one is at
least one, so the eigenvalue is at most s; χ1(U1) attains it. For k odd entries, at least k labels
are half-integers, hence their product eigenvalue is at most rk; the product of the corresponding
fundamental characters attains it.
For H100 the unique leading label is (1/2, 0, 0). Conjugation invariance in the single irreducible
matrix space leaves only its trace, proving simplicity. Every other labeling either has j1 ≥ 3/2,
bounded by t, or has j1 = 1/2 and a nonzero integer label elsewhere, bounded by rs. Both
bounds are attained by characters or products of characters, proving (4.14).
The neutral gap consequently obeys
δneutral ≥ log I1(βt) I3(βt) − 9 4βs. (4.15)

4.5.1 Exact moments and arithmetic
In quaternion coordinates,

∑
i<j
|ui ×uj|2.
Powers of X are integer polynomials in nine real coordinates. Odd monomials integrate to zero.
For the three vector coordinates of one Haar SU(2) quaternion,
E[u2a 1 u2b 2 u2c 3 ] = (2a)!(2b)!(2c)! 4a+b+ca!b!c!(a +b +c + 1)!. (4.21)
Multiplication by 4u2 0 changes this moment by the factor 2/(a + b + c + 2). These formulas give
E0Vk and E0f 2Vk exactly as rational numbers.

The accompanying calculation uses k≤ 8. For either normalized positive measure and γ≥ 0,
⏐⏐⏐⏐⏐EeγV − 8∑ k=0 γk k! EVk ⏐⏐⏐⏐⏐≤e3γγ9 9! E|V|9 ≤e3γ 3γ9 9! EV 8. (4.22)

moment is used for the appropriate unweighted or f 2-weighted measure. Modified Bessel functions
and exponentials are enclosed by positive power series with geometric tail bounds; logarithms
use the positive arctanh series after range reduction; square roots use integer-square-root bounds.
Every interval operation rounds outwards using rational arithmetic.
The polynomial generator uses signed 64-bit integer coefficients; all subsequent integration and
interval operations use arbitrary-precision rational arithmetic. Its base polynomial has sum
of absolute coefficients 36, so every degree-eight intermediate coefficient and collected sum is
bounded by 368 < 263. Each coordinate exponent is at most 16, below the five-bit packing limit.
Thus this part of the computation has no integer-overflow ambiguity. The stored coefficient files
allow the Haar integrations to be rerun without regenerating the polynomial expansion.

4.7 Relation to finite-volume spectroscopy
Earlier studies include nonperturbative finite-volume glueball and electric-flux analysis by Koller
and van Baal [22], single-cube variational work by Carlsson and McKellar [23], and femtouniverse
simulation by Butt, Draper and Shen [24]. Those models and approximation schemes differ from
the present full Wilson-transfer enclosure. The calculation here provides an explicit benchmark
with a complete remainder bound and proved center-sector ordering; it makes no priority claim
for finite-volume gauge-theory spectroscopy as a subject.

This is an exact analytical example, not a computation extrapolated to infinite volume.

SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
For indicators depending on A, each coordinate oscillation is at most one. Hence the marginal
laws on GA are Cauchy in total variation. The space of finite signed measures is complete in
the total-variation norm, and a total-variation limit of probability measures is a probability
measure. The limiting finite-dimensional laws are consistent, since taking marginals commutes
with total-variation convergence. The countable-product extension theorem on the standard
Borel space G now gives a probability measure µβ on GE.
It remains to verify the Gibbs property and uniqueness, rather than assume them. For fixed
finite ∆, a bounded observable F supported on ∆, and a bounded local observable H outside ∆,
finite-volume conditioning gives
γηn Λn(FH) =γηn Λn(Hγ∆F )
once ∆ ⊂ Λn. The function γ∆F is bounded and depends on only finitely many exterior links,
because the interaction has finite range. Total-variation convergence on finite sets passes this
identity to µβ. A monotone-class argument in H extends it to every bounded exterior-measurable
H. This is the Dobrushin–Lanford–Ruelle conditional-law equation.
If ν is any other Gibbs measure for the same specification, condition it outside Λn and use (L5)
against γηn Λn. For each bounded local F, the resulting difference tends to zero. Thus νF = µβF
for all bounded cylinder functions; these determine the measure, so ν = µβ. This also proves
independence of the exhaustion and all boundary choices.
The specification is translation covariant. It is also covariant under lattice time reflection:
reflection permutes geometric links, replacing a link variable by its inverse when the chosen
positive orientation is reversed. Haar measure is invariant under inversion, and w(U−1 p ) = w(Up),
so the reflected specification is unchanged after relabeling. Finally, it is gauge covariant under
every finite vertex gauge transformation Uxy ↦→gxUxyg−1 y , by bi-invariance of Haar measure and
conjugation invariance of each plaquette trace. Each transformed measure is another Gibbs
measure for the same specification. Uniqueness therefore proves translation, time-reflection, and
local gauge invariance of µβ. Time-reflection invariance is a symmetry statement; it is not by
itself reflection positivity. Passing the finite-volume expectations of F,H,FH to their limits
proves (L4) in infinite volume. □
5.7 Nonzero lattice fluctuations
Let K be the four links of an elementary square p. At most 24 squares meet K, because each
of its four links meets six squares. For any outside configuration, the conditional density γη K
relative to hK is bounded below by
e−2β|P(K)|≥e−48β.
Averaging the Gibbs conditional law implies the same lower domination for the K-marginal of
µβ. Thus, for every real constant c,
µβ[(w(Up)−c)2]≥e−48βhK[(w(Up)−c)2].
Under independent Haar variables on the four links, their oriented product Up has Haar law.
Taking the infimum over c on both sides gives (L6).
For a nontrivial faithful unitary representation, w(e) = 1 and w is not identically one: a unitary
matrix whose real trace is N must be the identity. Continuity and the full support of Haar
measure then imply vG > 0. This checks that the lattice theory is not merely a Dirac measure on

=== PAGE 61 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
a single gauge orbit or a zero-variance construction. It says nothing by itself about nontriviality
after removal of the lattice cutoff. □
6 Local comparison estimates, unbounded observables and nec-
essary continuum scaling
The useful question after a fixed-lattice covariance theorem is how its constants behave when
observables, supports and couplings depend on the cutoff. A bounded plaquette trace is not
the same object as a renormalized smeared field: the latter may involve a growing number of
links and a normalization diverging as the lattice spacing decreases. This section keeps these
changes explicit. It sharpens the one-link coefficient for the actual Wilson specification, develops
weighted comparison estimates, treats observables controlled by moments rather than supremum
norms, and proves necessary scaling inequalities for a surviving connected correlation.
The comparison method is classical. Rebeschini and van Handel give a general account, including
block comparison theorems [11]. Covariance estimates in terms of mixing coefficients and moments
belong to the established theory represented by Davydov and Rio [25, 26]. The arguments below
are supplied in full with the normalizations used here. Their application to a continuum limit
always retains the displayed assumptions on moments, support, convergence and the class of
observables.
6.1 The precise local model
Let G be a compact Lie group with normalized Haar measure h. Fix a continuous unitary
representation ρ :G→U(N) and write
w(g) =N−1 Re Trρ(g), |w(g)|≤ 1.
Every geometric nearest-neighbor edge of Z4 carries one variable, stored in its positive coordinate
orientation. The variable on a reversed edge is its inverse. A plaquette is one elementary
unoriented square, counted once. The value w(Up) is well defined independently of its chosen
orientation and initial vertex, because real trace is unchanged by inversion and conjugation.
For a finite set of variable edges Λ and fixed exterior configuration η, consider

Allowing nonuniform couplings is useful for local perturbations and anisotropic estimates; it does
not change the underlying group-valued variables.
For a real bounded local function F, let

most one, whereas a function bounded in absolute value by M has coordinate oscillation at most
2M. Retaining that distinction improves the subsequent bound on event mixing. All kernels

in this section are given by their explicit Haar densities, so they are jointly measurable in the

The interaction graph has the links as its vertices. Distinct links are adjacent when they occur
in one plaquette. Its distance is denoted by dG. Distances between supports mean the minimum
over the two supports. Empty supports correspond to constant functions and can be omitted
from covariance estimates.
6.2 Geometry of the sharper influence coefficient
The previous lattice argument used the sum of common-plaquette multiplicities. On the ordinary
hypercubic lattice one can identify those multiplicities exactly.
Lemma LC.1 (distinct neighbors of a link). Two distinct geometric links of Z4 belong to
at most one elementary plaquette. Every link has exactly eighteen neighbors in the interaction
graph.
Proof. Fix the link from x to x + ei. A plaquette containing it is specified by another coordinate
direction j̸=i and a sign ε∈{−1, 1}. Its four vertices are
x, x + ei, x +εej, x + ei +εej.
The other link parallel to ei is the translate of the fixed link by εej. These six parallel links are
distinct: their displacements recover j and ε. The remaining two links are perpendicular to the
fixed link and meet, respectively, x and x + ei. Their direction, endpoint on the fixed link and
other endpoint again recover j and ε. These twelve links are all distinct, and none is parallel to
the fixed link. Thus the six incident plaquettes supply eighteen distinct other links. Any other
link belonging to a common plaquette has already appeared in this list, and its place in the list
determines the plaquette uniquely. □
The statement concerns ordinary subsets of Z4. Very small periodic quotients can identify
different geometric edges or squares; one must count their incidences afresh. No such quotient is
used in this section.
For neighboring links e,f, let p(e,f) be their unique common plaquette. Define

The numerical improvement over 18β < 1 is small, but it is exact: the unnecessary last relaxation

is a sufficient condition for this comparison argument, not a determination of a physical critical
coupling.
To be explicit about the infinite-volume assertion, the boundary comparison proof requires only
a finite interaction range and a uniform row bound q < 1. A disagreement outside a finite
region reaches a fixed interior support through a path of at least its distance to the boundary.
The total path weight is at most qs/(1 −q). Substitution of q = 18 tanhβ therefore gives the
same local total-variation Cauchy estimate as before. The consistent marginal limit satisfies
the local conditioning identities, and comparison with any other Gibbs law makes their local
expectations equal. Thus existence, boundary independence and uniqueness extend with the
sharpened coefficient; no unproved infinite-volume interchange is being inferred merely from a
smaller displayed number.

6.8 A direct truncation estimate for unbounded observables
At a fixed cutoff, every polynomial in bounded matrix entries is bounded, but a convenient family

6.10 Moment-controlled observables in the shrinking lattice
The preceding results can now be combined without a supremum-norm assumption. Let a↓ 0

This theorem allows the support to contain a polynomially growing number of links and the

positive margin from the comparison boundary is assumed.

from the control of one observable, nor does it claim the existence of the limiting functional. It
identifies precisely which moment-controlled families cannot generate a nontrivial physical limit
while remaining inside a fixed contractive regime.

6.12 Why enlarging blocks is not an automatic repair
Block comparison methods can improve single-link conditions, but a useful block theorem
must exploit the actual conditional block law. Merely grouping variables and repeating the
supremum oscillation estimate need not improve the criterion. The following calculation makes
this distinction concrete for the Wilson action.
For an integer L≥ 2, partition lattice vertices into cubes
Bz =Lz +{0, 1,...,L− 1}4, z∈ Z4.
74
=== PAGE 75 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Assign each positively oriented link to the block containing its initial vertex. This gives disjoint
blocks of link variables. For two blocks B,B′, let NBB′ be the number of plaquettes containing
at least one link assigned to each block. Conditional on the remaining blocks, changing all links
of B′ changes the log density on B by a function with oscillation at most 4βNBB′. Thus a valid,
but crude, block influence certificate is
Cblock BB′ = tanh(βNBB′).
The coefficient is a chosen upper bound on the true block influence. A lower bound on this
certificate is not a lower bound on the true influence.
Proposition LC.9 (failure of the crude large-block certificate). For every fixed β > 0,
the ordinary maximum-row-sum contraction test for this block matrix fails for all sufficiently
large L. In fact, for every block,
∑
B′̸=B
Cblock BB′ ≥ 2 tanh ( 3βL2(L− 1) ) ,
whose right side tends to two.
Proof. Consider B0 and one coordinate direction i. Across its positive i-face, use plaquettes in
the (i,j)-plane for each j̸= i. Choose the base vertex x with xi = L− 1, xj ∈{0,...,L− 2},
and the remaining two coordinates in {0,...,L− 1}. Three positively represented edges of such
a square have initial vertices in B0, while the edge in direction j based at x + ei is assigned to
the neighboring block Bei. These are distinct plaquettes, and their number is 3(L− 1)L2. Hence
NB0,Bei ≥ 3(L− 1)L2.
Across the negative i-face, choose xi = −1 with the same ranges in the other coordinates. The
square then has its direction-j edge based at x + ei in B0 and its other three edges assigned to
B−ei. The same count gives
NB0,B−ei ≥ 3(L− 1)L2.
Since tanh is increasing, these two distinct neighboring blocks alone supply the asserted lower
bound on the row sum. As L→∞, its argument tends to infinity and tanh tends to one. The
bound eventually exceeds one, contradicting the strict row-contraction requirement for this
chosen matrix. Translation gives the same calculation for every block. □
The proposition does not rule out a refined block coupling, a weighted criterion, or a
renormalization-group argument. It rules out one specific shortcut: grouping ever larger cubes
while retaining only the worst-case oscillation of every crossing plaquette does not itself provide
the desired contraction. The crossing surface grows as L3, and this crude estimate adds its entire
strength before applying the tilt bound.
A successful replacement would need a quantitative property of conditional block distributions
that the worst-case calculation discards: for example, cancellation, concentration after a suitable
gauge choice, or a controlled effective interaction. Such a property has to be proved for the
distributions in question. Naming it as a block-decay assumption does not establish it.
6.13 What can be recovered at the second-moment boundary
The rare-event example shows that second moments alone are insufficient. It does not mean that
an L2+ε hypothesis is logically necessary. Uniform control of second-moment tails can replace it,

renormalized composite field has borderline moment behavior.

Proof. The layer representation of the positive and negative parts of the clipped variables gives

consequently O(aγ/2), rather than faster than every power. A polynomial normalization of total
degree u can be absorbed by this bound only when u<γ/2; the displayed inequality alone gives
no vanishing conclusion at or beyond that threshold.
For non-unit variables, apply the statement to normalized variables and multiply by the two
normalization factors. The logarithmic moment condition must then be imposed on those
normalized variables. Writing it for the unnormalized variables instead would be a different

assumption. This gives a practical way to record borderline tail information without confusing it
with the stronger moment hypothesis in Theorem LC.7.
6.14 Stability of the moment condition under finite polynomial observables
A physical observable class must be rich enough to generate states; controlling one scalar field
does not settle that requirement. The moment condition of Theorem LC.7 is stable under finite
sums and products when enough individual moments are available. The following elementary
verification identifies exactly how much moment information each polynomial uses.
Suppose Xa,1,...,Xa,m are local real lattice observables. For every finite r≥ 1, assume bounds
∥Xa,k∥r ≤Ck,ra−uk,r
with finite constants and nonnegative exponents independent of a. Assume each support has at
most a polynomial number of links. Let
Pa =
L∑
ℓ=1
cℓ,a
m∏
k=1
Xnℓ,k a,k
be a fixed finite polynomial pattern, with nonnegative integer exponents nℓ,k and coefficients
satisfying|cℓ,a|≤Cℓa−vℓ. The numbers of terms and the exponents are fixed as a↓ 0.
Proposition LC.11 (polynomial closure). For each fixed finite p≥ 1, there are finite
constants CP,p,uP,p such that
∥Pa∥p ≤CP,pa−uP,p.
The support of Pa is contained in a finite union of the individual supports and therefore also
has polynomial cardinality. Thus every fixed pair of such polynomial observables at separated
physical supports satisfies Theorem LC.7 whenever the underlying Wilson comparison margin
remains uniformly positive.
Proof. Consider one monomial of total degree n = ∑ knℓ,k > 0. Regard it as a product of n
factors, allowing repeated factors. Hölder’s inequality with n equal exponents gives
‖‖‖‖‖ ∏ k Xnℓ,k a,k ‖‖‖‖‖ p ≤ ∏ k ∥Xa,k∥nℓ,k pn .
The assumed moment estimates make this a constant times a power of a−1. Multiplying by the
coefficient contributes another such power. A degree-zero term is covered by its coefficient alone.
The triangle inequality in Lp bounds the finite sum by the sum of these estimates. For 0 <a≤ 1,
their maximum exponent and the sum of their constants give uP,p and CP,p. No number of terms
depends on a. The support assertion is immediate because multiplication and addition cannot
introduce a dependence on a link outside the union. Apply Theorem LC.7 with, for example,
moment exponents p =q = 4 for the two resulting polynomial observables. □
The proposition does not prove density of the polynomial classes in any continuum Hilbert space.
It permits a precise conditional statement: if their centered positive-time classes are total and
the corresponding reflected correlations converge, then the moment-controlled strong-coupling
obstruction applies to the entire fixed polynomial class, not merely to its generators. All moments
of a primary field are not required to control one chosen polynomial; only the finitely many
orders used in the displayed Hölder estimate are needed. To handle polynomials of arbitrarily

=== PAGE 78 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
high degree in one common algebra, however, those finite requirements range over unbounded
moment orders.
6.15 How these bounds constrain a constructive attempt
The results now provide a sequence of concrete tests for any proposed limit. At the finite cutoff,
one can verify the Wilson normalization and count the conditional influences without referring
to a formal continuum path integral. If a comparison condition holds, one obtains both graph
and directional decay. Observable supports and either supremum norms or stronger moments
then determine the complete prefactor.
If the prefactor grows only polynomially and the comparison margin stays fixed, separated
connected correlations vanish faster than any power. If a nonzero separated covariance is
independently established, Theorem LC.8 instead forces the comparison margin toward zero at an
explicit scale. Neither outcome supplies a physical mass by itself. They restrict which estimates
can be compatible with a nontrivial limit and identify the place where additional information is
required.
The distinction between a Euclidean moment and a physical-state norm is particularly important.
A positive variance of a plaquette at one cutoff is an equal-location statement. A centered
Osterwalder–Schrader norm is a reflected two-point statement across a positive time separation.
The latter can vanish even when local variances grow. The moment-controlled theorem makes
this issue quantitative rather than leaving it as an informal warning.
There are also useful positive consequences. A proposed family of renormalized observables with
uniform L2+ε bounds immediately satisfies the tail hypothesis of Theorem LC.6. A proposed
anisotropic action can be tested using its weighted influence rows. A purported local discretization
errorcanbepropagatedbytheperturbationboundifitsactualplaquettecoefficientsarecontrolled.
Each of these is a finite, explicit calculation that can be independently checked before an infinite
limiting argument is attempted.
The complete theorems of this section establish sharper locality bounds and precise compatibility
conditions. The missing input for the intended four-dimensional continuum construction is a
family of estimates that remains valid along that construction while preserving a nonzero dense
family of reflected states. No claim that this input has been proved is made by replacing it with
one of the conditional consequences above.

7.5.1 Proof of the single-link estimate
Condition on every link except e. The six plaquette terms containing e can each be written as
1
2 Tr(UeSp), after using cyclicity and inversion if necessary, with Sp ∈SU(2) a staple formed by
the other three link matrices. Under the quaternion identification, this expression is u·vp for a
unit vector vp ∈S3. Thus the exact conditional law is ph, with
h =β
∑
p∋e
vp.
Changing a second link f that shares exactly one plaquette with e changes exactly one unit
vector in this sum. Consequently |h−h′|≤ 2β. Theorem IH.2 and monotonicity of Z give the
claimed coefficient. On the ordinary lattice each link belongs to six plaquettes, each containing
three other links, and these eighteen neighbors are distinct. Hence the row sum bound is (IH.9).
In general lattice dimension d≥ 2, the identical count gives 2(d− 1) incident plaquettes and
6(d− 1) distinct neighbors per link. The SU(2) coefficient itself is dimension independent,
and the corresponding row bound is 6(d− 1)cH(β). The number eighteen in the displayed
four-dimensional theorem is therefore exact for this incidence graph, rather than an unspecified
coordination constant.
Existence and uniqueness of βH follow from continuity, strict monotonicity and unboundedness
of Z, with Z(0) = 1. From (IH.7),
qH(β)≤ 18
√
1−e−β2/4 < 9β (β > 0).
At β = 1/9 this is strictly less than one. The exact rational procedure below verifies (IH.11).
For clarity, the constant in the covariance estimate is obtained as follows. Let Cef = cH on
adjacent distinct links and zero otherwise, and write D = (I−C)−1 = ∑ n≥0 Cn. The comparison
covariance inequality proved earlier is
| Cov(F,G)|≤ 1 4 ∑ e,f δeFDef δfG.
Since Cn ef = 0 for n<dG(e,f), its row sums are at most qn H, and δeF≤ 2∥F∥∞, summing first
over the support with fewer links proves (IH.12). Symmetry of C permits interchanging the
two supports. For boundary influence, the one-step forcing vector is at most be = ∑ f/∈Λ Cef.
Every path in Db leaving Λ from e has at least dG(e, Λc) steps, so its total weight is at most
qdG(e,Λc) H /(1 −qH). The same comparison theorem gives (IH.12a). In particular the right side
tends to zero in an exhaustion for each fixed local F, proving boundary independence and
uniqueness. Existence follows from compactness of the product of compact single-link spaces and
continuity of finite-volume conditional densities, as already established in the manuscript. No
limiting constants depend on the lattice volume. At β = 0, the product Haar measure supplies
all statements directly. □

8 Chordal transport estimates for the SU(2) single-link law
This section proves the quarter-contraction estimate on the field range needed for the lattice
comparison below, together with an explicit strict improvement away from the zero field. The
quarter theorem and the harmonic Neumann method are present in the work of Bhattacharjee
and Bhattacharya [5]. We give the details, replace its coefficient-sign argument by a short ratio
recurrence, and use an elementary rational estimate for the zonal component. The normalization
of the modified Bessel functions is the standard one [19].
8.1 Definitions and the local transport theorem
Let σ denote uniform probability measure on S3 ={u∈ R4 :|u| = 1}. For h∈ R4, define
dµh(u) =ρh(u)dσ(u), ρh(u) = eh·u Z(|h|), Z(r) = 2I1(r) r , Z(0) = 1. (8.1)
Here and throughout this section the metric on S3 is the chordal metric d(u,u′) = |u−u′|, not
the intrinsic geodesic metric. Write W1 for the Wasserstein distance with this cost and put
F (h,v) = sup
Lipchord(f)≤1
Covµh(f,v·u), |v| = 1. (8.2)
Because changing f to −f preserves the admissible class, the same supremum bounds the absolute
value of every displayed covariance.
Theorem 8.1 (Quarter bound with an explicit strict margin). For every h∈ R4 with |h|≤ 4/3
and every unit vector v,
F (h,v)≤ 1 4 − |h|4 24000. (8.3)
Moreover F (0,v) = 1/4. Consequently the uniform constant 1/4 is sharp, although the estimate
is strictly smaller at every nonzero field in the stated ball.
The coefficient 1/24000 is deliberately conservative. Its purpose is to give a transparent analytic
margin, not a numerical approximation to the optimal sensitivity. The proof occupies the next
subsections and uses no discretized transport computation.

with value 1/4 at h = 0. Directly, reflection through v⊥ leaves µh invariant and bounds the
covariance by Eµh(v·u)2, attained by f = v·u. This variance is A(r)/r, either by differentiating
logZ(|h|) in a transverse direction or by the rotational symmetry of the Hessian.
These identities do not prove the stronger proposed bound F (h,v) ≤A(|h|)/|h| for every direction
v. What has been established here is the full-direction quarter bound on |h|≤ 4/3, its explicit
strict margin, and the exact finite transport formula when the two fields have equal norms.
These are estimates for a single compact-group conditional law; their role in a lattice comparison
argument does not by itself supply a continuum construction.

9.2 Sharpness of this comparison and its limits
At an interior link, the staples use disjoint other links. Their quaternion products can be set
independently and paired with opposite values, producing he = 0. An infinitesimal variation of
any neighboring link changes the field at speed β in a unit direction. Since F (0,v) = 1/4, the
supremum influence coefficient is at least β/4. Together with (9.3), it equals β/4 in the stated
range.
The off-zero improvement does not lower this worst-case supremum. Thus 2/[3(d− 1)] is the
ceiling of this uniform row-sum contraction on the original links with the chordal metric. This
statement does not exclude gauge reduction, collective updates, block comparison, or multiscale
estimates. For all larger β, the same infinitesimal zero-field example still supplies the lower
bound Cef ≥β/4, whether or not our restricted-radius upper bound applies.
The heat-bath generator L used to prove covariance estimates is an auxiliary sampling dynamics.
Its relaxation gap is not the physical Hamiltonian gap. For 0 <β < 2/[3(d− 1)], a fixed-spacing
physical-gap inference uses the reflection-positive Wilson reconstruction and its positive transfer
operator [6, 9]. Each adjacency step in G changes the link midpoint’s time coordinate by at
most one lattice unit. Thus the graph distance between fixed local supports separated by n
time steps is at least n−cF, with cF depending only on the original supports. The covariance
bound is therefore O(qn). If the corresponding centered local gauge-invariant states are total in
the reconstructed excitation space, the positive spectral-measure argument in Theorem GT.1
excludes transfer spectrum above q. This yields the dimensionless lower threshold − logq. None
of these steps removes the lattice cutoff.
