10.2 A perfect gauge-fixing forest in Z4
Definition 10.3. A set F of links of Z4 is a perfect forest if it contains no cycle and every
plaquette contains exactly one link of F.
For x∈ Z4 put si = (−1)xi, and let µ(x)∈{1, 2, 3, 4} be defined by
µ(x) =



1 if s2 =s3 =s4,
2 if s1 =s3 =−s4,
3 if s1 =s4 =−s2,
4 if s1 =s2 =−s3.
(10.3)
Set F∗ := {(x,µ(x)) : x∈ Z4}, so that exactly one link of F∗ leaves each site in a positive
direction.
Proposition 10.4. The rule (10.3) is well defined, and F∗ is a perfect forest. Every component
of F∗ is infinite. Every link e /∈ F∗ lies in exactly 12 pairs (p,f) with p∋ e a plaquette and
f∈p\{e}, f /∈F∗; these 12 links f are distinct.
Proof. Well defined. Each of the four conditions in (10.3) constrains three of the four signs. Each
holds on exactly four of the sixteen parity classes, and no class satisfies two of them.
Perfect. The links of P (x; a,b) that leave a corner in a positive direction are (x,a), (x,b),
(x+ea,b) and (x+eb,a). The first two lie in F∗ exactly when µ(x) = a, respectively µ(x) = b; the
link (x + ea,b) lies in F∗ exactly when µ(x + ea) = b; and (x + eb,a) exactly when µ(x + eb) = a.
95
=== PAGE 96 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
These conditions depend only on the parity class of x and on the plane (a,b): 16 × 6 = 96 cases.
Table 21 in Appendix B lists, for each case, the unique link that satisfies its condition.
Acyclic. Suppose F∗ contained a cycle. Let y be a vertex of the cycle with the smallest coordinate
sum. Both cycle edges at y would leave y in positive directions. That contradicts the fact that
each site has only one outgoing link in F∗.
Infinite components. Following outgoing links never terminates.
Twelve neighbours. Each of the six plaquettes through e contains one link of F∗, which is not e,
and two further non-forest links. Two distinct plaquettes through e share no link other than
e.
Remark 10.5. For a periodic forest in Zd, or in a bulk density limit with negligible boundary
contributions, its density satisfies ρ≤ 1 links per site. Each link lies in 2(d− 1) plaquettes and
there are d(d− 1)/2 plaquettes per site, so the average number of forest links per plaquette is
4ρ/d. Exactly one per plaquette therefore requires ρ = d/4, hence d≤ 4. Within the subclass
with one positive outgoing link at every site, ρ = 1, so this counting identity forces d = 4. It
does not exclude constructions with lower density in dimensions below four. In d = 4 the perfect
forest also gives the least possible average neighbour count (Remark 10.12). A finite exhaustive
calculation classifies the period-two rules with exactly one positive outgoing link per site and
exactly one such link per plaquette: there are eight, and all are related to (10.3) by coordinate
permutations and translations modulo two. The calculation assigns one of four directions to
each of the sixteen parity classes, discarding a partial assignment only when a plaquette already
has more than one selected link or when a fully assigned plaquette does not have exactly one.
Hence every admissible assignment is retained. The reproducible integer enumeration is supplied
as code/v4/verify_forest_classification.py; this finite classification is separate from the
analytical infinite-lattice argument.
10.3 Gauge fixing at the level of specifications
Let E be the set of links of Z4, γ = (γΛ) the Wilson specification for (10.1), andG(γ) its set of
Gibbs measures. For a forest F⊂E, the gauge-fixed specification γF lives on ΩF = SU(2)E\F
and is defined by substituting the identity for every forest link in each local Wilson plaquette
interaction. This is a definition of a new local specification, not conditioning on the probability-
zero event that infinitely many links equal the identity. The underlying lattice is Z4, not a finite
periodic quotient: a forest in Z4 may acquire cycles after a periodic identification.
Lemma 10.6 (Gauge fixing). Let F be a forest. In each component of F choose a vertex o (for
instance the one closest to the origin, with ties broken lexicographically). For a vertex y joined to
o by the path o = y0,...,yk = y in F, put g(y) = Uy0y1 ···Uyk−1yk. Define Φ(U) = Ug, where
(Ug)xy =g(x)Uxyg(y)−1. Then:
(i) Φ(U)e = 1 for every e∈F, andO◦ Φ =O for every gauge-invariant local functionO;
(ii) Φ∗µ∈G(γF ) for every µ∈G(γ).
Proof. (i) The definition gives g(yj+1) = g(yj)Uyjyj+1, so every link of F is mapped to 1. Paths
in a tree are unique and finite between any two specified vertices, so g is well defined; it depends
only on U|F. Each coordinate of g is a finite product of link variables. Thus Φ is measurable
(indeed continuous in the product topology). The roots are fixed once and for all from the
graph; no measurable choice depending on U is needed. Distinct components have separate
roots. Residual root transformations do not affect gauge-invariant observables. A local function
depends on finitely many links, so invariance under all gauge transformations is the same as
invariance under the finitely many values of g it sees.
96
=== PAGE 97 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
(ii) Let Λ ⊂E\F be finite and let A be bounded and measurable on ΩF. The DLR equation for
µ gives Eµ[A◦Φ] = Eµ[γΛ(A◦Φ)]. In γΛ( ·|UΛc) the transformation g is fixed, because it depends
only on links of F ⊂ Λc. Change variables Ve ↦→ g(xe)Veg(ye)−1 for e∈ Λ. Haar measure is
invariant under this change, and the plaquette weights are gauge invariant. Hence
γΛ(A◦ Φ)(U) =γF Λ (A)(Φ(U)).
So EΦ∗µ[A] = EΦ∗µ[γF Λ A] for all finite Λ.
Lemma 10.7 (Elitzur). Every µ∈G(γ) is invariant under finitely supported gauge transforma-
tions. Consequently µ is determined by its values on gauge-invariant local functions.
Proof. Let g be supported on a finite set X of sites, and let Λ be the set of links incident to X.
The transformation g changes only links in Λ, and it leaves γΛ( ·|UΛc) invariant. So µ = µγΛ
is g-invariant. For a local function O, average over Haar-distributed g on the endpoints of its
support. This produces a gauge-invariant local function with the same µ-expectation.
Corollary 10.8. If γF has at most one Gibbs measure, then γ has exactly one. Moreover, for
gauge-invariant local O1,O2 and ν = Φ∗µ, we have Covµ(O1,O2) = Covν(O1|ΩF,O2|ΩF ), and
ℓe(Oi|ΩF )≤ℓe(Oi).
Proof. Existence follows by compactness. Uniqueness follows from Lemmas 10.6 and 10.7. The
covariance identity is Lemma 10.6(i). Restricting the configuration space cannot increase a
Lipschitz seminorm.

Remark 10.12 (Sharpness and comparison). The ceiling for this comparison matrix. The six
staples of a non-forest link can be prescribed independently: the two free links in each staple are
distinct from the free links in the other five staples. Prescribe cancelling pairs so that he = 0. An
infinitesimal change of any chosen neighbour gives a tangent field perturbation of size β times
the chordal displacement. At zero field the exact directional sensitivity is 1/4, so every optimal
coordinate influence coefficient is at least β/4. For β≤ 1/3 the upper bound proved above agrees
with this lower bound. For β > 1/3, the same local lower bound still applies even though the
radius-two upper-bound theorem need not cover all backgrounds.
Here is the required infinite-graph argument for weighted comparison. Let C0 have entries β/4
on the twelve neighbours and zero otherwise. It is a symmetric finite-range, period-two matrix.
For the set ΛL of non-forest links with base points in a cube of side L,
⟨1ΛL,C01ΛL⟩
∥1ΛL∥2 2 = 3β−O(L−1).
99
=== PAGE 100 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Indeed only O(L3) links are within the finite interaction range of the cube boundary, whereas
|ΛL| is of order L4; every remaining row has all twelve neighbours inside. The largest eigenvalue
of the finite principal matrix therefore tends to 3β, with the reverse bound following from its
row sums.
If arbitrary strictly positive weights we obeyed C0w≤ qw, their restriction to each finite ΛL
would obey C0,ΛLw≤ qw. Diagonal conjugation by those finitely many weights gives a finite
nonnegative matrix with row sums at most q, so its spectral radius is at most q. Passing
L→∞ gives q≥ 3β. Thus weights cannot turn this exact original-coordinate comparison into
a contraction at or above β = 1/3. This is a limitation of this particular forest and influence
criterion; it is not an obstruction to other gauge choices, blocks, multiscale estimates, or physical
mass gaps.
Any forest. In a bulk limit with a well-defined forest density and negligible boundary contributions,
let ρ ≤ 1 be the forest density per site and kp the number of forest links in plaquette p.
Convexity of k↦→ (4 −k)(3 −k) bounds the average number of non-forest neighbours below by
6(4 −ρ)(3 −ρ)/(4 −ρ) = 6(3 −ρ) ≥ 12. We therefore expect 1/3 to bound every single-link
forest-gauge comparison. A general proof would have to treat links whose staples are partly
frozen; we do not give one.
Ranges in normalization (10.1). Shen–Zhu–Zhu [10]: β < 1/12. Ungauged comparison Theo-
rem 9.1: β < 2/9. Axial gauge: β < 2/7. Perfect forest: β < 1/3.
Gap bounds. Theorem 10.10(c) improves the bound − log(9β/2) of the ungauged comparison
theorem by the additive constant log 18 as β→ 0. No sharpness of the physical spectral lower
bound is asserted.
Remark 10.13 (What Theorem 10.10 is not). It is a fixed-spacing statement deep in the strong-
coupling region. The theorem supplies no useful weak-coupling estimate along β→∞, and no
continuum construction follows from it.
Scope of finite-volume and boundary assertions. The finite Dobrushin comparison bound
applies uniformly to finite subsets of the gauge-fixed non-forest link space with arbitrary fixed
non-forest exterior values. The transfer to the original Wilson theory proved above concerns
infinite-volume Gibbs measures and their gauge-invariant local correlations. A gauge transform
depending on forest links need not preserve an arbitrary originally prescribed finite-box boundary
condition. No uniform original-boundary covariance estimate is asserted without a separate
treatment of that transformation.
Attribution. Bhattacharjee and Bhattacharya report a twelve-neighbour forest gauge and the
range β < 1/3 [5]. The present proof gives the explicit parity rule, conditional-law change of
variables, directional comparison bound and transfer interpretation. The forest method and this
coupling range retain that prior attribution.
11 Site-plane norms and positive-time survival
This result is unconditional once the stated site-reflection positivity and Wilson Gibbs measure
have been constructed. It establishes nontriviality of the site-reflection Hilbert space. The variance
argument alone does not establish a nonzero finite-energy sector for a possibly noninjective
discrete transfer operator. The adjacent-time theorem in the following section supplies that
additional argument in the stated strong-coupling range.

11.1 Proposition SP.1: explicit site-plane excitation norm
Let µ be a four-dimensional fundamental SU(2) Wilson Gibbs measure at finite coupling β≥ 0,
with normalized plaquette weight w(U) = Tr(U)/2. Suppose µ is reflection positive for the site
reflection θ : t↦→−t, on an algebra that contains bounded gauge-invariant observables of the
spatial links in the plane t = 0. Let p be one spatial plaquette in that plane and define
F =w(Up)− Eµw(Up).
In the corresponding Osterwalder–Schrader quotient and completion, the class [F ] is orthogonal
to the vacuum vector Ω = [1] and obeys
∥[F ]∥2 OS = Varµ(w(Up))≥ 1 4e−48β > 0.
11.1.1 Proof
Because the plaquette is spatial and lies in the reflection plane, θF = F. Therefore its reflection
form is its ordinary second moment, and centering gives⟨Ω, [F ]⟩ = EF = 0.
For the lower bound, condition on every link except the four links of p. At most twenty-
four geometric plaquettes contain at least one of these links, since each link belongs to six
plaquettes; overcounting only weakens the estimate. Each normalized trace lies in [−1, 1]. Thus
the conditional density on the four free links, relative to product probability Haar measure h⊗4,
is bounded below by e−48β: its numerator is at least e−24β, and its normalizing integral is at
most e24β.
For every real constant c, this implies
E[(w(Up)−c)2 |Upc]≥e−48β
∫
(w(Up)−c)2 dh⊗4.
Take the infimum over c on both sides. The plaquette product under product Haar measure is
Haar distributed. Its normalized fundamental SU(2) character has Haar mean zero and variance
1/4. Hence the conditional variance is at least e−48β/4. The law of total variance gives the same
lower bound for the unconditional variance. This proves the claim.
The estimate also holds for a gauge-fixed representation of this state when the gauge-fixing
construction preserves gauge-invariant expectations: apply the argument before fixing the gauge
and transfer the expectation identity. No product-Haar domination on the already gauge-fixed
four-link set is assumed.
11.2 What this proves about the transfer operator
Suppose link-reflection positivity and the transfer construction supply a positive self-adjoint
contraction T on the site-reflection space. The proposition proves that Ω⊥ is nonzero. It does
not prove that T [F ]̸= 0, or that T is injective on Ω⊥.
This distinction cannot be removed by functional calculus alone. If T has a kernel, − logT is not
an everywhere densely defined self-adjoint Hamiltonian on the entire Hilbert space: the natural
finite-energy space is (kerT )⊥. A nonzero vector lying wholly in kerT has positive norm at time
zero but zero correlation at every strictly positive lattice time.
101
=== PAGE 102 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
For example, on CΩ ⊕ Ce, the positive contraction T = |Ω⟩⟨Ω| has a nonzero vacuum orthocom-
plement, while ⟨e,Tne⟩ = 0 for every integer n≥ 1. The zero-coupling Wilson product measure
has the corresponding loss of centered spatial-slice information after one time step. Thus a proof
based only on the site-plane variance would incorrectly bypass a real distinction.
Any one of the following facts is sufficient to close this fixed-spacing nontriviality issue:
1. Injectivity of the reconstructed infinite-volume positive transfer operator on the nonzero
site-plane sector.
2. One nonzero centered physical state v with⟨v,Tv⟩> 0.
3. A quantitative positive-time lower bound that survives the spatial-volume limit for the
same state family.
These are alternative sufficient conditions, not conclusions of the variance argument. The
following adjacent-time theorem establishes a quantitative instance of the second and third
conditions for 0 <β < 1/3. Finite-spatial-volume transfer injectivity at each volume does not
establish infinite-volume injectivity or survival by itself. Likewise, positivity of every local Wilson
character coefficient does not on its own justify passing an infinite product of transfer kernels
through the thermodynamic limit.
Once a positive-time centered state exists and a decay bound holds on a total family in the
relevant transfer sector, the spectral argument applies there. This still concerns a fixed lattice
spacing. Continuum survival requires further bounds along the spacing and coupling trajectory.

does not provide a cutoff-uniform continuum survival bound: its constants depend strongly on
the bare coupling, and its two layers are one lattice spacing apart.

spectral conclusion uses only the range in which the preceding free-boundary limit and forest decay
arguments have been established. Neither bound remains a finite nonzero continuum scale under
an uncontrolled removal of the lattice spacing. The positive-time witness therefore completes a

13 Finite-volume approximation and sensitivity estimates
Approximation errors, boundary sensitivity and physical spectral estimates are separate quantities.

include gauge directions; a bound or obstruction for those metrics acquires physical spectral
meaning only through a stated comparison and reconstruction argument.

gives λ0 = 3. If the log-density tilt has oscillation at most 2βP, comparison of numerator and
denominator in the variational Poincare quotient gives λ≥ 3e−2βP. This is a rigorous but
potentially very small denominator in the residual allowance.

13.5 Gauge directions and marginal diagnostics
Proposition 13.8 (Gauge-localized boundary changes). Let V be the internal links of a non-
degenerate four-dimensional box. At a boundary site with exactly one exterior incident link b,
changing only b can be matched by a gauge transformation of the seven internal incident links.
The conditional laws are related by this pushforward. Their chordal product Wasserstein distance
is at most 7|τb −τ′ b|, and all gauge-invariant internal observables have identical expectations.
Proof. Choose the site gauge transformation that maps τb to τ′ b. Gauge invariance of every
plaquette weight gives the pushforward identity. Couple an internal configuration with its
transformed configuration. Exactly seven links can move, and bi-invariance of chordal distance
makes each displacement equal to |τb −τ′ b|. A gauge-invariant observable is unchanged pointwise.
Proposition 13.9 (Haar plaquette marginals do not imply clustering). There exists a translation-
invariant, gauge-invariant random link field on Z4 whose individual positively oriented plaquette
holonomies are Haar-distributed up to conjugation, while their adjoint-character covariance is
one at arbitrarily large separation.
Proof. Draw a single Haar element h∈ SU(2) and set Ux,µ = hsµ(x), where sµ(x) = ∑ ν<µxν.
Every positively oriented plaquette is h or h−1 according to the orientation convention. Indepen-
dently draw Haar site gauges gx and replace Ux,µ by gxUx,µg−1 x+eµ. This gives gauge invariance.
Translation changes the original link field by a gauge transformation made from powers of h, so
the gauge-averaged law is translation-invariant. The adjoint character χ2 is real, conjugation
invariant, has Haar mean zero and Haar square mean one. It has the identical value χ2(h) on
every plaquette. Thus its covariance between any two plaquettes is one.

This field is an obstruction to an inference from marginal distributions; it is not asserted to be a
Wilson Gibbs state.

14 Coarse graining: proved comparisons and missing controls
The results of this section distinguish three operations: comparing partition functions, condi-
tioning on a blocked field, and controlling the covariances discarded by that conditioning. A
partition comparison alone supplies none of the last operation’s estimates.

14.3 A rigorous polymer criterion without uncertified endpoints
For a normalized positive plaquette weight w = 1 + f, assume
∫
f = 0 and ∥f∥∞ ≤ ϵ. In
scale-two decimation, condition on the coarse link products and integrate the remaining fine links.
Skeleton half-link variables can be removed by gauge transformations at their midpoints; the
residual integrated variables retain product Haar measure. Expanding ∏ p(1 +f(Up)) produces
polymers: plaquette sets connected through integrated links. Their activity is the corresponding
Haar integral of a product of f factors.
Lemma 14.5 (Uniform polymer estimates). An activity vanishes if an integrated link belongs
to exactly one of its plaquettes. Every nonzero polymer γ has at most 2|γ| distinct integrated
links, and |z(γ)|≤ϵ|γ|. The plaquette adjacency graph through integrated links has degree at most
D = 20. The number of connected size-n sets containing a fixed plaquette is at most
An = 1 (D− 1)n + 1
(
Dn
n
)
.
Proof. If an integrated link occurs only once, integrate that link first; the factor has Haar mean
zero irrespective of its fixed neighboring variables. Each plaquette has at most two skeleton links,
since a pair of parallel opposite edges has opposite parity in the transverse plaquette direction.
At least two edges are integrated. In a nonvanishing polymer every integrated link is counted
at least twice among at most 4|γ| incidences, proving the bound 2|γ|. The activity bound is
immediate. Each plaquette has at most four integrated edges, each in five other plaquettes,
giving degree at most twenty. Fix a deterministic neighbor ordering at each plaquette and encode
each connected set by its breadth-first rooted spanning tree, including the neighbor labels. The
set is recoverable from this tree. These trees are subtrees of the ordered D-ary tree, counted by
the displayed Fuss–Catalan number.

half offset, and one of each unit offset; its row is the stated polynomial. The temporal-edge row
is smaller.

16 Replica sectors and finite moment certificates
An independent replica reformulates connected correlations without eliminating the need to
control the complete physical vacuum complement. The distinction can be stated exactly at the
operator level.
Theorem 16.1 (The antisymmetric replica sector). Let T be a positive self-adjoint contraction
on a Hilbert space H = CΩ ⊕H0, with ∥Ω∥ = 1, T Ω = Ω, and H0 = Ω⊥ invariant. Write
λ =∥T|H0∥. On the antisymmetric sectorH−⊂H⊗H,
∥(T⊗T )|H−∥ =λ.
Proof. The orthogonal decomposition is H− = (Ω∧H0)⊕∧2H0. The map v↦→ (Ω⊗v−v⊗Ω)/ √ 2
intertwines T|H0 with the operator on the first summand, whose norm is λ. The second summand
has norm at most λ2 ≤λ.
Proposition 16.2 (Connected matrices and product positivity). For real time-zero observables
Fi, let mi =⟨Fi⟩, Gij =⟨Fi,Fj⟩ and Kij =⟨Fi,TFj⟩. For Ψi =Fi ⊗ Ω− Ω⊗Fi,
[⟨Ψi, Ψj⟩] = 2(G−mmT), [⟨Ψi, (T⊗T )Ψj⟩] = 2(K−mmT).
More generally, if M is the Gram matrix of vectors ha, the Gram matrix of ha ⊗hb −hb ⊗ha,
indexed by a<b, is 2[MacMbd −MadMbc]. It is positive whenever M is positive.
Proof. Expand the tensor inner products and use T Ω = Ω. For the last assertion, factor
M = R∗R; the displayed matrix is twice the second compound matrix of M, equal by Cauchy–
Binet to 2C2(R)∗C2(R). Equivalently, it is a restriction of the positive product Gram matrix
M⊗M.
Thus these replica positivity conditions follow from single-copy positivity and exact independence.
Treating replica mixed moments as unrestricted new variables discards the independence relations.
The proposition does not compare different truncation degrees or different sets of extra identities.
Proposition 16.3 (Direction of a finite variational estimate). Let Ψ1,..., Ψn ∈ H− have
positive-definite Gram matrix G−, and let K− be their one-step matrix. Then
λmax(G−1/2 − K−G−1/2 − )≤λ.
A lower bound r > 0 on the left therefore gives the upper mass bound − logλ≤− logr. An
inequality K−≤qG− on this finite family alone does not give λ≤q.
119
=== PAGE 120 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Proof. The generalized eigenvalue is the largest Rayleigh quotient on the span of the chosen
family, hence at most the operator norm. To see the limitation, realize the finite Gram and
step data on their span and append an orthogonal vacuum-complement eigenvector with any
eigenvalue λ′∈ (q, 1). The recorded finite matrices do not change. A global gap bound requires
additional control of the omitted subspace, or extension of the inequality to a total set with a
uniform constant.
16.1 Loop identities and the finite relaxation
The loop bootstrap in this application follows the lattice moment approach of [35]. Write
W [C] =⟨ 1 2 TrU(C)⟩. For SU(2),
TrA TrB = Tr(AB) + Tr(AB−1),
so products of normalized traces reduce to half-sums of single-loop expectations. Haar integration
by parts at an edge, with the sphere normalization ∆u = −3u, generates exact rational linear
equations in loop expectations when the Wilson coupling is rational. The relevant positivity
constraints are path Gram positivity, reflection positivity, and 0 ≤T≤I on time-zero observables.
For example, with a time link γ joining two spatial slices,
Gab = 1 2 {W [ab] +W [ab−1]}, Kab = 1 2 {W [aγbγ−1] +W [aγb−1γ−1]}.
The valid finite inequalities include G≥ 0, K≥ 0, G−K≥ 0 and |W [C]|≤ 1. The source
package records the exact generated linear systems and matrix entries, so the arithmetic claim
below can be checked without rerunning an optimization algorithm.

17 A certified three-link conditioning functional
The aim of the following construction is to bound an entire finite-dimensional field domain,
including all response directions, with the error from every series and interval evaluation controlled.
The local block geometry and single-link transport estimate are those of [34]. The refinement
uses a banded harmonic energy and a uniform moment expansion. Its strongest certified coupling
range is stated in Section 18. For clarity, the complete two-backend certificate at κ = 7/20 is
proved first; its moment decomposition is then strengthened without changing the underlying
functional.
The accompanying source package contains the exact certificate inputs, complete verifier programs,
and explicit series-tail allowances. The original two-backend certificate in this section is retained
with its integer and Arb evaluators. Section 18 specifies the final strengthened certificate and its
reproducible verification scope.

19.1 Two transport lemmas
Lemma 19.1 (Free-link reparametrisation). Fix j∈{2,...,n} and the links yi, i /∈{1,j}. The
map yj ↦→ w := y2 ···yn is an isometry of Sp−1 that preserves σ, and Re(y1 ···yn) = ⟨y1,w⟩.
Consequently, under σ⊗n the variable w is Haar-distributed and independent of (yi)i̸=j. Moving w
to w′ while keeping all yi, i̸= j, fixed costs exactly |w−w′| in dB. Finally, |w−w′|≤∑ i≥2 |yi−y′ i|
for arbitrary moves.
Proof. w = Pyj Q with P = y2 ···yj−1, Q = yj+1 ···yn fixed unit elements. Left and right
multiplication by unit elements and conjugation are isometries preserving σ. Next, Re(y1 ¯w) =
⟨y1,w⟩. The last claim is|ab−a′b′|≤|a−a′| +|b−b′| for unit elements, iterated.
Lemma 19.2 (Equal-concentration vMF laws). Let p≥ 1, κ≥ 0 and a,a′ ∈ Sp−1. For the
chordal metric,

is the following reflection-acceptance kernel: from w, stay with probability min{1,q′(w)/q(w)},
otherwise jump to Rew. Here q,q′ are the densities of the two laws. The potential ϕ(w) = ⟨w,e⟩
is optimal.
Proof. The kernel is a coupling. q(Rew) ∝ eκ⟨w,Rea⟩ = eκ⟨w,a′⟩, so q◦Re = q′ and q′◦Re = q,
and Re preserves σ. The image density at u is

19.6 A rigidity theorem for the reflection potential
The preceding transport construction shows that the explicit potential
F0 =⟨y1,h⟩ +⟨y2y3,h⟩
is optimal at zero field, and on the faces b2b3 = 0 for h⊥b1. There it gives K = (1+A(κ))A(r)/r.

Two-spin form. For independent x∼ vMF(a), z∼ vMF(c) on S3, let

G

Lemma 19.14 (Tight pairs). If s(u) −s(u′) = |x−x′| + |z−z′| with u = (x,z) ̸= u′, then
s(u) > 0 and u′∈{Txu,Tzu}. Here Tx(x,z) = (Rzx,z) and Tz(x,z) = (x,Rxz), where Rv is the
reflection across v⊥; both flips send s↦→−s.
Proof. Write s(u) −s(u′) = ⟨x−x′,z⟩ + ⟨x′,z−z′⟩. Each term is bounded by the corresponding
distance, so both must be tight:
x−x′ =λz, z−z′ =µx′, λ,µ≥ 0.
Case λ > 0. Unit length forces λ = 2s(u), so x′ = Rzx. If µ > 0, unit length would force
µ = 2⟨z,x′⟩ =−2s(u)< 0, a contradiction. Thus µ = 0, and u′ =Txu.
Case λ = 0. Then µ = 2s(u)> 0, and u′ =Tzu.
Theorem 19.15 (Rigidity). Let κ> 0.
(i) s attains N(a,c) if and only if a = 0 or c = 0.
(ii) On the slice b1 = 0, F0 attains K(0,b2,b3; h) if and only if b2 = 0 or b3 = 0. Off these faces
(on the slice), K(0,b2,b3;h)> Cov(F0,⟨y1,h⟩) strictly.
(iii) On the faces b2b3 = 0, F0 attains K(b;h) if and only if h⊥b1 (including b1 = 0).

19.7 A quantitative strict improvement over the reflection potential
19.7.1 Definitions and the precise claim
For unit vectors x,z∈S3 ⊂ R4, put
s(x,z) =x·z, d((x,z), (x′,z′)) =|x−x′| +|z−z′|.
For a probability law P of (x,z), let

Lipd(G)≤1
CovP (G,s), V = VarP (s).
The potential s is admissible, so NP ≥ V. We seek a quantitative lower bound for NP −V.
For independent x∼ vMF(a) and z∼ vMF(c), this NP is the quantity N(a,c) of the reflection-
potential problem.
The conclusions below use only Euclidean geometry, elementary covariance identities and von
Mises–Fisher moments. They do not use the imported lattice uniqueness or transfer-matrix
implications for the bond potential. They do not give a continuum Yang–Mills mass gap.
19.7.2 A general quantitative bound from an explicit potential
Let W =x∧z∈ Λ2R4, with coordinates

lemma.
Lemma 19.17 (A Euclidean Lipschitz embedding). The map
Φ(x,z) = (s(x,z),W (x,z))∈ R⊕ Λ2R4
is 1-Lipschitz for the metric d.
Proof. For fixed z and p =x−x′, the difference is (p·z,p∧z). Since|z| = 1,
(p·z)2 +∥p∧z∥2 =|p|2.
Thus Φ is an isometry when only x changes. The same identity applies when only z changes.
Inserting the intermediate point (x′,z) and applying the Euclidean triangle inequality proves
∥Φ(x,z)− Φ(x′,z′)∥≤|x−x′| +|z−z′|.

19.8 Finite-subgroup calculations and their interpretation
The retained numerical experiments replace SU(2) by the binary polyhedral groups 2T, 2O, 2I,
with 24, 48 and 120 elements. For the product chordal metric their finite transport problem is
a linear program, but the stored solutions use floating-point linear programming. At κ = 0.35,
the reported 2T corner value is approximately 0.2729280, compared with 0.2717644 at zero field.
The larger subgroup calculations also report positive corner excess. These values are numerical
evidence for the finite models, not rationally certified inequalities or a limiting theorem for SU(2).

=== PAGE 146 ===

Only three groups were sampled, and they do not form a controlled approximation sequence
with an available transport-error theorem. Fits of the excess to different mesh variables give
different intercepts. The analytic rigidity theorem settles the strict failure of the simple potential
on the continuous sphere independently of those fits. It does not settle the stronger inequality
supbK(b) =K(0), because the improved interior lower bound can remain below K(0).
19.9 A transverse total-variation estimate
Proposition 19.22. If y∼ vMF(κe) on S3 and u⊥e is unit, then
E|u·y| = 1 2 E √ 1−s2, s =e·y,
is strictly decreasing for κ> 0, and is at most 4/(3π). At κ = 0 the same value holds for every
unit direction u.
Proof. Conditionally on s, the transverse direction is uniform on S2. Its projection onto u is
uniform on [−1, 1], giving the factor 1/2. The density of s is proportional to eκs√ 1−s2. For
the even decreasing function g(s) =
√
1−s2, differentiation gives ∂κEg = Cov(g,s). After
folding to [0, 1], let π have density proportional to cosh(κs)
√
1−s2 and ρ density proportional to
s sinh(κs)
√
1−s2. Then Cov(g,s) = E[s](Eρg− Eπg). The likelihood ratio dρ/dπ is proportional
to s tanh(κs), strictly increasing. The elementary association inequality, obtained by integrating
(g(s) − g(t))(s tanh(κs) − t tanh(κt)) ≤ 0 against π(ds)π(dt), makes the covariance strictly
negative. At zero concentration, direct Haar integration yields 4/(3π).
The corresponding bound for arbitrary nontransverse directions is not proved by this argument;
numerical scans of that stronger statement remain numerical evidence.

Hamiltonian dynamics and spatial refinement
21 Kinetic temporal limit with complete representation control
This section constructs the time-continuum limit of the normalized SU(2) Wilson kinetic operator,
including an explicit operator-norm error bound. There is no representation truncation in the
result. The number of spatial links remains finite. The final proposition shows precisely why this
kinetic limit does not directly approximate the full isotropic Wilson transfer operator at large
coupling.

21.2 Uniform operator control over the complete representation space

Proof. Let m =⌊βt⌋ and N =⌈√β⌉. For β≥ 9,

For the entire omitted set n>N, strict monotonicity of the coefficients and cN ≥ (β−1)/2 ≥ 4β/9

their norm difference is also at most one.
For strong convergence at the time origin, first take a vector supported on finitely many
representations. Ordinary telescoping without damping, (21.3), and the rounding bound show
uniform convergence on [0,T ] on this finite-dimensional subspace. For an arbitrary vector,
approximate it by such a finite sum; the error on the remaining vector is at most twice its norm
because both operators are contractions. This proves the final assertion. Uniform operator-norm
convergence down to t = 0 is neither asserted nor true: if 0 <t< 1/β, the discrete operator is I
and∥I−e−tG∥ = 1.

The proposition rules out a direct operator-norm substitution of the kinetic factor for the
normalized isotropic transfer operator in this Hilbert-space identification. It does not rule out
scale-dependent embeddings, an interacting spatial renormalization construction, or a positive

β = 4ϵ g2a, β βt = (ϵ a )2 , ββt = 16 g4 .

spatial-cutoff limit. The constructed time-continuum theory retains its finite spatial lattice.
For an additional precise distinction, the unprojected one-link kinetic operator Cβ has nonvacuum
gap − logρ2. On a nonconstant tensor-product representation, at least one link is nontrivial, so
its eigenvalue is at most ρ2. Consequently − logρ2 remains a lower bound after restriction to the
nonconstant locally gauge-invariant sector; equality need not hold because the gauge constraints
require allowed representation networks. For β≥ 3, Lemma 21.1 gives

If a proposed time spacing aβ obeys βaβ → 0, this kinetic-only gap divided by aβ diverges. It
cannot by itself give a nontrivial, strongly continuous physical-time limit on the fixed nonvacuum
Hilbert space at that spacing. This statement is conditional on the displayed spacing hypothesis;
it supplies neither a full interacting mass estimate nor a spatial continuum construction.
22 Interacting temporal continuum at fixed spatial cutoff
The result in this section removes the temporal lattice spacing from an explicit anisotropic
Wilson theory. The spatial lattice is retained. The Hamiltonian formulation and its relation to
the Wilson transfer matrix are due to Kogut–Susskind and Creutz [3, 4]. The arguments below
specify the normalizations and prove convergence in operator norm, including the vacuum and
every fixed low eigenvalue. No finite representation truncation is made.
22.1 The model and its physical Hilbert space
Fix a spatial spacing a> 0, a coupling g > 0 and an integer L≥ 2. The periodic spatial lattice
is (Z/LZ)3. It has E = 3L3 positively oriented links and P = 3L3 unoriented elementary spatial
plaquettes, one orientation chosen for each plaquette. For L = 2, the periodic parallel links are
distinct link variables. The configuration space and normalized measure are
X =SU(2)E, dµ(U) =
E∏
e=1
dUe.
The vertex gauge groupG =SU(2)L3 acts by Uxy ↦→qxUxyq−1 y . The physical Hilbert space is
Hphys =L2(X,dµ)G. (22.1)
This imposes Gauss’s law and retains all physical center-flux sectors. Let Ce be the nonnegative
one-link Casimir, with eigenvalue j(j + 1) in spin j. In the unit-quaternion realization of SU(2),
Ce =−∆S3,e/4.
Set
b = 4a g2 , κ = g2 2a, H0 =κ E∑ e=1 Ce, (22.2)
V (U) = 4 g2a P∑ p=1 ( 1− 1 2 TrUp ) , V∗ = 8P g2a, H =H0 +V. (22.3)
Here V denotes multiplication by the displayed function, and 0 ≤V ≤V∗. The trace is real for
SU(2). The operator H is selfadjoint on D(H0), nonnegative and has compact resolvent. These
properties hold both on L2(X) and on (22.1). Indeed, the Casimir sum has a complete product
Peter–Weyl basis with finite multiplicities below each fixed energy, and adding the bounded
selfadjoint V preserves its domain and compact resolvent. Gauge transformations commute
with both summands. The interaction is nonconstant: all identity links give V = 0, whereas
changing one link to −I changes its adjacent plaquette traces and gives V > 0. In particular,
the constant function is not an eigenfunction of H; the vacuum constructed below includes this
nonzero interaction.
For a temporal spacing ϵ> 0, choose the anisotropic Wilson couplings
βt = 4a g2ϵ = b ϵ, β = 4ϵ g2a. (22.4)

the same physical eigenvalue ratios as the unfixed Wilson transfer operator. A different overall
positive normalization changes the unnormalized vacuum energy but cancels from Fϵ/λ0(Fϵ).

eigenfunctions could not be orthogonal. Gauge transformations preserve positivity and commute
with these operators, so uniqueness forces the positive normalized ground states to be gauge
invariant.

around the circle proves norm convergence of the vacuum projectors. Their positive normalized
representatives therefore converge in Hilbert norm. The top eigenvalue limit and scalar division
prove (22.19); subtracting the two lowest energy limits proves (22.20). Positivity and compactness
already give E1 >E0; the next subsection provides an explicit bound.

follows by inserting the convergent normalized vacua and telescoping the finite product of bounded
operators. Thus this construction supplies states and transfer correlations as well as a formal
Hamiltonian. The convergence is on a fixed spatial configuration space; it does not identify
Hilbert spaces associated with different spatial cutoffs.

at each fixed spatial cutoff and finite volume. A four-dimensional continuum conclusion would
still require a spatial-cutoff construction, convergence of appropriately renormalized observables
across those different Hilbert spaces, and a positive physical lower bound that survives that
construction and growing physical volume. None of those missing spatial estimates is assumed or
inferred from (22.24).

24 Full-complement finite-volume gap from heat-kernel compar-
ison
This section supplies a full physical-sector spectral inequality. It does not restrict trial vectors to
plaquette functions or a finite operator basis. The estimate is positive for every fixed lattice, but
its explicit constant still tends to zero in spatial cutoff removal. The heat-kernel and measure-
comparison ingredients are classical; the quantitative specialization and comparison with the
fixed-time certificate are the calculation made here.
24.1 Hamiltonian and theorem
Let the spatial lattice be a periodic cube of side L≥ 2 in lattice units. Put N = 3L3, the number
of independent link variables and also the number of elementary plaquettes. Let µ be normalized
product Haar measure on SU(2)N. For a> 0 and s =g2 ∈ (0, 1], consider
H =κD +V, κ = s 2a, D = ∑ e Ce, V = 4 sa ∑ p (1−Fp), Fp = 1 2 TrUp. (24.1)
Each CasimirCe has eigenvalues j(j + 1). In particular,
0≤V ≤Vmax = 8N sa. (24.2)
The physical Hilbert space is the vertex-gauge-invariant subspace of L2(µ). The unique normalized
positive ground state is h, with energy E0. Write K =H−E0 and dν =h2dµ.

Theorem 24.1 (Global finite-lattice physical gap). In the setting above, define
BH(a,L,s) = 3s 8a (π 16 )3L3 exp ( −48πL3 s ) > 0. (24.3)

Proposition 26.5 (The vacuum is not a single Wilson Gibbs weight). At every g > 0, no real

26.5 Explicit hidden-mode examples with the vacuum handled exactly
First, take
Kε = diag(0, 1,ε) on C3, 0<ε< 1,
and let U : C2 → C3 include the first two coordinates. The vacuum is preserved exactly,
U∗KεU = diag(0, 1), and the retained space is exactly invariant: QKεU = 0. Even U∗e−tKεU =
e−t diag(0,1) holds for every t≥ 0. Nevertheless the full gap is ε, while the compressed gap is one.
The entire missing information is the discarded eigenvalue.
There is an infinite-dimensional compact-group version. On two SU(2) class-function rotors, let
Kε = 4 3 ( C1 +εC2 ) .
Its unique vacuum is the constant function. The map Uf(U1,U2) = f(U1) preserves that vacuum,
has exactly vanishing residual, and compresses to (4/3)C1, with gap one. The physical class-
function state χ1/2(U2) has energy ε, so the full gap is ε. These two rotors are a counterexample
to a proposed spectral inference, not a replacement for the specified Wilson model.
Second, knowledge that both diagonal blocks are uniformly gapped is also insufficient without
the cross correction. With the same vacuum and retained space, set

renormalization construction; they specify what such a construction must actually verify.

29 Exact spatial refinement maps and their eliminated dynamics
This section constructs maps between different spatial cutoffs and computes their compression
and discarded terms exactly. The bare Haar map and the map adapted to the true fine vacuum
have different coarse vacua. Neither compression is identified with a continuum Hamiltonian. All
calculations retain the full representation space.
29.1 Spatial geometry, gauge symmetry and Haar isometry
Fix an integer L≥ 2, an integer refinement factor r≥ 2, and a coarse spacing a> 0. The coarse
graph is the periodic cubic lattice Λc = (Z/LZ)3 and the fine graph is Λf = (Z/(rL)Z)3, of
spacing af = a/r. They describe the same physical three-torus. Each graph has three positively
oriented links and three elementary plaquettes per vertex. Write
Ec =Pc = 3L3, Ef =Pf = 3(rL)3, Xc =SU(2)Ec, Xf =SU(2)Ef,
and let µc,µf be normalized product Haar measures. Opposite orientations refer to inverse group
elements, not additional variables.
For a coarse positive link e = (x,i), its fine skeleton path is
Pe ={(rx +sˆi,i) :s = 0,...,r− 1}.
These paths are pairwise disjoint as sets of fine link variables. They may meet at vertices. In fine
integer coordinates, a direction i link belongs to the skeleton precisely when its two transverse
coordinates are multiples of r. Define the blocking map
(BU)e =Ue,1Ue,2 ···Ue,r. (29.1)
The factors are in their path order. The Haar pullback is
(Iψ)(U) =ψ(BU). (29.2)
Proposition 29.1 (Exact Haar and gauge structure). The map I : L2(Xc,µc) →L2(Xf,µf) is
an isometry. Its adjoint is Haar conditional expectation on B:
I∗F (v) = Eµf [F|BU =v].
It intertwines the fine gauge action with its restriction to the coarse vertices. In particular it
maps the full coarse gauge-invariant Hilbert space into the full fine gauge-invariant Hilbert space.
No center-flux sector is removed.
Proof. For each disjoint skeleton path, replace its last variable by its ordered product ve. Given
the other r− 1 variables, the last is (Ue,1 ···Ue,r−1)−1ve. Haar invariance makes this a smooth
global product-coordinate change with Jacobian one. Together with all unused fine links, these
remaining coordinates form Z =SU(2)Ef−Ec, and
Xf ≃Xc ×Z, dµf =dµcdµZ. (29.3)
Consequently B∗µf =µc, proving the isometry and adjoint.
Under a fine vertex gauge transformation q, all intermediate endpoint factors on a path cancel,
leaving
B(q·U)(x,i) =qrx(BU)(x,i)q−1 r(x+ˆi).
Every coarse gauge transformation can be extended to the fine vertices. This proves equivariance
and the assertion about the physical subspaces.

identity just proved. Completeness in RanI shows that this range and its orthogonal complement
are spectral invariant for Df. Equivalently the identity e−tDfI = Ie−rtDc holds on the entire
Hilbert space. Closedness gives the operator-domain intertwining.
Every elementary fine plaquette has at least two links outside the skeleton. In an i,j plaquette,
its two i links have transverse j coordinates differing by one; they cannot both be multiples of
r≥ 2. The two j links give a second unused link by the same argument. Such variables are
absent from BU and are independent Haar variables under (29.3). Integration over any one of
them yields
Eµf [fp |B] = 0, Eµf [f 2 p |B] = 1 4 .
The first identity is the vanishing Haar integral of a fundamental matrix coefficient. The second
is
∫
(TrU/2)2 dU = 1/4, since the real fundamental character has squared Haar norm one.
Two distinct elementary fine plaquettes share at most one unoriented link when rL≥ 4. In
different coordinate planes their common edges can lie on only one unit line segment; in the
same plane two distinct unit squares share at most one edge. The periodic identification at side
length at least four creates no additional coincidences between these unit squares. Since each
plaquette has at least two unused links, for p̸= q there is an unused link belonging to p but not
q. Integrating it proves
Eµf [fpfq |B] = 0.
The conditional mean and second moment of Wf −Pf = −∑ pfp are consequently 0 and Pf/4.
This proves (29.6)–(29.7). The reducing electric subspace and these identities give (29.8)–(29.10).
Finally Wf, the gauge projectors and Df preserve the physical spaces, so restriction does not
change any of the computations.
The magnetic interaction is thus erased by the compressed bare expectation, while the coupling
to the discarded space has the nonzero exact norm
∥Q0HfI∥ = vf

No exact interacting eigenvector of Hf can lie entirely in RanI: if HfIψ = EIψ, its Q0

The compressed electric coefficient is rκf = r2g2 f/(2a). Matching it to an unmodified coarse
coefficient g2 c/(2a) by compression alone would require g2 c = r2g2 f. This is not a renormalization-
group law: the full eliminated dynamics can also alter the effective kinetic operator, as the
nonzero discarded term already shows.

29.5 Exact finite-scale consistency
Consider three aligned nested spatial lattices c,m,f with blocking maps Bcm and Bmf. Ordered
products give Bcf = Bcm ◦Bmf exactly. Start with one fine-vacuum measure νf, and define
νm = (Bmf)∗νf and νc = (Bcm)∗νm. Their positive square-root Haar densities hf,hm,hc give
maps of the form (29.15), and direct cancellation proves
UmfUcm =Ucf. (29.31)
The corresponding compressed forms also agree under this further compression. This consistency
is exact when all intermediate states are marginals of the same fine state. It does not assert
equality between those marginals and the separately chosen vacua of intermediate Wilson
Hamiltonians.
30 Subsequential equal-time spatial holonomy construction
There is an unconditional compactness construction for spatial holonomies. It is useful to specify
exactly what it produces and which physical conclusions it does not supply.
Fix a physical three-torus with initial spacing a0 and initial side length L0 ≥ 2. Choose integers
rk ≥ 2, set Rk = r1 ···rk, and let ak = a0/Rk and Lk = L0Rk. Let Bjk : Xk → Xj be the
aligned ordered-path blocking maps for k≥j. At each level choose any finite gk > 0 and take
the actual positive normalized ground state hk of the corresponding finite spatial Hamiltonian.
Write νk =h2 kµk.
Theorem 30.1 (Subsequential vacuum holonomy measure). There is a subsequence kℓ →∞
and probability measures ν∞ j on every fixed Xj such that
(Bj,kℓ)∗νkℓ =⇒ ν∞ j for every fixed j, (Bj,j+1)∗ν∞ j+1 =ν∞ j .
185
=== PAGE 186 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Each limiting measure is gauge invariant. These measures determine a unique gauge-invariant
probability measure ν∞ on the compact inverse-limit configuration space
X∞ ={(v0,v1,...) :Bj,j+1vj+1 =vj for every j}. (30.1)
For every continuous cylinder observable F◦πj,
∫
Fdν∞ j = lim ℓ→∞ ⟨hkℓ, (F◦Bj,kℓ)hkℓ⟩. (30.2)
The same holds for every finite product of such observables. If, in addition, gk ≥gmin > 0, every
fixed coarse Wilson loop that contains an edge exactly once satisfies
Varν∞ j (F )≥ 9 100 exp ( − 512 g4 min ) > 0. (30.3)
In particular, fixed-g refinement has an actual nontrivial gauge-invariant equal-time limit along
this subsequence.
Proof. Each Xj is a compact metric space, so its probability measures are sequentially compact
for weak convergence. This can also be proved directly by taking convergent subsequences of
the integrals against a countable dense subset of C(Xj) and extending the resulting positive
normalized functional. Apply this compactness successively at j = 0, 1,... and take a diagonal
subsequence. Continuity of the blocking maps passes Bj,j+1Bj+1,k = Bjk to the weak limits and
proves consistency. Gauge invariance passes to the limit because each gauge action is continuous
and the blocking maps are equivariant.
The space (30.1) is a closed subset of a countable product of compact metric spaces. The blocking
maps are surjective, so every coordinate projection πj is surjective. On its continuous cylinder
algebra define L(F◦πj) =
∫
Fdν∞ j . Consistency makes this definition independent of the cylinder
representation. It is positive, normalized and bounded in supremum norm. The cylinder algebra
contains constants and separates points, so its uniform closure is C(X∞). The positive-functional
representation theorem gives a unique probability measure ν∞. This proves the assertions and
the equal-time convergence. Gauge equivariance gives invariance under compatible vertex gauge
transformations. Finally, apply Corollary 29.5 to each direct blocking map Bj,kℓ. Its variance
lower bound is uniform when gkℓ ≥gmin. Both F and F 2 are continuous and bounded, so weak
convergence passes the variance inequality to the limit and proves (30.3).
The consistent limiting measures give actual weighted Hilbert isometries by pullback,
L2(Xj,ν∞ j ) → L2(Xj+1,ν∞ j+1). Their cylinder subspaces are dense in L2(X∞,ν∞), and the
constant function is the normalized vacuum vector for this equal-time probability representation.
The construction is on generalized spatial holonomies. The unrestricted compactness argument
supplies no positive smooth limiting Haar density and by itself does not exclude singular
finite-level limits. If gk ≥ gmin, the inherited one-link ratios instead bound every fixed-level
limiting density between R∗(gmin)−2Ej and R∗(gmin)2Ej. To see this, change the Ej coarse
coordinates one at a time, normalize the resulting global density-ratio bound, and pass the two
measure inequalities to the weak limit. Even then no derivative bound has been proved, so the
smooth density formulas cannot simply be differentiated after taking the limit.
This theorem supplies actual subsequential equal-time vacuum moments, and nonzero coarse-loop
variance when the couplings stay bounded away from zero. For unrestricted weak-coupling
sequences gk → 0, the displayed lower bound degenerates and does not establish continuum
nontriviality. The theorem does not prove that different subsequences give the same state or
that renormalized local fields exist. It does not construct a strongly continuous physical time
semigroup on the limiting Hilbert space, a continuum Hamiltonian, Euclidean rotation symmetry,
186
=== PAGE 187 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
an infinite-volume limit, or a positive continuum spectral gap. Along the intended weak-coupling
sequence, compactness and the finite-volume positive densities do not supply a uniform positive
variance or a uniform coercive spectral estimate after spatial refinement.
The precise remaining spectral task is to control the full vacuum-complement energy, including
the covariance residual and discarded sector, under compatible spatial limits and renormalized
observables. The equal-time compactness construction does not supply those estimates. It can
be combined with local conditional vacuum estimates, but it cannot replace their missing global
and dynamical control.
31 Local physical states, exact loop energies, and spectral tight-
ness
The results here concern the actual interacting vacuum of the spatial SU(2) Hamiltonian. They
provide volume-independent bounds on energies and time correlations of specified physical states.
They also prove a restricted failure of spectral tightness under spatial refinement at fixed coupling.
Neither positive spectral weight at some positive energies nor a finite-state variational energy is
a lower bound on the entire physical spectrum.

31.4 Obstruction to bare fixed-coupling spatial refinement

zero. It also does not exclude operator mixing, smoothing, or other renormalization constructions.
The physical times in (31.23) are those of (31.1); a new scale-dependent redefinition of time
would be a different construction.

observable by Gk = ZkFk + ckI, where Zk ̸= 0 and ck are arbitrary scalars. After actual-vacuum
centering, its state is Zk(Fk−νkFk)hk. Its normalized spectral measure and normalized connected
time correlation are exactly unchanged. Therefore such multiplicative normalization and identity
subtraction cannot turn the non-tight family in Proposition 31.5 into a tight, nontrivial normalized
family.

31.6 Exact scale covariance and a dimensionful mass value
Proposition 31.8 (Scale covariance of the full physical spectrum). Under the canonical identifi-
cation of the same finite graph’s Haar Hilbert spaces,
Ha,L,g = 1 aH1,L,g, ha,L,g =h1,L,g, ∆a,L,g = 1 a∆1,L,g. (31.25)
Changing every spatial and temporal length by a common constant s> 0 leaves all dimensionless
lattice data unchanged and divides every energy by s.
Proof. Both coefficients in (31.1) contain the same factor a−1, while D,W, Haar measure and
the gauge constraints depend on the graph, not on the assigned physical length. The spectral
theorem and positive normalized ground-state uniqueness prove all identities. In particular
e−tKsa,L,g =e−(t/s)Ka,L,g.
Consequently dimensionless bare data alone cannot select one numerical mass in a specified
physical unit. If a continuum construction with a mass M and an inverse-length reference scale
Λ were established, a common dilation would replace them by M/s and Λ/s while preserving
M/Λ. Specifying a reference scale removes this dimensionful ambiguity; it does not determine
the dimensionless ratio. Reference-length scale setting in SU(2) gauge theory is discussed, for
example, by Sommer, arXiv:hep-lat/9310022. No value of the unknown continuum ratio is
inferred here, and this dimensional observation is separate from proving a positive continuum
gap.

representations and all spectator links are retained.

32.5 Sharpness and a precise limit of the local inputs
The powers in the Fisher lower bounds cannot be improved using only an upper bound on the
one-link electric energy. To see this within the physical Hilbert space, fix a simple loop and
consider the smooth gauge-invariant wavefunction
hβ =Z−1/2 β eβF/2.
The Haar marginal of F is the usual one-link trace marginal, since a link occurring once can be
changed to the full loop holonomy. The variational identities proved above therefore give, for
each link in the loop,
⟨hβ,Cehβ⟩ = 3βrβ 16 ≤ 3β 16 , Eβ(1−F 2) = 3rβ β ≤ 3 β.
The same decreasing Gamma tilt, now with the increasing function z2, gives
VarβF≤ Eβ(1−F )2 ≤ 15 4β2 .
Choosing β = 16M/3 gives electric energy at most M and variance at most 135/(1024M 2). Thus
no universal lower variance bound with a slower decay than M−2 can hold for this class. Likewise
the order M−1 for ν(1 −F 2) is optimal for this class. These comparison states are not asserted
to be the interacting Wilson-Hamiltonian vacuum.
There is also a fully explicit reason why the electric bound and the chosen plaquette’s mean
bound alone do not provide the missing O(s2) upper variance. For s∈ (0, 1], set β = 8/s,
w =s/4, and let

For a chosen plaquette F, this is a positive smooth gauge-invariant wavefunction on the same
configuration space. Fisher information is convex: pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives

does not assert the mean bound for every other plaquette. It isolates exactly why additional
ground-state information is needed for that inference. The bounded nonlinear renormalization
developed in the following analysis uses a different consequence of Lemma 32.1 and does not
require such a fourth moment estimate.

strongly continuous semigroup acting on a unit vector has correlation tending to one as t↓ 0,
so such a norm-preserving limiting state is impossible for this family. The proof uses an actual
positive escaping spectral weight; it does not infer non-tightness merely from a divergent mean
or upper bound.
Exact scope. The norm construction is unconditional for the stated SU(2) vacuum. It is a
bounded nonlinear renormalization of a shrinking elementary plaquette. The spectral theorem
shows why it cannot be promoted to the requested four-dimensional local state merely because its
norm stays nonzero. This does not exclude renormalized observables with appropriate space-time
smearing, other operator mixing, or a continuum theory with a mass gap. It does not prove that
the physical mass gap closes. The escaping energies concern this ultraviolet state family, not the
lowest energy in the full vacuum complement.
Multiplicative rescaling and additive identity subtraction leave the normalized spectral measures
of this family unchanged. Thus they cannot repair (33.8). A construction that does repair it
must supply additional physical-time and locality control for a different family of states.
Reproduction. The standard-library script certify_bounded_states.py checks every ratio-
nal constant above, the polynomial inequalities, the complete interval-probability accounting,
and the first/second moment spectral-weight calculation. It records exact fractions and outward
decimal intervals. These are certified bounds on the actual Hamiltonian states, not measured
masses or numerical samples of the unknown vacuum.
34 Infinite-volume dynamics at fixed spatial cutoff
Fix the spatial spacing a> 0 and the coupling g > 0 throughout this section. The physical side
length aL tends to infinity, while the spatial ultraviolet cutoff remains a. We construct the limit
from the actual finite periodic Hamiltonian vacua. The Hilbert space and time semigroup are
reconstructed from all positive-time histories, so the argument does not assume that an equal-time
limit is already cyclic or that a Markov property survives the limit. The reflection-positive
construction follows the Osterwalder–Schrader framework [8, 9]; the time-continuity and domain
estimates needed here are proved directly for this lattice Hamiltonian.

34.6 Extent of the fixed-cutoff construction
The physical spatial size tends to infinity in this construction: aLn →∞. At each fixed a,g, it
supplies a stationary infinite-volume state, all-time Euclidean and real-time local correlations, a
nonnegative selfadjoint physical Hamiltonian, a dense operator core, exact local energies and
nontrivial time-dependent gauge-invariant states. It is a vacuum representation on Rtime ×aZ3.
The subsequence can depend on a and g. No uniqueness of phase, clustering, or full vacuum-
complement spectral gap has been proved. A continuum claim would require compatible control
as a↓ 0 and the coupling and local observables are renormalized. The local ratio and energy
constants displayed here are finite at fixed a,g but do not provide those uniform weak-coupling
estimates. In particular, neither a positive first spectral moment nor a nonzero amount of positive-
energy weight excludes other spectral weight arbitrarily close to zero. No exact continuum mass
is determined by the construction.

35 Conditional projection angles and collective physical-gap
criteria
Nonzero local states and a collective spectral lower bound are different requirements. This section
supplies a sufficient collective estimate in terms of the actual vacuum’s conditional projection
angles. It also gives an overlapping-block hierarchy for which summable losses suffice. The
projection argument is part of the established subspace-angle framework [40]; conditional variance
factorization is likewise an established framework [38]. All constants and implications used here
are proved below. Neither reference supplies the unverified SU(2) weak-coupling angles.
35.1 The actual measure, physical sector, and conditional blocks
On a finite periodic spatial lattice, write

35.4 Complete two-block dependence estimates
Fix exterior links z outside A∪B, write x = UA\B and y = UB\A, and integrate the overlap

Indeed, after removing the common exterior projection, PAPB is precisely the conditional-
expectation operator from centered x-functions to centered y-functions. It acts fiber by fiber
over z; its norm is the essential supremum of these fiber norms. Taking input functions already
in ranPB attains the same operator norm, so this is an equality, not just a correlation bound for
a selected list of observables.

To prove (35.14), subtract one from the kernel when acting on a centered function, then apply
Cauchy–Schwarz and integrate. Equation (35.15) follows immediately. For (35.16), write the joint
measure as δpx zpy z + (1 −δ)~pz. The remainder has the same marginals; its conditional-expectation
operator is an L2 contraction by Jensen’s inequality. On centered functions the independent part
vanishes, proving the bound.
These tests concern every centered function of the exclusive blocks. A finite table of Wilson-
loop covariances gives no upper bound on (35.13) unless the omitted subspace is also bounded.
Similarly, weak correlation of selected observables, a fitted correlation length, or a sampling
synchronization rate does not certify the required operator norm. For the quantum Hamiltonian,
h2dµ must not be replaced by the four-dimensional classical Wilson density or by a product of
local plaquette factors.

These inequalities do not construct a spatial continuum state or its time correlations. They specify

For the actual SU(2) vacuum the analytic block seeds (35.5) are available, and the improved

missing estimate; it is not an application of that criterion to an unconstructed SU(2) continuum.

36 Uniform Gram control and a physical-time obstruction for
finite operator mixing
This section gives a quantitative result for a specified family of renormalized point-plaquette
observables in the actual SU(2) Hamiltonian vacuum. It treats every complex, cutoff-dependent
linear combination of a fixed polynomial basis at once, and then extends the certificate to
linear combinations on edge-disjoint elementary plaquettes. It does not concern arbitrary local
composite operators, cross-products between different plaquettes, or overlapping link supports.
It gives necessary resource bounds for the specified averages, not a sufficient construction of
physical-scale smeared fields.

explicitly specified class of point operators in the actual interacting vacuum. The constants
are uniform in weak coupling and spatial volume. The result does not show that the physical
gap closes, does not exclude finite-energy states outside this family, and does not exclude a
continuum theory. It says that any successful repair must leave the fixed-degree polynomial family,
for example through physical-scale smearing, different local variables, or increasing operator
complexity. None of those alternatives is proved sufficient by this theorem.

37.5 Why the same pointwise argument stops at closed sheets
Select all L2 xy-plaquettes in one periodic xy-plane. Every selected link is shared twice and
the graph has no anchor, so λ = 0. This is not just a defect of the graph estimate: a positive
pointwise comparison to the sum of individual gradient energies is false for this family.
Set θ = 2π/L2 and choose diagonal link matrices in the plane:
Ux(x,y) =e−iθyσ3,
Uy(x,y) =I (y <L− 1), Uy(x,L− 1) =eiθLxσ3.
All other links may be set to I. Periodicity and eiθL2σ3 = I give Up = eiθσ3 for every selected
plaquette. Put s = 1 − cosθ∈ (0, 1]. Then every selected Yp = (1 −Fp)/s equals one, so it lies
strictly inside the favorable interval used in the single-plaquette proof, and Gp = 1/2.
For b = 1, 2, all link derivatives of these traces vanish at this diagonal configuration. For b = 3, the
two incident plaquettes have opposite orientation at a shared link and the same trace derivative
magnitude. Their G derivatives cancel because their Fp values are equal. Therefore

The ratio of these two continuous functions is arbitrarily small in an open neighborhood of
this configuration. That neighborhood can be chosen inside the same favorable Y interval.
Since the actual finite-volume vacuum density h2 is strictly positive, every such nonempty open
neighborhood has positive ν measure. Thus no strictly positive pointwise comparison constant
can hold almost everywhere, even on this favorable event.
This does not disprove a lower bound after integration against the actual vacuum. Such a bound
would need additional information about the joint vacuum law or a different collective argument.
At L = 2, s = 1, every matrix entry in this example lies in Q + iQ; the companion checker verifies
all link derivatives and cancellations exactly, with ∑ p ΓGp = 1/4.
Scope. The positive estimate uses an explicit incidence condition and the actual vacuum
single-plaquette inputs. It does not cover arbitrary three- or four-plaquette link multiplicities,
cross-products between different plaquettes, all physical operators, or a continuum mass gap.
The closed-sheet example excludes a proposed pointwise extension, not a continuum construction
or an integrated spectral inequality.

conditions. The result concerns the specified plaquette-state family; it is not a lower bound on

38.6 Certified calculations and scope
The checker constructs every actual torus link incidence, verifies the private counts and higher
multiplicities, and verifies the elimination order and integer inverse R. Positive definiteness is
checked by exact rational LDL∗ pivots. Bisection encloses the smallest retained-matrix eigenvalue,
the largest eigenvalue of R∗R, and the weighted roots, without floating-point arithmetic. Every
reported decimal is rounded outward. The companion JSON records matrices, pivots, exact
rational endpoints, and source hashes; the CSV contains the derived constants.
For the two central examples, the resulting intervals are

and the thirteen-face ansatz has aq/v > 0.0000091713776547918. These are selected-family
bounds, not numerical approximations to the global mass gap.
The method still does not certify a closed unanchored periodic sheet: it has no free link, the
retained matrix has a constant kernel vector, and elimination cannot begin. The previously
established closed-sheet cancellation remains relevant. This section broadens the admissible
overlapping families; it neither constructs nonzero continuum states nor supplies a uniform gap
on the full physical vacuum complement. The ingredients are elementary norm inequalities and
finite incidence calculations. Historical priority for this application has not been established.
39 Sharp electric-cutoff obstruction for Wilson-loop expectations
This section gives a necessary test for an approximation made by retaining only SU(2) electric
representations j≤J. It does not assume that the truncated state approximates the vacuum,
and it allows arbitrary entanglement with the rest of the lattice. The test is a sharp bound on
the original Wilson-loop observable, followed by an explicit consequence of the actual-vacuum
plaquette estimate.
The underlying ingredients are standard SU(2) harmonic analysis and orthogonal-polynomial
recurrences. The known difficulty of fixed electric cutoffs at weak coupling is discussed in
[41, 42, 43]. The calculation below provides a self-contained sharp observable bound and an
explicit volume-independent application. Historical priority for that combined formulation has
not been established.

Proof. Write ξ for all spectator links. At fixed ξ, the loop holonomy is A(ξ)U±1 e B(ξ). Left

For an elementary plaquette, replace U in (39.3) by Up. The resulting wavefunction ΦJ = ϕJ(Up)
is gauge invariant because each character is a class function. Its norm is one: integration over

gives⟨ΦJ,F ΦJ⟩ =cJ. No claim that this saturator is a ground state is made.

40 Extensive relative entropy of the interacting vacuum
This section quantifies how the actual interacting vacuum probability measure differs from product
Haar measure. The entropy below is a classical relative entropy of configuration probabilities. It
is not a von Neumann entropy or an entanglement entropy of the pure vacuum state.

elliptic operator has a unique smooth positive normalized ground state h. Positivity and gauge
invariance imply that h is physical. Set K =H−E0 and dν =h2dµ.
The actual-vacuum input is Lemma 31.1.

41 Vacuum fidelity under a hard electric cutoff

vacuum plaquettes nor an approximate vacuum wavefunction.

Scope and attribution. The argument uses standard Peter–Weyl projection kernels, expo-

specialization combines those tools with the actual SU(2) vacuum input. Historical priority is not
established. These necessary conditions apply to the stated standard hard electric cutoff and the
original vacuum. They do not bound coupling-adapted mixed bases, arbitrary effective encodings,
or universal qubit counts. The fixed-fidelity condition is a different accuracy requirement from the
earlier o(g2) Wilson-observable error criterion; the numerical constants from those two criteria
should not be ranked as improvements of the same statement. No continuum mass gap is inferred.

43 The finite-torus sectors invisible to contractible loop states
There is an exact structural reason why proving ever larger contractible-plaquette certificates
does not, by itself, control the entire physical finite-torus Hilbert space. This section states that
reason as a theorem, supplies explicitly nonzero missing vectors, and distinguishes it from the
infinite-volume local-vacuum question.
43.1 Three commuting center transformations
For each spatial direction α = 1, 2, 3, define zα on link configurations by multiplying by −I every
positively oriented α-link whose starting coordinate obeys xα = L− 1. All other links remain
unchanged. On L2(µ) let
(Zαψ)(U) =ψ(zαU).
The Zα are commuting self-adjoint unitaries with Z2 α = I. They commute with every gauge
transformation, because the inserted sign is central, and therefore preserve the physical Hilbert
space. Each elementary plaquette contains either zero or two links crossing the relevant cut. Its
holonomy trace is unchanged. Haar measure, the link Casimirs, the magnetic potential, and the
Hamiltonian are consequently invariant:
[Zα,H] = [Zα,K] = 0. (43.1)
Uniqueness and positivity of the full vacuum imply Zαh = h: applying Zα gives another
normalizedpositivegroundstate. Thisusesthefinitelatticeonlyanddoesnotassumespontaneous
symmetry breaking or its absence in an infinite system.
For χ∈{0, 1}3, define
Pχ = 1 8 ∑ b∈{0,1}3 (−1)χ·bZb1 1 Zb2 2 Zb3 3 . (43.2)

Finite character orthogonality proves that these are pairwise orthogonal projectors summing to
the identity. On the physical Hilbert space,
Hphys =

Hχ, Hχ =PχHphys, h∈H0. (43.3)
All eight subspaces reduce K.
For an oriented closed lattice loop C, a cut transformation changes its fundamental trace by
ZαFC = (−1)wα(C)FC, (43.4)
where wα(C) is its winding number modulo two in direction α. Reversed crossings have the same
sign modulo two. In particular, every contractible loop is neutral.
Theorem 43.1 (Contractible observables miss seven physical sectors). Let Actr be the algebra
generated by multiplication by contractible Wilson-loop traces, bounded functions of those traces,
and the identity. Then
Actrh⊂H0. (43.5)
The same inclusion holds if one also applies bounded spectral functions of K or forms finite
products of such functions with the specified observables. Every nontrivial Hχ contains an explicit
nonzero smooth gauge-invariant vector orthogonal to this entire closure. Consequently, arbitrary
polynomial degree, spatial support growth, operator mixing, and physical-energy filtering within
this neutral family cannot make it dense in the full physical vacuum complement on a finite torus.
Proof. Every generating observable commutes with all Zα, and the same is true of bounded
functions of K by (43.1). Since h is neutral, every generated vector lies in the closed subspace
H0.
At the origin choose the three straight fundamental winding loops C1,C2,C3, each of length L,
and write their based holonomies as P1,P2,P3. For each nonzero χ, concatenate the loops with
χα = 1 in the fixed order 1, 2, 3, and set
Fχ = 1 2 Tr(Pχ1 1 Pχ2 2 Pχ3 3 ), ψχ =Fχh. (43.6)
All factors are based at the origin, so the product trace is gauge invariant. The concatenated loop
contains L|χ| distinct link variables, each exactly once, even though its base vertex is revisited.
Equation (43.4) gives Zαψχ = (−1)χαψχ. At the identity configuration Fχ = 1; continuity and
h > 0 imply ψχ ̸= 0. Distinct characters give mutually orthogonal vectors, and all seven are
orthogonal toH0.

43.3 The exact target for a global finite-torus gap
The finite-lattice operator has compact resolvent, and its vacuum is unique. Define
m0 = inf spec(K|H0∩h⊥), mχ = inf spec(K|Hχ) (χ̸= 0).
Each is positive for fixed finite parameters, and the full physical gap is exactly
mphys = min
(
m0, min χ̸=0 mχ
)
. (43.9)
Consequently a global inequality on the whole physical vacuum complement is equivalent to the
corresponding inequality in all eight blocks, with the vacuum removed from the neutral block.
The contractible-loop estimates supply no charged-block lower bound. Inclusion in the neutral
block also does not, by itself, prove completeness or a lower gap throughout that block.
There is an exact information-theoretic illustration of the distinction. At fixed parameters and
any ϵ> 0, define
~Kϵ =K + ∑
χ̸=0
(ϵ−mχ)Pχ.
This is a self-adjoint nonnegative operator with the same unique vacuum and the same neutral
restriction as K. Its full gap is min(m0,ϵ). All vacuum correlations made from neutral bounded
observables and physical-time evolution are exactly the same as for K, since they never leave
H0. Thus even exact knowledge of those correlations alone cannot determine the gap in sectors
invisible to them. This modified operator contains nonlocal sector projectors and is not asserted
to be the Wilson Hamiltonian or a new local gauge theory. It is a logical counterexample to an
inference from the restricted data, not a counterexample to a Yang–Mills gap.

43.4 Passage from finite-torus sectors to infinite volume
The preceding statements concern the full gauge-invariant Hilbert space on a periodic finite
spatial lattice. A winding loop extends around the entire torus. When the physical torus grows
without bound, these vectors need not survive as states in the vacuum representation generated
by bounded-region local observables. The local infinite-volume vacuum theory may therefore ask
for a gap in a different, smaller representation. The finite-torus sector obstruction does not rule
out that construction or its mass gap.
It does identify a precise missing condition for the stronger route posed here: a certificate for the
full finite-torus physical complement must control the charged blocks as well as the neutral one.
If the intended target is instead the local infinite-volume vacuum representation, the construction
must specify that representation, establish its nontrivial local states and time correlations, and
prove the required inequality on a dense form core there. Neither an overlap certificate nor a
sector decomposition supplies these continuum steps.
Attribution boundary. Electric center sectors and winding-loop charges are established
lattice-gauge structures. No historical novelty is claimed for the decomposition. The application
here makes the missing blocks in the proposed certificate explicit and adds the quantitative
one-link norm estimate (43.7). The companion checker certifies the finite character and incidence
arithmetic; the operator and integration-by-parts assertions are proved above.
44 Finite-matrix certification of the full physical spectrum
The following construction controls every omitted electric representation. Unlike a Gram
inequality on a selected operator family, it is an eigenvalue enclosure for the entire gauge-
invariant Hilbert space of a fixed spatial lattice. Its ingredients are standard operator comparison,
min–max, and Schur-complement methods; the specialization below makes their required inputs
and representation tails explicit for the Wilson Hamiltonian. Related rigorous Feshbach–Schur
discretization methods are described in [44, 39]. No historical priority for the general spectral
method is claimed.

Proof. Consider the self-adjoint operator

44.3 An equivalent Schur test and finite-arithmetic error bounds
For any real z <τm, every omitted electric denominator is positive. The finite Schur matrix is
Sm(z) =A−zI−B(κDh −zI)−1B∗. (44.9)
All terms here are finite. Block completion of squares, together with positivity of the omitted
electric block, shows that if Sm(z) has at most one strictly negative eigenvalue, then H has at
most one eigenvalue below z. If also u0 <z, it follows that E1 ≥z and the full gap is at least
z−u0. For rational matrices, exact LDL∗ inertia is one way to check this; algebraic or interval
enclosures give the same rigorous test. Zero pivots must be treated by an exact pivoting or
Sturm rule, not silently rounded away.
Suppose a Hermitian numerical matrix ˆM has a rigorously bounded residual ∥Mm − ˆM∥≤ϵM.
Then µ1 ≥λ1( ˆM) −ϵM. Entrywise interval bounds imply such a residual, for example through
the largest absolute row sum of a symmetric entrywise error bound. Any error in the finite
eigenvalue calculation must be included as well. The analytic representation remainder is already
controlled by the theorem; it is separate from this finite-arithmetic error.

At a fixed finite lattice and fixed a,s> 0, this is an eventually successful finite procedure when the
parameters are rational or supplied with arbitrarily refinable certified enclosures. The operator
estimates themselves hold for all real a,s > 0. Completeness does not assume an unproved

βm is bounded uniformly in m. The right side of (44.12) therefore converges to E1 −E0 > 0.
With increasing finite precision, a strict positive certificate is eventually obtained. This proves
completeness of the procedure at fixed parameters; it does not give a small computational budget.
Why this does not finish the continuum step. The projection must contain the complete
physical electric space, not only a small chosen operator basis. Its dimension grows quickly
with volume and electric threshold. A scalar test using the unconditional bound (44.10) has an
extensive coupling scale 4Np/(sa). Even the requirement z <τm puts the electric cutoff above
the absolute energy threshold being tested. The vacuum energy cannot simply be subtracted
from D using an unknown or truncated vacuum. No estimate here proves that the resulting
positive lower gap remains bounded away from zero as a→ 0, s→ 0, and physical volume grows.
Proving that property requires actual bounds along such a sequence, as well as a compatible
nontrivial continuum construction.
A full three-dimensional scalar check. There is a simple nontruncated check on the periodic
L = 2 lattice. It has Np = 24. Every nonconstant physical electric eigenstate has D≥ 3/2: an
invariant spin network with a nonzero edge cannot have a vertex of support degree one, so its
support contains at least a two-edge cycle; each nonzero spin contributes at least 3/4. A straight
two-link winding loop attains D = 3/2. Thus E1 ≥ 3s/(4a) by V ≥ 0, while the constant Haar
trial gives E0 ≤ 96/(sa). At s = 16 this certifies
E1 −E0 ≥ 6 a (44.13)
on the full physical complement, with every representation and sector included. This is a strong-
coupling example, not a weak-coupling or continuum result. The following separate one-plaquette
calculation illustrates much tighter spectral enclosures in a smaller model.
45 Certified infinite-representation one-plaquette benchmark
This section computes rigorous spectral intervals for a single plaquette graph: four distinct links
forming one cycle, gauge invariance at all four vertices, and no external charges. It is a reduced
model, not a three-dimensional spatial box or a four-dimensional continuum theory. Its purpose
is to demonstrate a complete physical-spectrum calculation in which the infinite electric tail is
