SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
certified. The single-plaquette character and Mathieu descriptions have established precedents,
including [45]; the numerical bounds below are independently calculated in the normalization
stated here.
45.1 The exact infinite physical Jacobi matrix
Gauge invariance reduces the physical Hilbert space to class functions of the plaquette holonomy.
Its complete orthonormal basis is en(U) = χn/2(U), n = 0, 1,.... All four links carry the same
spin, so Den = n(n + 2)en. The fundamental character recurrence gives Fen = (en+1 + en−1)/2,
with e−1 = 0. Hence the dimensionless operator Js =aH has entries
(Js)nn = s 2n(n + 2) + 4 s, (Js)n,n+1 = (Js)n+1,n =−2 s. (45.1)
It is self-adjoint on the electric domain and has compact resolvent, because its diagonal grows
quadratically and its remaining terms are bounded. These are all physical states of this graph,
not just a chosen variational operator family.

The companion checker uses only Python’s standard library. At a rational spectral test point

The number of negative eigenvalues is the number of sign changes in P0,P1,..., with zero entries

The calculation starts with N = max{16,⌈2/s⌉} and doubles N only if necessary to reduce the
final gap interval width below 10−12. It uses 64 exact bisections per finite eigenvalue in the
listed parameter range. The interval width includes both the finite bisection error and the entire
analytic representation remainder.

Part VI
Continuum construction and spectral passage
46 A physical-scale block criterion and an exact obstruction to
naive blocking
The preceding comparison theorems concern microscopic links or links remaining after a specified
gauge fixing. A continuum application needs decay measured in physical distance. This section
proves an explicit sufficient criterion at a fixed physical block scale, including all support and
normalization constants. It then gives a compact-group example in which replacing individual
variables by large blocks makes a total-variation comparison fail, even though the underlying
correlations have finite range. These results clarify what a successful block construction would
have to improve.
The comparison framework is classical; generalized block formulations are developed by Rebeschini
and van Handel [11]. The finite proof below is included to specify the constants and hypotheses
used here. The criterion is not asserted to hold for the four-dimensional Wilson theory along a
continuum trajectory.

The example does not disprove a multiscale Yang–Mills argument. It rules out the general
inference that large blocks must have a small whole-block total-variation influence merely
because the original local model mixes well. Overlapping update schemes, weighted transport
costs, observables adapted to interior regions, and exact renormalized effective interactions can
behave differently. Each requires its own quantitative estimate rather than the replacement of a
microscopic variable by a large tuple with no further analysis.

the full block variable, uniformly over all exterior configurations. All omitted interactions have

local plaquette form.
A scalar bound on the global partition function is also insufficient for (PB.20). The proposition
needs control of conditional densities, up to constants independent of the variable u. Conversely,
exterior-dependent additive constants in ri cancel from the conditional normalization and need
not be bounded. This is why the oscillation, rather than an arbitrary absolute action offset, is
the appropriate error quantity.
46.7 What would be needed for a continuum application
Theorem PB.4 replaces a desired infinite-distance correlation estimate by a local conditional-
kernel inequality at a specified physical scale. For each fixed cutoff it is a statement about
finitely many block variables and boundary fields. It is not one finite computation whose validity
automatically extends to all cutoffs.
The missing model-specific task is to construct exact block or effective variables for the relevant
continuum trajectory and prove, with constants independent of a,
sup
i
∑
j
C(a) ij ≤q < 1, (PB.24)
together with the required observable bounds. Even in the finite-range Wilson action, the
boundary configurations in these suprema range over compact sets of increasing dimension. A
proof at a list of couplings, on a finite boundary grid, or at one block size does not establish
(PB.24). An interval computation would require a valid finite reduction with controlled covering
error, and a separate argument giving uniformity over the unbounded cutoff sequence.
The microscopic transport estimate in the companion section controls fields of radius bounded
by a fixed constant. Its four-dimensional single-link range β < 2/9 therefore supplies no direct
estimate on a trajectory with β(a) →∞. A forest-gauge comparison may improve a fixed-spacing
constant, but any such constant remains separate from (PB.24). A gauge transformation is not
an ultraviolet renormalization step; it does not by itself give a controlled effective action at fixed
physical resolution.
For an exact renormalization map, three additional points matter. First, the effective conditional
law must actually equal the pushforward or marginal law being studied, including all generated
interactions. Second, the mapped observables and their supports must be followed through the
map. Third, any approximation error must be summable or otherwise controlled over all scales.
If a coarse observable is nonlocal in the fine variables, its nominal coarse label is not proof of
physical locality. If the effective state space has constraints, a product-space comparison theorem
needs an appropriate representation or a different update construction.
Once the actual block condition, renormalized moment bounds, a nonzero limiting reflected norm,
and the required reconstruction properties have all been proved, (PB.11) or (PB.15) supplies
physical-distance decay with an explicit positive exponent. The spectral criteria elsewhere in the
manuscript can then be applied to a total family of physical states. Neither a Gibbs-sampler
update count nor the existence of the block comparison theorem is substituted for physical
Euclidean time.
The completed result of this section is therefore precise: a sufficient physical-scale criterion, its
full proof with constants, and a solvable obstruction to one naive way of trying to satisfy it. The
258
=== PAGE 259 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
required estimate (PB.24) for four-dimensional Yang–Mills at weak coupling is not established
here.
47 Continuumconstruction: weak-couplingcontrol, compactness
and exact elimination
This section develops three parts of a possible continuum argument that can be proved without
assuming the desired continuum theory. The first is an estimate for the actual Wilson measure
at weak bare coupling: on ordinary periodic four-dimensional boxes, the mean plaquette defect
is bounded uniformly in volume by a constant times (1 + logβ)/β. The second is a collection
of compactness criteria that state precisely which uniform bounds would produce limits of
renormalized observables. The third is an exact calculation of coarse-graining and its errors in
models where every integration can be justified.
These results have different logical roles. The Wilson estimate is unconditional in its displayed
finite-lattice setting. The compactness results are theorems about probability laws; their hy-
potheses must be verified for the chosen Yang–Mills observables. Gaussian elimination is exact
for Gaussian measures, and the nonlinear extensions retain explicit integrability assumptions.
Keeping these roles visible makes it possible to identify a failed estimate instead of transferring a
conclusion from one model to another.
The methods are standard probability, compact Lie group geometry and finite-dimensional
integration, written out here with the constants and limiting operations required by this in-
vestigation. Bałaban’s four-dimensional small-field effective-action work supplies an important
constructive context [13]; the present elementary estimates do not reproduce that construction.
Chatterjee’s work obtains substantially more precise leading free-energy information in specified
lattice regimes [46]. Neither reference is used as an unstated premise of the proofs below.
47.1 A volume-uniform weak-coupling estimate for the Wilson action
Let G be a connected compact Lie group of positive dimension dG, with normalized Haar measure
h. Fix a faithful smooth unitary representation ρ :G→U(N). Its normalized real character is
w(g) = 1 N Re Trρ(g).
For a complex N×N matrix define the normalized Hilbert–Schmidt norm
∥A∥2 ∗ = 1 N Tr(A∗A).

Choose a bi-invariant Riemannian metric on G. Such a metric is obtained by averaging any inner

give a finite constant Lρ satisfying

norm of its matrix increment by M times the geodesic length. The representation takes values in
a finite-dimensional Euclidean matrix space, so the ordinary fundamental theorem of calculus
applies to that path. One can take Lρ =M.
There are constants ε0 ∈ (0, 1] and cG ∈ (0, 1] such that
h{g : distG(g,e)≤ε}≥cGεdG (0<ε≤ε0).
Here is the local reason. The exponential map is a diffeomorphism on a sufficiently small Lie

value at the origin is positive. On a smaller closed ball that density has a positive minimum.
The integral over the Euclidean ball is therefore at least a positive constant times its radius to
the power dG. The Riemannian and coordinate distances agree to first order and are uniformly
comparable on this smaller neighborhood. Decreasing the constant, and replacing it by its
minimum with one, gives the displayed estimate. Neither cG nor ε0 depends on a lattice volume.

Corollary CT.1a (fixed-spacing Gibbs limits at weak coupling). For each fixed β > 0,
periodic Wilson measures have subsequences converging locally weakly to infinite-volume Gibbs
measures on GE(Z4). These limits are invariant under translations and the coordinate symmetries
of the lattice. If β≥ε−2 0 , every such limit µβ satisfies
Eµβ[1−w(Up)]≤ Kρ − 2 3 logcG + dG 3 logβ β .
Uniqueness at these large values of β is not asserted.
Proof. Extend a periodic configuration periodically to all links of Z4. Its law is a probability
measure on the countable product of the compact metrizable space G. That product is compact
and metrizable, for example by a weighted sum of bounded coordinate metrics. Its probability
laws are therefore tight, and a sequence of periods L→∞ has a weakly convergent subsequence.
To verify the Gibbs property, fix a finite link set Λ, a continuous function F depending on its
links, and a continuous cylinder function H depending on a finite set of links outside Λ. Take
L sufficiently large that reduction modulo L is injective on the union of these supports and all
links in plaquettes meeting Λ. The torus conditional-density formula then gives
µβ,L(HF ) =µβ,L(HγΛF ),
where γΛ is the ordinary finite-volume Wilson specification on Z4. The function γΛF depends
only on a finite neighborhood of Λ and is continuous there. Indeed, its numerator and strictly
positive denominator are integrals over a compact finite product of a jointly continuous bounded
density; uniform continuity justifies continuity of the integrals, and positivity permits division.
Both sides therefore pass to the weak limit.
For each fixed finite Λ, continuous functions on GΛ determine finite measures, and continuous
cylinder functions generate the exterior Borel sigma-algebra. Applying the monotone-class
theorem first to the exterior tests and then to the interior tests extends the limiting identity to
all bounded measurable tests. This is the Dobrushin–Lanford–Ruelle conditional expectation
identity. Notice that the periodically extended finite-volume law itself was not declared a Gibbs
measure on the whole infinite lattice: its repeated coordinates create global constraints. Only
the finite local identities, valid once the quotient is injective on their supports, were passed to
the limit.
Translations and coordinate symmetries act continuously on the configuration product, with
inversion on links when an orientation is reversed. Each periodic law is invariant under these
transformations, because the action and product Haar measure are invariant. Their weak limits
inherit the same invariances. Finally, 1 −w(Up) is a continuous bounded local function. Pass
Theorem CT.1 to the convergent subsequence and let L→∞ in its coefficient. This proves the
estimate. □
The corollary removes the volume cutoff at fixed lattice spacing. It supplies actual weak-coupling
infinite-volume states and a local bound on those states. It neither removes the lattice spacing
nor proves that distinct possible Gibbs states coincide. Those are different assertions from the
compactness argument just established.
47.2 What the local-action estimate does and does not control
The preceding expectation estimate is stronger than a finite-dimensional Laplace statement
with an uncontrolled volume-dependent constant. Its coefficient after division by the number

Proof. A rectangular disk can be built by successively adjoining plaquettes along a connected

boundary segment with the other part of the plaquette boundary. Its holonomy is consequently
the product of the old boundary holonomy and a conjugate of the new plaquette holonomy or
its inverse, with the location of multiplication determined by the common base path. Induction
expresses UC as a product of A conjugated plaquette holonomies, each possibly inverted. This is
a group identity; commutativity is not used.

For fixed A, Theorem CT.1 forces the right side to zero at weak coupling. At a fixed physical

can then be of order a−4(1 + logβ(a))/β(a). No decay follows from the displayed bound along a
logarithmically growing inverse-coupling trajectory. This calculation identifies the quantifier that
changes: a bound for every fixed lattice loop does not control a family of loops whose lattice
area tends to infinity.
A second limitation comes from topology. On a periodic lattice choose one direction and a group
element g. Assign the same link value g to every link in that direction and identity to all other
links. Every plaquette holonomy is identity, because a plaquette containing that direction has
product gIg−1I. Yet a loop winding once around that periodic direction has holonomy gL, which
need not be identity. Thus a zero plaquette action does not eliminate global holonomy sectors.
The example is exact for nonabelian as well as abelian groups; only one nontrivial group element
is being used. It is not a statement that this single configuration dominates the Gibbs law. It
shows why local action control is not a global gauge-coordinate theorem.

differentiating an asymptotic expression illegally. Let F (β) = logZβ. Since S is bounded on a

47.3 Countably many observables: a genuine probability-law limit
A lattice observable can be a smeared plaquette expression, a Wilson loop, a finite product
of such quantities, or another prescribed gauge-invariant function. Before speaking about a
field-valued limit, fix a countable collection O1,O2,... and specify a real representative Xj,k
at each cutoff j. Complex observables can be replaced by their real and imaginary parts. The
laws at different cutoffs may live on completely different original configuration spaces; only their
observable vectors are compared.
Put Xj = (Xj,1,Xj,2,...), considered as a random element of RN with its product topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. A convenient complete separable metric is

convergence of the first m coordinates proves convergence in the metric. Sequential compactness
and compactness coincide in a metric space.
Thus the laws are tight. The probability compactness theorem supplies a weakly convergent
subsequence and a probability law ν on the same space. Coordinate projections are continuous,
so their finite-dimensional laws converge to the corresponding marginals of ν. Those marginals
are automatically consistent because they come from one law, rather than from unrelated choices
of subsequences.

of nonnegative expectations. □
The hypothesis can be weakened: coordinate tightness suffices for the probability-law conclusion,
and appropriate uniform integrability suffices for each chosen polynomial. Requiring all coordinate
moments is convenient when the intended object is a full correlation hierarchy. It is not a hidden
theorem that Wilson renormalizations satisfy these bounds.
This theorem makes no assertion of uniqueness of the limit. A sequence of deterministic one-
coordinate laws alternating between zero and one has all moments bounded, but has two different
subsequential limits. Establishing a universal continuum theory requires an additional uniqueness
or comparison argument. It also makes no assertion that the coordinates form a distribution on
spacetime. A countable list may satisfy no linearity relation in the test functions, no continuity
estimate, and no transformation law. Those issues are addressed by additional structure rather
than by calling the product law a quantum field.
There is a simple stability principle for algebraic relations. If a polynomial Q in finitely many
coordinates vanishes almost surely at every cutoff, then Theorem CT.4 gives
∫
Q2dν = 0, so
Q = 0 almost surely in the limit. This preserves any exact finite polynomial relation included in
the chosen coordinate representation. For approximate relations, the same conclusion follows if
E|Q(Xj)|2 → 0. Thus linearity on a countable rational test-function space can be encoded and
passed to the limit. Extending it continuously to all smooth test functions still needs a bound in
a test-function norm.

Uniform control on each compact box can be combined through a countable exhaustion, but
compatibility must be retained. One can choose restrictions of a single lattice field to nested
boxes, prove tightness in each local weaker space, and use a diagonal subsequence. Continuous
restriction maps ensure that the limiting restrictions agree. An alternative is to define a local
negative-Sobolev topology by a countable set of compactly supported cutoffs. Either construction
requires uniform estimates for the same observable normalization across boxes; independently
renormalizing each box would not automatically produce compatible restrictions.
For Yang–Mills, raw connection coordinates are gauge dependent. A use of this theorem must
say whether Xj represents a gauge-fixed field with a proved gauge treatment or a specified
gauge-invariant composite observable. The compactness theorem does not choose a gauge,
remove singular composite products, or identify the resulting distribution as curvature. These
are mathematical definitions and estimates to be supplied before invoking it.
47.5 Why bounded action is insufficient for renormalized tightness
The action estimate gives Es(Up) = O((logβ)/β), while a smooth classical expansion suggests
s(Up) is of order a4|F|2 under a suitable field convention. Multiplication by a−4 therefore
transforms the proved upper bound into O(a−4(logβ)/β), which diverges along many natural
trajectories. This calculation does not prove that a correctly renormalized energy density diverges;
it proves that the present upper bound does not control it.
The distinction survives even in one dimension of probability. Let Yn equal n with probability
n−2 and zero otherwise. Then E|Yn| = n−1 → 0, but E|Yn|2 = 1, and E|Yn|3 = n→∞. An
L1 concentration statement alone does not control higher correlations. If instead Zn is an
independent centered Gaussian with variance n−1, then Zn → 0 in every fixed finite moment,
yet √nZn has a nondegenerate limit. Choosing a normalization changes the question and its
required estimates.
For a spatial family there is an additional accumulation issue. Suppose Na bounded local
observables are averaged with weights ca,x. The exact variance is
Var
(∑
x
ca,xYa,x
)
=
∑
x,y
ca,xca,y Cov(Ya,x,Ya,y).
Bounding only diagonal variances does not estimate the double sum sharply. Perfectly correlated
variables give variance of order N 2 a for their unnormalized sum; independent variables of equal
variance give order Na. The two models have identical one-point laws. Consequently, a one-
plaquette concentration theorem cannot determine the normalization or tightness of a smeared
continuum observable. The missing covariance estimates are not a technical rephrasing of the
proved action bound.
An exact example makes this point without asymptotics. Let B be a centered variance-one
variable and put Yx = B for every site in a finite set of size N. Compare this with independent

47.7 Nonlinear elimination: an exact identity and a controlled expansion

The following bounded-interaction lemma makes one perturbative estimate fully rigorous. Its
boundedness hypothesis is deliberately explicit and is not asserted for an arbitrary polynomial
field interaction.
Proposition CT.7 (third-order control of an effective interaction). Let W be a real
random variable on a probability space with|W|≤M. For real t, define
F (t) =− log Ee−tW.

2 Var(W ) +R3(t), |R3(t)|≤ 4 3M 3|t|3.
The bound is uniform over the underlying probability law, including a conditional Gaussian law
depending on retained variables.
Proof. Boundedness permits repeated differentiation under the expectation for every real t.
Let Et denote expectation under the tilted probability proportional to e−tW. Direct quotient
differentiation gives
F′(t) = EtW, F′′(t) =− Vart(W ), F′′′(t) = Et[(W− EtW )3].
Since |W− EtW|≤ 2M, one has |F′′′(t)|≤ 8M 3. Taylor’s theorem with integral remainder gives
|R3(t)|≤ 8M 3|t|3/6 = 4 3 M 3|t|3. The first two derivatives at zero give the stated coefficients. □
For an unbounded W, the derivative identities require exponential integrability and uniform
control of the tilted centered third moment. Merely knowing all ordinary moments is insufficient
to justify a nonzero radius of convergence of its moment-generating function. The lognormal
distribution is a familiar source of this distinction, but a simpler series argument also suffices:
tails can decay faster than every inverse power while slower than every exponential. In that
situation all polynomial moments exist, whereas Eet|W| =∞ for every t> 0.
Even the bounded lemma needs a size estimate under repeated elimination. If W is a sum of V
local terms each bounded by one, the crude choice M = V gives a remainder of order V 3|t|3. It
does not yield an extensive bound proportional to V. A cluster or connected-cumulant argument
would have to exploit locality to replace that cubic volume growth. This is precisely where a
formal cumulant series can conceal the missing uniform estimate. The exact identity remains
valid, but its approximation is not automatically useful.
47.8 Accumulation over scales and why errors need a summable budget
A continuum construction typically requires a number of scale transformations tending to infinity.
An estimate that is small at each individual scale can still fail after their errors accumulate. The
following deterministic lemma describes the bookkeeping without assuming any field theory.

space, and let Rk : X → X be maps with Lipschitz constants Lk ≥ 0. Suppose exact and
approximate sequences satisfy
xk+1 =Rkxk, d(yk+1,Rkyk)≤εk.

the per-scale estimates are proved in a norm controlling the observables of interest.
The summability condition cannot be replaced by εN → 0. Take FN = ∑N k=1 k−1. Its increments
tend to zero, but the sequence diverges. Nor does a bounded total error automatically preserve a
positive lower bound: if a target squared norm starts at c> 0, a perturbation estimate of size 2c
gives no nontriviality information. To preserve positivity one needs an error budget smaller than
the known positive margin.
There is a parallel normalization issue. If each coarse-graining step rescales an observable by
zk > 0, then after N steps the factor is ∏ k<N zk. Uniform closeness of each zk to one does
not control that product. Its logarithm is ∑ k<N logzk. For example, zk = 1 + 1/(k + 1) has
product N + 1, while zk = 1 − 1/(k + 2) has product 1/(N + 1). Both factors approach one. A
construction must track these products alongside action errors, because they determine whether
observable norms survive, diverge, or vanish.
These elementary statements do not claim that a Yang–Mills renormalization map is a contraction
in a suitable norm. Such a norm, the map, and the constants must be defined and estimated.
They identify the exact place where a phrase such as “the small errors disappear in the limit”
needs a proof.

calculation identifies the scaling distinction without using a perturbative quantum series.

lattice field whose coordinate size or higher moments grow as the cutoff is removed need not
satisfy the same uniform bound. Controlling the exceptional configurations and the normalization
of composite observables is necessary before integrating the expansion and passing to a continuum
limit. The exact finite-dimensional algebra remains valid, but the limiting interchange requires
additional estimates.
47.10 Removing the two regulators in a justified order
A lattice calculation has both an ultraviolet cutoff and a physical-volume cutoff. Let n index
decreasing lattice spacings an ↓ 0, and let R index increasing physical boxes. The number
of lattice sites in a physical box depends on both n and R; treating that number as a single
parameter can obscure the order of limits. For a fixed observable supported in a fixed compact
physical region, denote its normalized expectation by fn,R. The same notation can represent a
finite correlation, provided its normalization and support have already been fixed.
Theorem CT.10 (uniform removal of the volume regulator). Suppose that for each n the
limit fn,∞ = limR→∞fn,R exists. Suppose there is a deterministic function ϵ(R)→ 0 such that
sup
n
|fn,R −fn,∞|≤ϵ(R).
Suppose also that for every fixed R, the limit gR = limn→∞fn,R exists. Then gR has a limit g∞
as R→∞, fn,∞→g∞, and for every joint sequence nj →∞, Rj →∞,
fnj,Rj −→g∞.
The conclusion and proof hold for values in any complete normed space, with absolute values
replaced by norms.
Proof. For fixed R,S and every n,
|fn,R −fn,S|≤|fn,R −fn,∞| +|fn,S −fn,∞|≤ϵ(R) +ϵ(S).
Pass to the n→∞ limit to obtain |gR −gS|≤ϵ(R) + ϵ(S). Thus gR is Cauchy and has a limit
g∞. Sending S→∞ gives|gR −g∞|≤ϵ(R).
For each fixed R,
|fn,∞−g∞|≤|fn,∞−fn,R| +|fn,R −gR| +|gR −g∞|≤ 2ϵ(R) +|fn,R −gR|.

|fnj,Rj −g∞|≤ϵ(Rj) +|fnj,∞−g∞|−→ 0.
Every step used only triangle inequalities and completeness, so the normed-space statement
follows as well. □

Without the uniform estimate, the two iterated limits need not agree. Define fn,R = 1{R≥n} for
positive integer indices. At fixed n, the large-volume limit is one. At fixed R, the ultraviolet-index
limit is zero. Consequently
limn→∞ lim R→∞ fn,R = 1, lim R→∞ limn→∞fn,R = 0.
The diagonal R =n has value one, whereas R =⌊n/2⌋ has value zero. Every scalar is bounded
by one; the failure comes entirely from lack of uniformity. Boundedness, therefore, is not enough
to exchange the regulators.
The theorem can be used without an explicit infinite-volume limit at the outset if one proves the
equivalent Cauchy estimate
sup

Completeness gives fn,∞ for every n, and passing S→∞ supplies the displayed hypothesis
of CT.10. This formulation often matches a boundary-influence estimate more directly. The
observable must remain supported a controlled physical distance from the boundary; a support
moving toward the boundary is a different family.
In a lattice strong-coupling argument, influence might decay exponentially in a graph distance
measured in lattice steps. A continuum use of CT.10 requires translating that estimate to the
actual observable normalization and physical geometry uniformly in n. The strong-coupling
constants can cease to apply along the intended bare-coupling trajectory. Even when they do
apply, they can force the triviality mechanism proved elsewhere in the manuscript. The regulator
theorem itself neither repairs that loss of applicability nor identifies a nontrivial limit; it ensures
that a valid uniform estimate is used with the correct order of quantifiers.
For a correlation hierarchy, CT.10 should be applied to each member of a countable family whose
moment and continuity bounds are sufficient to recover the desired distributions. One can allow
the function ϵ to depend on that fixed member. A single rate for all unbounded composite
observables is not required by this elementary interchange theorem. A common physical decay
rate across a total family of centered states is a different requirement, arising in the spectral-gap
theorem. Distinguishing these constants avoids demanding an unnecessarily strong compactness
estimate while inadvertently weakening the essential mass-gap estimate.
47.11 A constructive route stated in verifiable stages
The actual Wilson weak-coupling estimate and the abstract compactness criteria can be con-
nected only through further analytic work. A precise route is to choose a sequence of physical
lattices, specify renormalized gauge-invariant representatives for a countable dense family of test
observables, and prove uniform moment estimates in a local distribution topology. Theorems
CT.4 and CT.5 then supply subsequential probability laws and convergence of suitable correlation
functions. Their proofs show exactly which constants must be independent of cutoff and which
may depend on a fixed test observable or compact region.
The next requirements concern the limiting law, rather than its mere existence as a probability
measure. Algebraic consistency, reflection positivity, Euclidean covariance and the regularity
assumptions of a reconstruction theorem must be checked for the same limiting hierarchy. Exact
symmetries can pass to a limit when the corresponding transformed observables converge, but a
lattice symmetry group is smaller than the full Euclidean group. Restoring the missing continuous
transformations is a separate assertion. The spectral and reflection sections give the necessary
positive-form and semigroup arguments once their hypotheses are available.
275
=== PAGE 276 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Nontriviality requires at least one centered positive-time observable class with strictly positive
finite reflected norm. A nonzero equal-point variance does not provide that norm. A practical
strategy would be to prove a lower bound for a specific smeared reflected two-point function and
an upper bound that ensures finiteness, with both bounds stable under the cutoff removal. The
stability lemmas above explain how a known positive margin can survive controlled approximation
errors. They do not manufacture the initial lower bound.
Finally, a physical mass gap requires decay on a total class of reconstructed centered states,
with a positive rate in physical time and constants compatible with the continuum limit. The
weak-coupling action estimate does not establish that decay. It also does not exclude it. The
conclusion of the present calculation is narrower and useful: the actual Wilson family has
volume-uniform local concentration at large β, while the remaining continuum task is explicitly
a problem about renormalized multipoint control, nonzero reflected norms and physical-distance
decay.
There are therefore proved additions to the investigation: an unconditional weak-coupling
local-action estimate, exact fixed-loop consequences, probability-law and distribution-valued
compactness criteria, exact Gaussian coarse-graining with transformed observables, a bounded
nonlinear remainder estimate, and a scale-error convergence criterion. The hypotheses needed to
apply the latter tools to four-dimensional continuum Yang–Mills are left visible. None of them is
renamed as an established Yang–Mills estimate merely because it would complete the intended
argument.
48 Gap transfer, continuum scaling, and precise obstructions
The distinction is between a regulator-dependent gap and a positive, finite mass in a nontrivial
continuum quantum field theory. A lattice estimate does not supply the continuum theory whose
spectrum one wishes to study. Once that theory and sufficiently strong uniform correlation
estimates exist, the final spectral deduction is short.
48.1 Exponential decay on a total set implies a Hamiltonian gap
Let H be a complex Hilbert space, H ≥ 0 self-adjoint, and Ω ∈ kerH a unit vector. A set
D⊂ Ω⊥ is total if its complex linear span is dense in Ω⊥.

0≤⟨v,e−tHv⟩≤e−mt∥v∥2
for every v∈ Ω⊥ and every t≥ 0.

For finiteness, take 0 ̸= w∈ Ω⊥. Its spectral measure has mass ∥w∥2 > 0. Some finite interval

48.3 What reconstruction still requires
Theorem GT.2 is not a construction of the continuum triple it assumes. For a Euclidean
Yang–Mills programme, one must separately:
• Specify the renormalized smeared gauge-invariant observables corresponding to local curva-
ture polynomials and their covariant derivatives.
• Obtain the full hierarchy of limiting Schwinger distributions with the regularity and growth
conditions of an applicable reconstruction theorem.
• Establish reflection positivity, restored Euclidean symmetry and the remaining axioms.
Closed positivity inequalities pass to limits if all the necessary entries converge; that fact
does not establish convergence or the other axioms.
• Establish a total family of limiting observable states and a nonzero centered state.
• Identify the resulting theory as four-dimensional Yang–Mills, including the required short-
distance properties.
The applicable Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction hypotheses must hold for the limiting
correlations [8, 9]. The required Yang–Mills construction must identify its local observable theory,
nontrivial physical states and time-translation dynamics. A finite lattice integral or a Gaussian
comparison model supplies only its own stated conclusions.

=== PAGE 279 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
48.4 Fixed positive lattice decay can force a trivial limit
If mlat,j ≥κ> 0, then mphys,j ≥κ/aj →∞. A fixed lattice gap does not shrink to zero under
this scaling.
Theorem GT.3 (fixed lattice-rate obstruction). Retain the continuum triple, total set and

merely the existence of a random distribution.
This exact consequence does not extend strong-coupling estimates to the weak-bare-coupling

48.6 Every regulated model can be gapped while its limit is gapless
LetF be bosonic Fock space over L2(R3,dp) and define
Hε =dΓ(ωε), ωε(p) =
√
|p|2 +ε2.
On the n-particle sector, this is multiplication by ∑n i=1 ωε(pi). Every ε> 0 has unique vacuum
and excitation threshold ε: the n-particle energy is at least nε, and the one-particle spectrum
has infimum ε.
As ε↓ 0, the semigroups converge strongly to those of H0 = dΓ(|p|). On each finite-particle sector
the multipliers converge pointwise and are bounded by one, so dominated convergence proves
strong convergence. Finite-particle vectors are dense and all the semigroups are contractions,
extending convergence to the full Fock space.
The limiting vacuum remains unique because in any nonvacuum sector the zero-energy set consists
of all momenta vanishing, a measure-zero set. Yet every interval (0,η) contains one-particle
spectrum: use functions supported where 0<|p|<η. Thus the limit is gapless.
A purely finite-dimensional example is HN = span{Ω,e1,...,eN}, HNΩ = 0, HNek = k−1ek.
Each gap is 1/N; the natural limit on CΩ ⊕ℓ2(N) has positive eigenvalues accumulating at zero.
These examples refute a logical shortcut, not the Yang–Mills conjecture.
48.7 A uniform gap does not ensure a nontrivial observable limit
LetH = C2, Ω = (1, 0), H = diag(0, 1) and

48.8 A stochastic sampling gap is not automatically a physical gap
For any probability measure µ, the complete-resampling Markov generator
Lf =µ(f)−f
is self-adjoint on L2(µ), preserves constants and has invariant measure µ. Direct calculation gives
esLf =e−sf + (1−e−s)µ(f), ⟨f,−Lf⟩ = Varµ(f).
Thus −L has gap exactly one whenever the mean-zero subspace is nonzero, irrespective of the
equilibrium spatial correlations.

For an explicit measure, take the equal mixture of the all-plus and all-minus spin configurations
on Z4. Then µ(Xx) = 0 and Covµ(Xx,Xy) = 1 at every separation, although the resampling
generator has gap one. Multiplying L by a positive constant changes its mixing gap without
changing µ.
The parameter s is artificial sampling time. An implication for physical mass requires a proved
identification with physical Euclidean-time translation. This example does not rule out such an
identification in a particular model; it rules out treating it as automatic.
49 Quantitative spectral bounds and construction from time-
correlation kernels
This section treats the physical-time part of the continuum problem. Its purpose is to replace
several informal statements about exponential decay by precise estimates, and to construct
a Hilbert space and a nonnegative Hamiltonian from explicit limiting correlation data. The
construction is useful because the cutoff Hilbert spaces need not have been embedded in a
common space. It also makes visible two different losses that must be prevented: spectral weight
can approach zero energy, or it can escape to arbitrarily large energy.
The positive-kernel construction belongs to the established framework of reproducing kernels and
Euclidean reconstruction [48, 9, 49]. The elementary estimates and their proofs are given here in
the exact form used in this investigation. A physical-time semigroup is one part of a field theory;
this section does not identify a constructed abstract kernel with four-dimensional Yang–Mills
Schwinger functions. That application is considered explicitly at the end.
49.1 Positive spectral measures and the information in a correlation
Let H be a complex Hilbert space whose inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument.
Let H≥ 0 be self-adjoint. For v∈H, its spectral measure is
µv(B) =⟨v,EH(B)v⟩,
where EH is the projection-valued spectral resolution. It is a finite positive measure on [0,∞),
with total mass∥v∥2. Its Euclidean-time autocorrelation is
Kv(t) =⟨v,e−tHv⟩ =
∫ ∞
0

The measure is positive even when v represents a complicated product of observables. This
positivity is the decisive distinction between an autocorrelation and a general signed correlation.
It allows bounds on the transform to control actual spectral projections without cancellation
between different energy ranges.
If a vacuum Ω is specified, the vectors relevant to the excitation spectrum are centered vectors
v⊥ Ω. Centering removes the known vacuum component. It does not, before a uniqueness
theorem, remove a hypothetical additional zero-energy vector. Consequently intervals [0,b],
including zero, are the appropriate intervals for exclusion arguments.
Proposition SB.1 (elementary spectral regularity). For every v, Kv is continuous on

The word “probe” matters. A vector can be orthogonal to an entire low-energy subspace. Even
exact knowledge of Ev for one v gives the bottom of the spectral measure of that vector, not
automatically the bottom of the Hamiltonian on the complete excitation space. The totality
arguments below address that issue rather than assuming it away.
49.2 Finite-time bounds with explicit errors
A useful analytical estimate often has an additive error. The following result says exactly what
such an estimate proves. The error can represent a rigorously bounded discretization remainder,
a truncation of an analytic expansion, or an interval enclosure. It is not required to arise from
numerical computation.

49.3 Several probes, matrix inequalities, and conditioning
Let v1,...,vN be a finite list of vectors. Define their Gram matrix and time-correlation matrix
by
Gij =⟨vi,vj⟩, Kij(t) =⟨vi,e−tHvj⟩.

49.4 Passing from finite probe spaces to the full excitation space
The matrix certificate has an infinite-dimensional use when the geometry and errors are controlled
along a sequence of growing probe spaces. The necessary limiting statement can be given explicitly.
It does not require a single finite family to generate every state, and it does not confuse a finite
list of successful inequalities with a universal theorem.
Let K⊂H be a closed subspace invariant under the spectral projections of H. In a vacuum
theory the intended choice is K = Ω⊥. Let SN ⊂K be finite-dimensional subspaces whose
orthogonal projections QN tend strongly to the identity on K. Nested spaces with dense union
are one sufficient example. Let vN,1,...,vN,dN be a basis for SN, and write GN and KN(t) for
its Gram and correlation matrices.

No lower bound on γN uniform in N is required. Poor conditioning is allowed, but its growth
must be paid for in the error estimate. Likewise, the time TN may grow with the probe dimension,
provided the displayed matrix approximation is valid at that actual time. The theorem makes
these costs visible rather than absorbing them into a dimension-dependent unspecified constant.

One can derive a simple exact schedule. Suppose dN = N, aN ≤ Npe−mTN, γN ≥ N−q and

To obtain a full gap at m, one may prove exclusion for a countable sequence bk ↑m. The probe
spaces, time schedules and error rates may depend on k because each fixed lower interval is
excluded separately. The same physical Hilbert space and the same nonnegative Hamiltonian
must be used for all k. Allowing an unrelated limiting theory for each threshold would not
establish a gap for one theory.
There is a structural limitation here. The spaces SN are subspaces of an already defined target
excitation space, and their projections converge strongly by hypothesis. A sequence of cutoff
variational subspaces does not automatically satisfy that hypothesis after the cutoff is removed.
The kernel construction later in this section provides one way to define a generated limiting
Hilbert space, but identification of its dense family with the necessary gauge-observable states is
still a separate task. In particular, a list consisting only of small Wilson loops can miss sectors
generated by more general positive-time products.
The theorem can nevertheless be useful for a paper proof. It specifies how an analytic approxima-
tion scheme for the entire correlation matrix would have to improve with the number of probes.
Bounds on the Gram inverse, on the error matrix, and on the accessible physical-time window
become explicit mathematical targets. A finite computation can test such targets or falsify a
proposed rate, while the proof of (SB7) must cover the full unbounded sequence.
For a direct test of the prefactor requirement, take Hek = k−1ek on ℓ2(N) and
SN = span{e1,...,eN}. Then GN = I and KN(t) is diagonal, with largest entry e−t/N.
At any chosen finite time TN, one can formally write
KN(TN)≤CNe−TNGN, CN =e(1−1/N)TN.
Thus an exponential-looking estimate with a freely growing prefactor can always be manufactured
on a finite probe space. It provides no gap at rate one. The actual certificate factor for a fixed
b > 0 is ebTNCNe−TN = e(b−1/N)TN, which cannot tend to zero. The exact spectral formula
exposes the failure before any limit is taken. This example is not an obstruction to every
approximation method; it identifies why the dimension dependence of the prefactor belongs
inside the proof rather than inside an unnamed constant.

49.5 Short-time continuity and preventing escape to infinite energy
Low-energy exclusion alone does not ensure that a nonzero state survives a continuum limit. A
sequence of unit vectors can concentrate at energies tending to infinity. Then its correlations
vanish at every positive physical time, while its equal-time norms remain one. This is the spectral
form of a trivialization mechanism.
For a finite positive measure µ with transform K, the identity
K(0)−K(s) =
∫ ∞
0
(1−e−sλ)dµ(λ)
gives, for L,s> 0,
µ([L,∞))≤ K(0)−K(s) 1−e−sL . (SB10)
The denominator is positive. The estimate controls a high-energy tail using a short-time increment,
without requiring the vector to lie in the domain of H.
Theorem SB.7 (spectral tightness from a short-time modulus). Let {µj} be finite
positive measures on [0,∞) with uniformly bounded total masses, and let Kj be their Laplace
transforms. The following statements are equivalent:
1. For every ε> 0 there is L<∞ such that supj µj([L,∞))<ε.
2. lims↓0 supj[Kj(0)−Kj(s)] = 0.
Proof. Assume the second statement. Given ε> 0, choose s> 0 so that the supremum in that
statement is less than (1−e−1)ε. Apply (SB10) with L = 1/s. This proves the first statement.
Conversely, let the total masses be bounded by M. Given ε> 0, choose L with tail masses below
ε/2. Split the increment integral at L. For the lower part, 1 −e−sλ ≤sL; for the upper part it is
at most one. Therefore

Example SB.8 (positive-time limits can lose all norm). Take µj = δj. Then Kj(0) = 1

It explicitly prevents the surviving norm from being concentrated either near zero or at infinity.

49.6 A positive-time lower bound certifies finite-energy survival
A lower bound at one positive physical time gives another direct route to a surviving finite-energy
sector. It is often more useful than a pointwise variance because high-energy mass is exponentially
suppressed in the quantity being bounded below. The following estimate does not assume an
energy moment or a differentiability bound at zero.

physical-time correlation together locate a nonzero state in a finite positive-energy interval.
Proof. Since the semigroup is a contraction, Kv(t0) ≤∥v∥2 ≤B, so B≥c. Split the integral

For an exact example, take the probability measure

There is a useful distinction between this proposition and Theorem SB.7. A surviving positive-

any fixed amount of norm from escaping. The latter is what permits the norm-preserving kernel
construction below. For instance, µj = 1 2 δ1 + 1 2 δj has a positive limiting correlation at every
positive time, but half its unit norm escapes to infinity. The modulus criterion detects that
escape; the positive-time certificate correctly retains a finite-energy half without claiming to
retain the other half.

to a unitary. It carries the named vectors correctly and intertwines all rational shifts, hence all
real-time semigroups. □
This theorem does not require strictly positive Gram matrices. Null vectors are expected in
constrained theories, and the quotient handles them exactly. It also does not require a uniform
lower bound on B = S1. The logarithm is generally unbounded; injectivity, not bounded
invertibility, is what excludes an infinite-energy subspace from the Hilbert space constructed
here.
The shift-contraction hypothesis is independent of Hankel positivity. The scalar kernel K(t) = et
has positive Hankel matrices, since es+t = eset, but its time shifts grow and would produce
the negative generator H = −1. Conversely, a function that is positive at each time need not
have Hankel positivity: for K(t) = e−t2 , the two-point matrix at times 0,s has determinant
e−4s2 −e−2s2 < 0 when s> 0. Neither pointwise positivity nor appealing decay can replace the
precise matrix hypotheses.
49.8 Gap and nontriviality in the constructed space
The preceding construction creates the excitation space directly. Add a unit vector Ω orthogonal
to it and define
H = CΩ⊕Hex, H = 0⊕Hex.
This provides a distinguished vacuum vector. It does not yet prove that it is the only zero-energy
vector. The following theorem supplies that conclusion through the correlation estimates.
Theorem SB.10 (a generated family suffices for the gap). Under Theorem SB.9, suppose
one m> 0 has the property that, for every index i, there are finite Ci and ti ≥ 0 with
0≤Kii(t)≤Cie−mt (t≥ti). (SB17)
Then kerH = CΩ and σ(Hex) ⊂ [m,∞). If Kii(0) > 0 for some i, then Hex ̸= {0} and its
spectral infimum is finite as well as positive.
Proof. For a generator w =e−sHexvi, its autocorrelation is
⟨w,e−tHexw⟩ =Kii(t + 2s).
For sufficiently large t, (SB17) bounds this by Cie−2mse−mt. For every 0 ≤ b < m, positivity
gives

e−tb∥EHex([0,b])w∥2 ≤Cie−2mse−mt.
Let t→∞. The projection annihilates every such generator. Their span is dense, and the
projection is bounded, so it vanishes on the whole excitation space. A countable sequence b↑m
excludes [0,m), including zero. This proves the gap and vacuum uniqueness. If a diagonal norm
is positive, the corresponding vi is nonzero. Its finite positive spectral measure has positive mass
in some finite interval, proving that the excitation threshold cannot be infinite. □
It is not necessary to prove a common prefactor Ci or a common onset time ti over all probes. The
rate m is common. This distinction can make a research target weaker than an operator-norm
bound at every cutoff, while remaining strong enough for the spectral conclusion.
A short-time state can also be tested through a reflected covariance. If the index i corresponds to
a real centered positive-time observable F, its squared reconstructed norm is Kii(0). A rigorous
lower bound on that quantity establishes a surviving state only if it concerns the renormalized
reflected form that defines the Hilbert space. An ordinary same-point classical variance at fixed
lattice spacing need not be that quantity. The distinction is particularly important when contact
terms survive but separated reflected correlations vanish.
49.9 Constructing a subsequential semigroup limit from cutoff data
The kernel theorem can now be combined with compactness. The following result does not
assume a continuum Hamiltonian in advance. Its premises are scalar bounds and convergence
control for cutoff physical-time correlations.

For each j, let Hj ≥ 0 be self-adjoint on a Hilbert space Hj, and let vj,i, i∈ N, be a countable

consistency of the limits from different compact intervals.
For any finite list (ip,sp) with rational sp ≥ 0, the cutoff Hankel matrix is the Gram matrix

‖‖‖‖‖ ∑ p cpe−spHjvj,ip ‖‖‖‖‖ 2 − ‖‖‖‖‖e−rHj ∑ p cpe−spHjvj,ip ‖‖‖‖‖ 2 ≥ 0.

At t = 0, the limiting diagonal entry for i0 is at least η by assumption 3, so the excitation space
is nonzero. At each fixed t≥ti, the uniform estimate (SB19) passes to the limit. Theorem SB.10
then proves the spectral gap. All steps use the same diagonal subsequence, so the nonzero norm,
the kernel structure and the gap refer to one and the same limiting semigroup. □
This is an existence theorem for an abstract physical-time Hilbert model with a positive finite
excitation threshold. It is more than a deduction about a pre-existing continuum Hamiltonian:
it actually constructs that semigroup from cutoff correlations under the stated scalar conditions.
Its limitation is equally precise. It does not prove spacetime covariance, locality, existence of
field operators, a hierarchy of Schwinger distributions, or identification of those kernels with the
required Yang–Mills observable algebra.
The short-time modulus is not a cosmetic condition. Removing it allows the sequence in Example
SB.8: the norms survive at time zero, all positive-time correlations disappear, and no strongly
continuous limit preserving those norms results. Removing the nonzero norm condition allows
every limiting observable vector to vanish. Removing the uniform positive decay rate allows
excitation energies to approach zero. Each assumption therefore addresses a distinct failure mode
rather than duplicating another premise.
The theorem permits a weaker nontriviality premise when only a subsequence is desired. If
lim supj ∥vj,i0∥2 > 0, first select a subsequence with norms bounded below by some η > 0 and
then apply the theorem there. The uniform bounds and moduli remain valid on that subsequence.

=== PAGE 296 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
No assertion about uniqueness of all possible continuum subsequences follows without further
information.
49.10 A countable research target and the order of limits
The preceding arguments suggest a disciplined way to specify the spectral part of the Yang–
Mills investigation. Choose a countable family of renormalized gauge-invariant positive-time
observables containing a dense collection of the polynomial products and smearing functions
required by the eventual reconstruction. For each cutoff and volume, form their centered reflected
time kernels. The family must be sufficiently rich by a proved continuity and density argument;
choosing a countable collection does not automatically make it total in a separately defined
continuum theory.
The useful bounds are then of three kinds. First, uniform diagonal norm bounds prevent the
Gram data from diverging. Second, a short-time modulus prevents these bounded norms from
escaping to infinite energy. Third, a common positive decay rate, with probe-dependent but
cutoff-independent prefactors, excludes additional zero-energy states and low positive energies.
A surviving positive reflected norm provides nontriviality. Theorem SB.11 shows how these
statements fit together without requiring arbitrary identifications between different cutoff Hilbert
spaces.
There are two legitimate orders of argument. One may first construct the continuum correlations
and physical Hilbert space and then use a total-set spectral criterion. Alternatively, one may
prove the uniform scalar hypotheses of Theorem SB.11 and obtain a subsequential time-semigroup
limit while separately establishing the spacetime field structure. Neither order permits replacing
pointwise convergence at fixed t by convergence at a time tj →∞ unless an additional uniform
estimate has been proved.
To make that last issue explicit, suppose Kj(t) →K(t) for each fixed t. This alone places no
useful bound on |Kj(tj) −K(tj)| at growing times. If an argument uses a cutoff-dependent time
to optimize (SB2), it must have an error bound on the corresponding growing window. Otherwise
the order of limits has been changed without justification. The safe alternative is to pass a
cutoff-uniform estimate at each fixed time to the limit first, and only then send physical time to
infinity in the limiting spectral measure.
If rigorous window errors are available, they can be incorporated exactly. Suppose
|K(t)−Kj(t)|≤εj (0≤t≤Tj), Kj(t)≤Ce−mt +rj.
Then Theorem SB.3 applies to K with δj = εj + rj on the same window. The separate errors
add; neither may be dropped. A schedule satisfying Corollary SB.5 can then prove exclusion
of each fixed interval [0,b], and a countable sequence b↑ m yields a gap. This is a complete
analytical implication from explicit error bounds, but those bounds remain quantities to prove
for the actual renormalized gauge kernels.
The contribution of this section is therefore a set of proved interfaces between correlation
estimates, spectral weight, nontriviality and semigroup existence. It identifies a more quantitative
target than an informal assertion that correlations “look exponential,” while avoiding the stronger
and unnecessary demand for one universal prefactor over every physical state. The actual
four-dimensional gauge-field estimates required to instantiate these interfaces are not supplied by
the abstract arguments.

=== PAGE 297 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
50 Sparse-time certificates and a surviving continuum semigroup
This section gives complete auxiliary implications concerning positive physical-time correlations.
The transfer-matrix framework for Wilson lattice gauge theory is classical; see Lüscher [6]. The
purpose is to expose the precise time windows, positivity, normalization, and error estimates
that would make a cutoff calculation sufficient for a limiting spectral conclusion. The hypotheses
below are not asserted to have been verified for the four-dimensional Wilson family along a
continuum trajectory.
Throughout, Hj ≥ 0 is a self-adjoint cutoff Hamiltonian, and t denotes physical Euclidean
time. If a positive transfer operator advances time by aj, its nth power corresponds to t = naj.
Consequently the parameters b and m below have units of inverse physical time. We consider
diagonal correlations

states orthogonal to a vacuum. An arbitrary signed connected covariance does not satisfy the
argument merely because it has been given the same notation. For data obtained at integer
transfer steps, use the actual times Tj = njaj throughout; any time-rounding error belongs in
the certified bounds.
50.1 A spectral splitting inequality
Lemma 50.1 (From one late-time value to an earlier-time bound). Let H≥ 0 be self-adjoint,

50.3 Construction from positive-time survival
Equal-time norm bounds alone do not prevent spectral mass from escaping to infinite energy. A
positive lower bound at one strictly positive physical time is a stronger survival condition. It
also provides a way to obtain short-time regularity after propagation.

Propagation by e−sHj takes place inside an already positive physical semigroup. It is not four-
dimensional gradient-flow smoothing. If a full continuum Hilbert space and a total unshifted
family vi have separately been constructed, their positive-time translates remain total, because
e−sHvi → vi as s↓ 0. Without that identification, Theorem 50.4 constructs the surviving
generated space only. Adjoining a one-dimensional zero-energy vacuum gives an abstract vacuum
model with a nonzero excitation space and a gap; this operation supplies none of the missing
spacetime axioms. The constructed space also contains finite-energy spectral weight: the positive
spectral measure of any nonzero vector must assign positive mass to some bounded interval,
since the intervals [0,R] exhaust [0,∞). Thus its nontriviality does not merely retain states at
an infinite limiting energy.

50.5 Four exact failure modes
The following examples separate assumptions that cannot be conflated. All one- and two-
dimensional Hamiltonians act on the displayed probe space; a separate vacuum can be adjoined
if desired.
Vanishing late-time values without the exponential budget. Let Hj = (jτ0)−1I on C,
take vj = 1, and set Tj = j2τ0. Then Kj(Tj) = e−j → 0, while Kj(t) → 1 at every fixed physical
time. The limiting Hamiltonian is zero. For every b> 0, ebTjKj(Tj) = ebj2τ0−j diverges, so the
actual sparse-time condition correctly fails.
Equal-time norms without positive-time survival. Let Hj = (j/τ0)I on C, with vj = 1.
The squared norms are always one, and choosing Tj = jτ0 makes sparse-time exclusion hold for
every finite threshold m. Nevertheless Kj(t) → 0 for every fixed t > 0. There is no strongly
continuous limiting semigroup preserving the limiting norm one. Condition (50.8) excludes
exactly this example.

51 Conditional transfer of a continuum spectral gap
The result in this section proves the functional-analytic implication in the proposed continuum
argument. It does not assume that a four-dimensional SU(2) continuum construction has
already been obtained from the preceding strong-coupling certificate. Convergence of spectral
structures on varying Hilbert spaces is established theory; see, for example, Kuwae and Shioya
[50], especially their Theorem 2.4 and Proposition 2.5. The elementary proof below records
exactly the convergence needed here.
For each cutoff index k, let Hk be a Hilbert space, Ωk a unit vacuum vector, and Ak a positive
selfadjoint contraction such that AkΩk = Ωk. Write
Pk =|Ωk⟩⟨Ωk|, Qk =I−Pk.
For the physical lattice problem, Ak = Tk/λ0,k, where Tk is the physical Euclidean-time transfer
operator and λ0,k its vacuum eigenvalue. None of the statements below concerns a Monte Carlo
update operator.
Let ak > 0, ak → 0, and suppose that a certified number δk ≥ 0 satisfies
0≤AkQk ≤e−δkQk. (51.1)
The number δk may be a lower bound on the exact logarithmic gap. Equality with that gap is
not needed. When the exact gap is used, δk = − log∥AkQk∥. The case AkQk = 0 can be handled
directly; we use finite δk in the formulas to avoid an unnecessary 0·∞ convention. Set
nk(t) =⌊t/ak⌋, tk(t) =aknk(t), mk =δk/ak.
For every fixed t> 0, eventually nk(t) ≥ 1 and tk(t) →t. For isotropic periodic spatial boxes, the
infinite physical-volume application also requires akLk →∞. That geometric condition belongs
to the continuum construction; the abstract spectral implication below does not itself establish
it.
Lemma 51.1 (Vacuum subtraction and powers). For v∈Hk, put z = ⟨Ωk,v⟩ and η = Qkv.
For every integer n≥ 1,
⟨v,An kv⟩ =|z|2 +⟨η,An kη⟩, (51.2)
0≤⟨η,An kη⟩≤e−nδk∥η∥2. (51.3)
Thus the quantity controlled by the gap is the connected correlation, ⟨v,An kv⟩−|z|2, with connected
norm∥v∥2 −|z|2.
Proof. Selfadjointness and AkΩk = Ωk imply that Pk and Qk commute with Ak. The cross
terms between Pkv and Qkv therefore vanish. Spectral calculus on QkHk applied to (51.1) gives
0≤An kQk ≤e−nδkQk.

52 Spectral gap from total-family correlation envelopes
A uniform gap for every cutoff state is sufficient but can be stronger than necessary for the
continuum vacuum representation. A state that disappears from that representation can make
the full cutoff gap small. The following criterion avoids requiring control of such states, while
still requiring a total family of actual continuum states.

let S⊂ Ω⊥ have dense linear span. Fix M > 0 and a sequence tj →∞. Suppose that for each

for nonzero ψ.

Proof. For 0≤r<M, spectral positivity gives

The convergence follows from (52.2); for example, eventually Bψ(tj) ≤e(M−r)tj/2. The projection
argument in Theorem 51.2 completes the proof. The converse follows directly from the spectral
support condition.
An admissible envelope is Bψ(t) = Cψ(1 + t)pψ with finite Cψ > 0 and pψ ≥ 0. These constants
need not be uniform over ψ. One way to establish (52.1) from cutoff data is to prove, for every
fixed tj,
Ck,ψ(tj)≤Cψ(1 +tk(tj))pψe−Mtk(tj) +εk,ψ(tj), εk,ψ(tj)→ 0,
with Cψ,pψ independent of k, and then pass to the actual correlation limit. Prefactors that
diverge with the cutoff cannot simply be dropped. Neither finitely many measured times nor a
single glueball channel verifies this all-times, total-family requirement.
53 Exact counterexamples to missing premises
These examples are abstract spectral constructions, not SU(2) measurements. They show why the
hypotheses cannot be replaced by finite numerical evidence or by an incomplete set of observables.

53.3 A full-cutoff uniform gap is not necessary for a selected limit
Take Hk = CΩk ⊕ Cv⊕ Cwk, ak = 1/k, and physical energies 0, 1, 1/k. Let the continuum

to the two-level theory with energies 0, 1, which has gap 1. The full cutoff gap nevertheless
satisfies δk/ak = 1/k→ 0 because of wk, which is absent from the reconstructed observable
representation. This example motivates the total-family envelope theorem. It does not establish
that any particular SU(2) cutoff states decouple.
53.4 A fixed positive lattice gap can destroy time continuity
Let Ak = diag(1,e−c) with c> 0, and ak = 1/k. For the normalized excited vector v,
⟨v,A⌊kt⌋ k v⟩−→ 0 (t> 0), ∥v∥2 = 1.
The candidate limit equals the vacuum projection at every positive time but the identity at time
zero. It is not strongly continuous and cannot be e−tH for a selfadjoint Hamiltonian on this
nonzero excitation space. Alternatively, discarding the excitation leaves a trivial one-dimensional
vacuum theory. This is the explicit obstruction captured by Proposition 51.4.
Status. The transfer, dense-family and envelope results above are fully proved conditional
statements. They identify what an actual SU(2) continuum construction and a physical-rate
estimate would imply. They do not prove that the required limits or weak-coupling estimates exist
for four-dimensional SU(2). The abstract spectral principles and their reconstruction antecedents
are established mathematics; no historical priority claim is made here.
54 Conditional reconstruction of the physical time Hilbert space
The gap-transfer theorem starts with a constructed continuum Hamiltonian. The following
lemma spells out sufficient correlation-limit hypotheses that construct its time Hilbert space and
semigroup. It does not construct the required SU(2) limits. Nor does time-semigroup reconstruc-
tion alone prove the locality, Euclidean covariance, field regularity, gauge-observable structure
or other properties needed for a four-dimensional relativistic Yang–Mills theory. Full Euclidean
reconstruction has additional hypotheses; the corrected Osterwalder–Schrader framework is the
relevant classical reference [9].
Use the physical Ak, vacua Ωk, and projectors Qk from Section 51. For an index set F of
renormalized observable labels, suppose centered vectors uk(F ) ∈QkHk have been specified. For

55 What rescaling and exact time blocking can establish
The following results identify limitations of specific proposed extensions of the existing lattice
certificates. They do not exclude a continuum Yang–Mills construction, a different strong-coupling
estimate, or a controlled renormalization argument. All lengths below are numerical values in
one fixed physical reference unit; changing that unit does not change any assertion about a zero,
finite, or infinite limiting rate.
55.1 Exact time blocking preserves the physical spectral rate
Proposition 55.1 (Exact blocking identity). Let A be a positive selfadjoint contraction on a
Hilbert space, with a normalized vacuum Ω, AΩ = Ω, and vacuum projector P = |Ω⟩⟨Ω|. Put
Q =I−P and
q =∥AQ∥, δ =− logq,
where − log 0 = +∞. For every integer b≥ 1, the exact transfer operator across b time steps is
A[b] =Ab, and
∥A[b]Q∥ =qb, δ[b] =bδ.
If one original step has physical duration a, the blocked step has duration a[b] = ba. Consequently,
δ[b]
a[b] = δ a.
The statement includes volume-dependent operators and block sizes that vary along a sequence,
as an identity at each sequence index.
Proof. Selfadjointness and AΩ = Ω give AQ = QA, so the restriction AQ = A|QH is positive and
selfadjoint. The spectral theorem gives ∥Ab Q∥ = ∥AQ∥b. Taking logarithms proves the assertion.
For an unnormalized transfer operator T with vacuum eigenvalue λ0, the normalized blocked
operator is Tb/λb 0 = (T/λ0)b, giving precisely the same identity.

Thus exact grouping of time steps does not convert a fixed-cutoff spectral rate into a different
rate in physical units. Multiplying T by an overall normalization likewise leaves eigenvalue
ratios unchanged. A claimed effective coupling after blocking needs an identity or a controlled
approximation for the blocked operator; the blocking identity alone does not supply one.

57 Full-operator error budget for an approximate blocked trans-
fer
The following result gives a concrete sufficient error budget for a proposed blocking or spectral
approximation. It does not assert that this budget has been established for weak-coupling SU(2).
All operators in the comparison must act on the same full physical Hilbert space. A compression
to a finite basis supplies only part of the required hypothesis.
Theorem 57.1 (Normalized full-operator comparison). Let A be a positive selfadjoint compact
contraction on a physical Hilbert space of dimension at least two, with largest eigenvalue 1 and a
simple vacuum. Let b≥ 1 be an integer, let a> 0, and write

The vacuum eigenvectors of S and B need not agree.
Proof. Let v be the normalized leading eigenvector of B. For every unit x⊥v,
⟨x,Sx⟩≤⟨x,Bx⟩ +ε≤q +ε.
The min–max principle therefore gives λ1(S) ≤q + ε. Positivity implies λ1(S) = λ1(A)b = e−bδ.
Taking logarithms and dividing by τ = ba proves the claim. The use of min–max, rather than
identifying the approximate and exact vacuum vectors, is what makes the vacuum treatment
valid.

57.3 What remains unverified for SU(2)
No Bk, qk, and full operator errors εk satisfying (57.2) have been constructed here along a weak-
coupling, growing-volume SU(2) sequence. The theorem supplies a precise sufficient criterion and

must be combined with the continuum construction and nontriviality hypotheses in the preceding
sections.
58 Why a finite-error correlator fit cannot certify the missing

place of a uniform spectral theorem.
Choose 0<m<M and 0<ϵ< 1/2. On C3, let

This is why the continuum implication uses a true exponential upper bound on a total family
of states, with controlled prefactors and limiting norms. Ordinary finite-time fits and additive
Monte Carlo error bars do not supply that hypothesis.
For a reproducible illustration only, the companion rational checker uses M = 1, m = 1/10,
and ϵ = 10−6. It certifies the displayed crossover and sample correlator values using positive
exponential and logarithm series with explicit tails. These numbers describe the counterexample
above and have no SU(2) mass interpretation.

61 Cutoff gaps, surviving spectra, and physical scale calibration
61.1 Lattice mass gap
For each coupling under discussion, choose an infinite-volume Wilson Gibbs measure µβ on Z4
that is invariant under lattice translations and reflection positive for time reflections. Outside
a proved uniqueness range, this choice is part of the data and is not silently assumed to be
independent of the limiting sequence. A weak limit of periodic-box measures has these properties
[7]. The Osterwalder–Seiler construction [7] builds a Hilbert space Hβ from gauge-invariant local
functions supported at positive times. It comes with a vacuum vector Ω = [1] and a transfer
matrix Tβ, a positive self-adjoint contraction with TβΩ = Ω; see also Lüscher [6].
Definition 61.1. The lattice mass gap is m(β) := − log∥Tβ|Ω⊥∥∈ [0,∞]. Along a trajectory of
spacings aj ↓ 0 and couplings βj, the physical gap is ∆j :=m(βj)/aj.

Scale setting and nontriviality. Mass-based scale setting is legitimate when positivity of the

nontrivial surviving states, the appropriate spacetime axioms, and the required identification with
Yang–Mills dynamics. Any asserted asymptotic calibration must be proved or stated explicitly as
a further hypothesis. The definition of physical units and proof of physical content are separate
steps.

Physical scale calibration, smoothing and the choice of observable algebra impose separate

62.3 Model-specific tests using Abelian and finite groups
Applicability to an Abelian or finite group is not, by itself, a contradiction. Strong-coupling decay
may correctly apply to both groups. Moreover, exponential decay of gauge-invariant correlations
at weak coupling is proved for finite gauge groups, including Z2, by Adhikari–Cao; Forsström
treats finite Abelian groups directly. [52, 53]
The useful obstruction is narrower: an argument claiming a weak-coupling continuum gap in
a model with a proved massless phase has to identify an assumption that fails there. Fröhlich–
Spencer’s four-dimensional Abelian massless-phase theorem is a relevant check, with its exact
action, observables and hypotheses preserved. Its large-N cyclic-group statement must not be
replaced by a statement about Z2. [54]
A theorem using quaternion/S3 geometry is already specific to SU(2), even if some general
machinery also applies to Abelian groups. Applicability to another group is not itself an error.
62.4 Time smoothing and reflection positivity
Lüscher’s 2010 work motivates positive-flow-time gauge observables. Lüscher–Weisz prove their
finiteness to all orders in perturbation theory once the underlying four-dimensional theory is
renormalized. This does not by itself give a nonperturbative continuum construction or a uniform
physical mass gap. [55, 56]
Four-dimensional gradient flow smooths in the Euclidean time direction as well as space. Conse-
quently, a flowed observable nominally labelled by a point in positive time need not be measurable
with respect to the original positive-time field algebra. The original reflection-positivity proof
cannot simply be reused for the flowed algebra. The following direct counterexample makes that
obstruction precise; the calculation is explicit.
62.4.1 Proposition RV.1 (time heat smoothing need not preserve reflection positiv-
ity)
Let ω > 0, τ > 0, and define the stationary covariance
Kτ(t) = 1 2π ∫ R eipte−2τ(p2+ω2) p2 +ω2 dp.
The centered Gaussian process with covariance Kτ is not reflection positive with respect to
the positive-time algebra generated by its own time-labelled field. In contrast, the unsmoothed
covariance K0(t) =e−ω|t|/(2ω) is reflection positive.
Proof. The Gaussian multiplier makes every differentiated integral absolutely convergent.
Therefore Kτ is a real even smooth function, and
Kτ(0)> 0, K′ τ(0) = 0, K′′ τ (0) =− 1 2π ∫ R p2e−2τ(p2+ω2) p2 +ω2 dp< 0.
For small positive h, Taylor expansion gives

For each such h, continuity implies that, for a sufficiently small ϵ> 0,

The same calculation applies to each fixed spatial Fourier mode of a heat-smoothed free massive
scalar field. It does not show that flowed observables are useless, nor that Yang–Mills gradient
flow always violates a particular chosen physical construction. It shows that preservation of
a positive-time algebra is an additional issue. One can instead retain the original physical
Hilbert space, establish suitable approximation/localization theorems, or analyze an appropriate
spatial-only smoothing scheme; each route needs its own proof.
62.5 Gaussian fields and non-Gaussian composite observables
A continuum Yang–Mills identification requires the appropriate local observables and dynamics,
together with Euclidean symmetry, locality, clustering and nontriviality. Lattice symmetry alone
does not establish these limiting properties.
A blanket demand that “some observable have a nonzero fourth cumulant” is too weak to certify
interactions. For a standard normal variable X, the composite observable Y = X2 − 1 already
has fourth cumulant 48. Indeed,
log EetY =−t− 1 2 log(1− 2t) = ∑
n≥2
2n−1

so κn(Y ) = 2n−1(n− 1)! for n≥ 2. Thus non-Gaussian gauge-invariant composites can occur
even over a Gaussian underlying field. A claim of nontrivial interacting Yang–Mills behavior
must specify the fields, algebra and dynamical property being distinguished.
62.6 What an exact bootstrap certificate must establish
Kazakov–Zheng derive linear closed SU(2) loop equations and bootstrap plaquette bounds using
semidefinite optimization. Their paper identifies MOSEK and discusses numerical precision
limitations. These finite-dimensional constraints motivate exact certification of the resulting
bounds. [35]
A rigorous certificate must include the exact loop identities and all normalization conventions, a
mathematically valid feasible relaxation containing the actual Gibbs expectations, exact dual
coefficients, positive-semidefinite slack certificates, and a verified weak-duality calculation. An
interval eigenvalue bound is useful only after propagating every residual into an explicit objective
correction. A list of floating-point optima is not a certificate. Finite-loop plaquette bounds alone
also do not establish an infinite-distance mass gap.
The continuum application therefore requires renormalized correlation bounds and reconstruction
assumptions in addition to any fixed-spacing comparison estimate.
