63 Matter representations and screening
The comparison models in this part have different field content, geometry, or dimension from
four-dimensional pure Wilson theory. Their exact calculations identify sufficient estimates for the
specified models and the additional matching assumptions needed for a microscopic application.
Published semiclassical mechanisms and exactly solvable gauge theories retain their original
attribution.
63.1 Why the fermion representation matters
Proposition 63.1 (Centre-charge obstruction to screening). For SU(N), an external source in
a representation of nonzero N-ality cannot form a singlet by tensoring with any finite number of
adjoint particles.
Proof. Let z = e2πi/NI be the central generator. On a representation of N-ality k, z acts as
e2πik/N. It acts as 1 on every adjoint factor. Therefore it acts as e2πik/N ̸= 1 on the entire tensor
product. On a singlet it would act as 1, so no singlet subrepresentation can occur.
For SU(2) this is the familiar fact that tensoring an odd number of half-integer spins with integer
spins cannot produce spin zero. This is a kinematic obstruction to screening; it does not itself
prove a positive string tension.
Fundamental dynamical fermions change the conclusion. If finite-energy static-light colour
singlets exist, a separated pair supplies a variational state with
E0(R)≤ 2Mstatic−light +o(1), R→∞, (63.1)
after a common static self-energy subtraction. A potential E0(R) ∼σR with σ > 0 cannot then
persist to arbitrarily large R. This argument assumes the stated singlets and their asymptotic
separation; it is not a construction of them. String breaking is compatible with the absence of
isolated observable quarks.
63.2 Kinematics is not dynamics: the two-dimensional lesson
The centre-charge proposition is sometimes read as “adjoint matter cannot screen fundamental
probes”. That reading is false as a dynamical statement. Gross, Klebanov, Matytsin and Smilga
showed that in two-dimensional SU(N) gauge theory with massless adjoint Majorana fermions a
fundamental probe is screened: the string tension of the fundamental Wilson loop vanishes, even
though no finite number of adjoints can neutralise its N-ality [57]. For a small adjoint mass m
confinement returns with a string tension proportional to m times the fermion condensate. The
mechanism is that the string tension is a statement about the vacuum energy in the presence
of a background electric field, and with massless adjoints a chiral rotation can remove that
background; the asymptotic state carries the centre charge non-locally rather than in a finite
bound state. The lesson for the four-dimensional problem is that a proof of confinement must
control energies, not representation theory. Whether the massless four-dimensional adjoint theory
328
=== PAGE 329 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
confines fundamental probes in the sense of an area law is not settled by any result used in this
analysis.
64 Symmetries and the mixed anomaly of adjoint QCD
The gauge contribution to the mixed anomaly constrains possible infrared phases; the constraints
do not determine a mass gap by themselves.
Consider SU(N) Yang-Mills with nf massless adjoint Weyl fermions λa I, I = 1,...,nf. Because
the matter is adjoint, the ZN centre acts trivially on all fields and the theory has a Z(1) N one-form
(centre) symmetry [58]. The classical U(1) acting on all fermions by a common phase is broken
by the anomaly to the discrete subgroup under which the measure in a unit-charge instanton
background is invariant; an adjoint Weyl fermion has 2N zero modes in such a background, so the
surviving symmetry is Z2Nnf, containing fermion number (−1)F as its order-two element. The
faithful symmetry group also involves identifications with flavour transformations; the argument
below uses only this common axial transformation and the centre background.
Proposition 64.1 (Mixed centre–chiral anomaly phase). Work on a spin four-manifold with
vanishing gravitational index contribution, for example a flat four-torus, and couple the theory
to an admissible background Z(1) N gauge field. Assume the resulting PSU(N) gauge bundle has
topological charge Q∈ 1 N Z and adjoint Weyl index 2NQ. Under the generator of Z2Nnf the
fermion measure changes by the phase e−2πiQ. For Q = k/N with N ∤k this phase is nontrivial.
Proof. Under the stated geometric assumptions, the gauge part of the index theorem gives each
adjoint Weyl operator index nL −nR = 2NQ by the index theorem (the adjoint Dynkin index is
2N in the normalisation where the fundamental has index 1). The generator multiplies every
fermion by e2πi/(2Nnf ), so the zero-mode measure (whose transformation depends only on the
index) acquires e−2πinf 2NQ/(2Nnf ) = e−2πiQ. For integer Q this is 1, so this axial subgroup is
preserved in the absence of a centre background; for Q =k/N it equals e−2πik/N.
A phase that cannot be removed by a local counterterm is a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly between
Z(1) N and Z2Nnf [58, 59, 60]. The cited anomaly-matching arguments exclude a trivially gapped
infrared phase that preserves both symmetries. Symmetry breaking, gapless excitations, or a
nontrivial topological sector can instead match the anomaly. The following small-circle effective
potential realises one symmetry-breaking possibility. For SU(2) with nf = 2, the symmetry is
Z8 and the small-circle analysis of Section 68 realises its generator on the dual photon as
σ↦−→σ +π, (64.1)
because the monopole vertex carries eiσ times 2nf = 4 fermion zero modes, and e2πi·4/8 = −1
must be compensated. The bion potential ζ(1 − cos 2σ) is invariant under (64.1); its two minima
σ = 0,π are exchanged. Hence Z8 → Z4 with two vacua, in agreement with the anomaly. The
π-walls of Sections 69–73 are the domain walls between these vacua, and the deconfinement of
fundamental probes on them (Theorem 73.1) is the effective-model realisation of discrete anomaly
inflow on the wall [61, 62, 63].

Two physical comments, both attributed. First, the a field is sourced at order µu′′(0) in the

SU(2) theory distinguishes only the N-ality n mod 2: the n = 2 string must be able to break
by W-pair creation, which the abelian description cannot see. This was noted by Douglas and
Shenker [67] and is a general limitation of abelianised descriptions of confinement, including the
one in Sections 68–73, where the analogue is the two-wall structure of the fundamental interface.
This is a local effective Higgs calculation. The condensate notation is a gauge-fixed description.
The vacuum algebra does not prove the exact quantum spectrum or uniform control as |µ| becomes
large. Removing all superpartners also removes the protected structure used to determine (65.1);
the calculation cannot simply be continued to pure Yang-Mills.

isometric image of it. The cited linear-programming proof also excludes a tuple with repeated

labelled tuples as well as distinct sets, and each coincident off-diagonal pair contributes the
strictly positive discrepancy aq(1) −h(1). Thus equality cannot occur with repeated eigenvalues.

the summability assumption permit integration against ν≥ 0, giving V (Ω)≥V (Ωc).

66.2 Where the one-loop centre-symmetric minimum ends
With a common mass m for the adjoint fermions (periodic boundary conditions) the standard
one-loop potential becomes

h(0) = 1, h decreasing to zero. The coefficients are no longer of the form (66.4) (they be-

minimum is lost at a finite mass. For SU(2) the curvature at ϕ = π/2 is proportional to∑
n(−1)n+1[nfh(nmL) − 1]/n2. A 400-term numerical sum gives a local-stability threshold near

indicates that the global minimum moves earlier, near mL = 2.00 for nf = 2, consistent with a
first-order transition of this one-loop potential. These are numerical estimates with finite series
and angular discretisation, not certified transition values. They illustrate why fermion decoupling
at fixed small L requires an additional analysis of the holonomy potential.

67 Fermion exchange and an exactly evaluated pair integral
In the semiclassical description, a fundamental monopole has action S0 = 4π2/g2 and two zero
modes per adjoint Weyl flavour. Its vertex contains fermion fields. Pairing a monopole with the
appropriate anti-Kaluza-Klein monopole permits their contraction, leaving magnetic charge 2
and topological charge 0. This is the magnetic-bion mechanism [68].
We now isolate the actual mathematical calculation. A three-dimensional massless fermion
propagator scales as r−2. Contracting 2nf propagators contributes r−4nf. Let A> 0 denote the
Coulomb-repulsion length. Omitting overall determinants and core corrections, define

67.1 An explicit core-tail estimate
The fraction of the model integral coming from 0 <r<r0 is Γ(4nf − 3,A/r0)/Γ(4nf − 3). For
nf = 2 and A/r0 = 50, this is e−50 ∑4 j=0 50j/j! < 6 · 10−17. The support code certifies the
inequality with rational arithmetic, using e50 >∑150 j=0 50j/j!.
This tiny number does not bound the error of replacing the microscopic monopole core by
the model. The true core weight would require its own comparison estimate. The calculation
establishes integrability, a typical separation and an exact benchmark, not the complete bion
determinant or a convergent cluster expansion.

68.1 Quadratic theory
Expanding about σ = 0 gives V′′(0) = 4ζ. With canonical field φ = √ Kσ,
m2 0 = 4ζ K, ⟨σ(x)σ(0)⟩Gaussian = e−m0|x| 4πK|x|, x̸= 0. (68.3)
To check the propagator, (−∇2 + m2 0)e−m0r/(4πr) = 0 for r > 0; the integral of the out-
ward gradient at a small sphere fixes its unit delta-function source. Division by K gives the
normalization.
The dimensions are [K] = mass, [ζ] = mass3, [m0] = mass, and [T ] = mass2. Equation (68.3)
proves an exact Gaussian decay statement. It is not a nonperturbative spectral theorem for the
interacting microscopic theory. The Weyl identification and the physical observable algebra must
also be respected when interpreting a Cartan field as an observable.

68.2 The Wilson charge fixes the wall count
The insertion exp(iq
∫
Σ B·dS) shifts the dual gradient by a sheet of strength 4πq. A fundamental
probe thus imposes total monodromy 2π. Adjacent minima of (68.2) are separated by only π.
Consequently a fundamental-charge interface requires two elementary walls. This normalization
agrees with the double-wall structure studied in [61]; a single π wall is not the fundamental
string. Section 73 turns this counting into a theorem about the energy functional, including the
complementary statement that the excess energy on a wall stays bounded with probe separation.

Remark 69.4 (Threshold resonance ). The bounded solution ψ = tanh[m0(z−z0)] of Lψ = m2 0ψ
is a zero-energy resonance exactly at the continuum threshold (the reflectionless Pöschl–Teller
well). Under a generic perturbation of the potential or kinetic function this half-bound state
either dissolves into the continuum or becomes a genuine bound state. The numerical calculations
in Section 72 indicate a wall-localised mode just below threshold for the specified example.

Remark 70.4 (Distinct harmonic sensitivity of tension and curvature). The first derivative of
the tension at the unperturbed model has coefficients hn ∼ 1 2 logn, while V′′(0) has coefficients
proportional to n2. This is a local linear-response statement. A nonlinear tension estimate
under only a logarithmically weighted error requires additional control of the vacuum locations
and nonnegativity of the potential; that control does not follow from the derivative formula.
The weighted n2 hypothesis of Theorem 70.1 supplies the stated global positivity and curvature
bounds.

72 Linear stability of the perturbed wall

Remark 72.2 (Bound states). Unlike the leading model, the partner operator QQ† is not of
constant coefficients when Z or V is perturbed, so the theorem does not exclude further discrete
eigenvalues in (0,m2 curv). Such eigenvalues are internal (shape) modes of the wall. For the
certified example of Section 71 two numerical methods produce a candidate eigenvalue
λ1 = 4.08380 (threshold m2 curv = 4.088, binding m2 curv −λ1 = 0.0042), (72.4)
from a generalised finite-difference eigenproblem on boxes up to |z| ≤ 384 and a shooting
computation of the Jost mismatch, agreeing to 2 · 10−5. These calculations do not include
interval bounds on discretisation, tails, or the number of eigenvalues. Its wavefunction extends
over ∼ 1/

threshold resonance. The numerical result is consistent with its binding under this perturbation.
In the linearised 2 + 1-dimensional effective theory such a mode would propagate along the wall
with mass √λ1 below the bulk linear-fluctuation threshold. The translational branch remains
gapless along the wall, and no full interacting quantum spectral gap follows.

sector. Denote the infima of E over the two sectors by Ebulk(d; R) and Ewall(d; R); with no
probes (d = 0, no cut) the corresponding values are 0 and 2RTπ, the latter attained by σ∗(y).

E≥ 2Tπ[ |k|(2R−d− 2ϱ) + |k− 1|(d− 2ϱ) ]; for R≥ d the minimum over k∈ Z is at k = 0,
which is (a).
Upper bounds. Let ρ(y) = σ∗(−y)−π; it is a wall from 0 (at y = −∞) to −π (at y = +∞) and has
the same one-dimensional energy Tπ as σ∗, because Z and V are π-periodic and the energy density
is invariant under y→−y. Let M(y) = ρ(y) + 2π1y>0 −σ∗(y), i.e. M(y) = σ∗(−y) + π−σ∗(y)
for y > 0 and σ∗(−y) −π−σ∗(y) for y < 0; it decays exponentially at ±∞ by the pointwise
bounds and the first-order wall equation and M(0+) −M(0−) = 2π. Let λ∈C∞(R) increase
from 0 on (−∞,−1] to 1 on [1,∞), let χ(r) be a smooth cutoff equal to 1 for r≤ 1 and 0 for
r≥ 2, and let ϑ∈ (−π,π] be the polar angle. Define the junction function

smooth on R2 \{0}, equal to λ(x) for r≥ 2, with Λ(x, 0) = 1 for x> 0 and Λ(x, 0) = 0 for x< 0.

Remark 73.2. The constants CB,CW contain the logarithmically divergent Coulomb self-energy
of the probe lines (in the dual picture, the 1/r gradient of a vortex), which may be subtracted
using a common fixed-core convention when comparing configurations with the same probes.
The displayed bounds retain their stated ϱ dependence. In the one-component leading model the
two walls between bulk probes repel, so the minimiser pushes them apart as far as the geometry
allows; the excess Ebulk(d; R) − 2Tπd therefore grows slowly with d (Figure 6), the “double-string”
of [61]. On the wall the two half-walls 0 →π and 0 →−π are exactly degenerate, which is the
effective-model form of the statement that the probe’s 2π monodromy is absorbed by the Z2
shift (64.1) across the wall.

For a fully exact gauge-theory comparison, consider pure two-dimensional Yang-Mills on the plane
in its heat-kernel formulation [31, 72, 73, 74]. There are no added fermions in this subsection.
These results are established mathematics and physics, reproduced here as benchmarks.

the tensor-product channels occur in the inner area A1. For two fundamental SU(2) loops their
algebraic weights are 1/4 and 3/4, associated with the singlet and adjoint channels. As A1
grows the adjoint contribution is exponentially suppressed relative to the singlet term. These
coefficients are character-decomposition weights, not probabilities of dynamical screening events.
A single-loop area law and a singlet component in a two-loop correlator are distinct statements.

74.2 With fermions: the Gross–Klebanov–Matytsin–Smilga dichotomy
Adding dynamical adjoint fermions destroys the simple independent-face calculation, and the
result changes qualitatively [57]: for massless adjoint Majorana fermions the fundamental string
tension vanishes (screening), while for small mass m it is proportional to m⟨ ¯ψψ⟩. Together with
the proposition above, two-dimensional gauge theory supplies exact instances of three phenomena
that the four-dimensional discussion must distinguish—an area law for fundamental probes, pair
screening in the singlet channel, and dynamical screening by massless adjoint matter—none
of which is decided by representation theory alone. Two-dimensional pure Yang-Mills has no
propagating local gluons; its representation structure and continuum problem differ substantially
from four dimensions. None of these exact statements transfers to four dimensions without proof.
75 A finite Hamiltonian benchmark for the effective scalar theory
The static functional also motivates a quantum scalar model. This section specifies a finite
regularisation, proves its twist equivalence and a time-discretisation bound, and records numerical
spectra. A representation cutoff makes the Hamiltonian a finite matrix; the bounds below
concern that matrix and do not estimate the omitted rotor representations or identify it with
the microscopic Yang–Mills Hamiltonian.

75.2 Twists and sector-energy differences
Proposition 75.1 (Twist equivalence on a chain). Let Hθ be the compact Hamiltonian (75.1)
on a periodic chain, with every θℓ ∈{0,π}. Its spectrum depends on the link twists only through
Θ = ∑ ℓθℓ (mod 2π). The global operator C = ∏ x(−1)px commutes with Hθ, and reflection
|px⟩↦→|−px⟩ changes Θ to −Θ. These statements hold both before and after hard momentum
compression.
Proof. For a site set S, US = exp(iπ∑ x∈S px) is unitary, commutes with ΠP and the kinetic
terms, and conjugates Ux to −Ux precisely for x∈ S. Thus the on-site even harmonics are
unchanged, while a link twist changes by π precisely when that link crosses the boundary of S.
Successive choices of intervals move all twists to one link; their sum modulo 2π is the remaining
invariant. Taking S to be the whole chain proves the C symmetry. Momentum reflection replaces
every Ux by U† x and changes each twist to its negative. Since both unitaries commute with the
hard cutoff, the same conjugation identities hold for the compressed matrices.
On a cylinder the corresponding classification requires a flat Z2 link field, with zero twist around
each contractible plaquette; local plaquette fluxes are additional invariants for unrestricted twists.
For a periodic chain define the finite-size sector difference MP = E(π) 0,P −E(0) 0,P. For a flat twist
on a cylinder with physical extent L∥ parallel to the interface, define τP = (E(π) 0,P −E(0) 0,P )/L∥.
Identifying a limit of these quantities with an infinite-volume kink mass or wall tension requires
control of size and momentum cutoff. The twist changes signs of link terms without changing
the Hilbert-space dimension. The minimum register size at cutoff P is Ns⌈log2(2P + 1)⌉ qubits,
before auxiliary registers and error correction; this dimension count is not a gate-complexity
estimate.

76.2 Confining gauge dynamics need not gap all fermions
The small-circle theory retains neutral fermions. At weak coupling, the monopole vertex for
nf = 2 is a four-fermion operator; in three dimensions its free-field scaling dimension is 4 > 3.
The gauge-sector scalar mass calculation by itself therefore supplies no mass for every fermionic
or gauge-invariant composite channel. More generally, a full gap requires all physical low-energy
states to be controlled, not just one bosonic Hessian. The anomaly permits several infrared
realisations. The specified small-circle potential has degenerate vacua, but neither that feature
nor the anomaly supplies a gap in every channel.
76.3 The decoupling and decompactification steps are unproved
Increasing L to obtain R4 leaves the small-circle expansion. Positive masses at each finite
parameter do not imply a uniformly positive limit: m(L) = e−L is a counterexample to that
inference.
Decoupling the adjoint fermions while keeping a small circle is also nontrivial, and the numerical
one-loop calculation in Section 66 illustrates the obstruction: the centre-symmetric point ceases
to be the global minimum of (66.10) at mL ≈ 2.00 and ceases to be a local minimum at
mL = 2.280 (nf = 2). At the heavy-fermion endpoint the pure-gauge sign of (66.1) is recovered,
V1(π/2) −V1(0) = π2/(12L4) > 0. Thus the centre-symmetric mechanism used here cannot
simply be assumed to survive the fixed-small-L heavy-fermion limit. A joint path in mass,
circumference and possible deformations needs an actual phase and error analysis. Adiabatic
351
=== PAGE 352 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
continuity is a proposal to prove, not a substitute for such estimates; the quantum-simulation
formulation of Section 75 is one way to test it numerically, not to prove it.
The fixed-coupling pure-gauge contraction certificates do not supply the weighted Fourier,
fermionic or continuum bounds required here. Integrating fermions changes the effective measure,
so the pure-gauge comparison constants require a new derivation.
76.4 Uniform matching estimates needed for a microscopic application
The next useful target for this route is to derive the effective action from a defined microscopic
regularization and prove, for its actual coefficients,

and additional fields. Equation (76.3) is a sufficient target, not a claim that the microscopic
coefficients meet it. The local response in Theorem 70.2 has logarithmic harmonic weights;
a nonlinear replacement of the weighted n2 hypothesis requires additional nonnegativity and
fixed-vacuum assumptions.
A microscopic gap estimate must act on the full reconstructed physical vacuum complement.
The dense-subspace spectral passage in Section 48.1 applies once the corresponding physical-time
estimates and the nontrivial continuum construction have been supplied.
Uniform cutoff estimates must survive reconstruction, infinite volume, the change of geometry
and removal of added matter, while producing the intended nontrivial theory. Exponential decay
for a finite list of observables does not establish the dense-subspace premise. An exact wall
tension alone does not supply it either.

With the usual bare Wilson mass convention,

78.6 The exactly solvable electric Hamiltonian
An independent route starts from the electric part of the SU(2) lattice Hamiltonian. Unlike the
earlier static scalar functional, this is a quantum operator on a gauge-invariant Hilbert space.
Theorem 78.6 (Exact electric-limit string tension and gap). On a finite open cubic spatial
lattice with spacing a, impose Gauss law at every vertex, including its boundary, and let
HE = g2 2a ∑ e E2 e.
In the sector with two fundamental static sources separated by graph distance n, the ground energy
relative to the vacuum is 3g2n/(8a). Thus for collinear separation R =na,
VE(R) =σER, σE = 3g2 8a2 .
If the box contains a plaquette, the source-free physical gap is
∆E = 3g2 2a = 4aσE.
Both statements are independent of the box size once it contains the required path and plaquette.
Proof. Use the spin-network basis, on which E2 e has eigenvalue je(je + 1). The central element
−I in each Gauss constraint implies that the subgraph of half-integer-spin edges has odd degree
precisely at the source vertices. Such a subgraph contains a path connecting those vertices. At
least n edges therefore have Casimir at least 3/4. A shortest path carrying spin 1/2, with all
other edges trivial and the invariant source and internal intertwiners, attains that energy. The
vacuum with all spins zero has energy zero.
Without sources, a nonempty subgraph of nonzero-spin edges has no degree-one vertex: a single
nontrivial representation cannot contain a singlet. A finite graph of minimum nonzero degree at
least two has a cycle. On the cubic lattice every cycle has at least four edges, each with Casimir
at least 3/4. A spin-1/2 plaquette loop attains the lower bound 4(3/4)g2/(2a).
The exact identity ∆E = 4aσE is a sharp obstruction: finite positive string tension as a→ 0
forces the electric-model gap to zero. A positive lower bound on the gap instead forces its string
tension to diverge. This solved limit cannot supply both finite continuum string tension and a
positive gap.
Adding a positive magnetic term does not repair the proof. Ground energies in both
the vacuum and source sectors shift. For M >s> 0, take
Hv = diag(0,M), Hq = diag(s,M), B = diag(M, 0)≥ 0.
The ground-energy difference starts at s. Adding the same positive B makes both ground energies
equal M, so the difference becomes zero. Thus HE + HM ≥HE does not imply a lower bound
on the vacuum-subtracted static potential. This matrix example refutes that inference; it is not
a proposed Yang–Mills model.

79.3 Obstructions to absolute-error transport
Absolute accuracy does not preserve string tension. Fix 0 < δ < 1 and consider the
positive functions
w0(A) =e−σA, wδ(A) = (1−δ)e−σA +δ.
For every A≥ 0,|wδ(A)−w0(A)|≤δ. Nevertheless,
lim
A→∞
− 1 A logwδ(A) = 0.
This is a counterexample to an inference from absolute errors, not a claim that these functions
construct a Yang–Mills measure. Uniformly small errors in loop values can dominate an
exponentially small signal. The useful control is relative, logarithmic, or through mixed differences.
A positive limit cannot be inferred from positivity at finite size. The smooth function
σ(L) = σ0e−L/L0 is positive for every finite L and has zero limit. A proposal asserting no finite-L
phase transition still needs a quantitative lower bound at L =∞.
362
=== PAGE 363 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
A bulk action estimate is not automatically a defect estimate. Bounding the difference
of two actions by a small constant times the total volume does not control a loop free energy
after the infinite-volume limit. One must retain cancellation between the vacuum normalization
and the inserted expectation. The quantity Γs defined above does exactly that algebraically;
bounding it is the hard step.
Classical tension does not control quantum entropy. Theorem 77.2, Proposition 77.3, and
Theorem 77.4 concern a classical energy functional. A path integral also sums over fluctuations
and interfaces. A lower bound on a minimizing classical configuration is not a lower bound on
the logarithm of the normalized quantum integral. Treating these quantities as identical would
assume the required quantum estimate.
The small-circle expansion cannot be extended by substitution. In a centre-symmetric
SU(N) background,
mW = 2π NL, NLΛ≪ 1
is the semiclassical scale window. At fixed N and physical Λ, decompactification exits it.
Increasing N also worsens this particular scale separation. Centre-stabilized large-N volume
independence does not, by itself, preserve the abelian calculation across this loss of control [82].
Matter content matters. Removing adjoint fermions changes the holonomy potential and the
quantum measure. The effective-model analysis itself shows that its one-loop centre-symmetric
minimum is lost in the fixed-small-circle heavy-fermion limit. Fundamental dynamical matter
introduces possible string breaking, so an unscreened fundamental-probe area law is not the
universal definition of confinement for every theory with fermions.
These obstructions explain why solving a more accurate scalar wall, or simulating that same
scalar theory on more sites, does not close the stated four-dimensional target.
79.4 Boundary-uniform covariance as an external confinement criterion
Chatterjee’s lattice result [80], Definition 2.3 and Theorem 2.4, gives a useful alternative: expo-
nential decay of bounded local covariances, uniformly over the specified cubes and all boundary
conditions, implies rectangular Wilson area laws for irreducible representations nontrivial on the
centre. Schematically, its premise has the form
| CovB,δ(f,g)|≤K1e−K2 dist(f,g),
with |f|,|g|≤ 1, the support convention specified in that paper, and constants independent of
the cube and boundary data. A vacuum mass estimate does not establish this stronger premise.
Even a positive lattice area coefficient c(β) at each finite coupling does not suffice for a physical
continuum claim. Along a prescribed scaling trajectory one needs, at minimum, quantitative
control compatible with
lim inf
a↓0
c(β(a))
a2 > 0,
plus renormalized loop convergence and control of the lower-order terms. The physical area is
a2 times the lattice plaquette count. This requirement is not provided by the effective-model
analysis.

79.7 Twisted partition functions and sector normalization
The Tomboulis–Yaffe route provides an independent microscopic comparison. For a reflection-
positive Wilson SU(N) theory on a suitable torus, let Z[k] be its partition function with the
standard centre twist k on a plaquette stack winding around the d− 2 transverse periodic
directions, so its dual surface is closed and wraps the torus. Set
qΛ = 1− 1 N N−1∑ k=0 Z[k] Z .
For a normalized rectangular Wilson loop of nonzero N-ality, Kanazawa’s generalization gives
[83]
|⟨W (C)⟩|≤ 2qAlat(C)/(NµNν) Λ .

rectangle’s lattice side lengths. Thus a sufficient defect estimate would be
− logqΛ ≥σ∗a2NµNν

uniformly along appropriate thermodynamic and continuum sequences. A single finite-box value
qΛ < 1 does not establish this rate. The inequality controls bare lattice loops; renormalized
continuum observables still require their own limiting argument.
It is not legitimate to assume that a local RG interpolation can be continued over every required
scale. Ito and Seiler give the elementary counterexample Ψ(λ,t) = e−t − 1 + 2λ: its locally
regular solution t = − log(1 − 2λ) cannot reach λ = 1 [84]. Uniform continuation is a proof
obligation, not a consequence of the local implicit-function theorem.
79.8 The physical continuum scale
The weak-coupling trajectory imposes a different quantitative scale. For the normalized Wilson
action, βW = 2N/g2 0 →∞ as a→ 0. The universal perturbative coefficients are [85]

coefficients cannot be substituted without threshold matching.
Proposition 79.5 (Absolute perturbative accuracy does not resolve the target). For each finite
real p, gp/Φ(g) →∞ as g↓ 0. Extending Φ by zero at g = 0 gives a smooth function with every
derivative zero there. Consequently the functions sΦ(g), s≥ 0, have identical formal power series,
although their ratio to Φ(g) is s.
Proof. The logarithm of the first ratio is 1/(b0g2) plus a constant and a multiple of logg; the
positive inverse square dominates. Each derivative of Φ is Φ times a finite sum of inverse
powers of g, hence tends to zero by the same argument. Induction proves smooth extension and
flatness.
Thus an absolute error budget Cgp alone cannot certify a positive coefficient of order Φ(g). This
does not exclude a favorable one-sided estimate, exact cancellation, or a nonperturbative bound.
Nor is it an impossibility theorem for renormalization methods.
For a concrete illustration, the positive functions

have identical perturbative expansions at every fixed lattice rectangle. Their unit-increment
Creutz differences equal sΦ(g) exactly. When a2nm→ A and Φ(g) ∼ (aΛ)2, the area term
approaches sΛ2A. These functions illustrate nonuniformity in loop size; they are not asserted to
arise from Yang–Mills measures.

79.10 Exact blocking and the full action
For an integer block factor b, assign each coarse link the ordered product of the fine links in its
straight chain:

so its expectation is preserved exactly. The action SB generally contains many interactions; it is
not asserted to be another Wilson plaquette action. For nonaligned observables the exact coarse
insertion is instead Eµ[W|B].
Reflection positivity is also preserved if B intertwines the reflections and pulls the coarse
positive-half algebra into the fine positive-half algebra: for such G,
(B∗µ)(G◦θcG) =µ((G◦B)◦θ(G◦B))≥ 0.
This identity gives no contraction or area coefficient for SB.
For a centre twist S[k] = S + ∆Sk, put hk = e−∆Sk. The exact coarse insertion and twisted

One must retain sector normalizations. For instance, actions S and S+c have identical normalized
measures but partition functions differing by e−c.
A common bulk residual does not cancel automatically. Let approximate weights on two

a Z2 2-chain σ with ∂σ = C. Project σ onto the (µ,ν) coordinate torus of C. The projection

its complement. Since RT≤ N 2/4 < N 2 −RT, σ contains at least RT plaquettes. At order

the rectangle. If two neighbouring plaquettes had different transverse positions, a link strictly
inside the rectangle would occur once in ∂σ. Hence σ is the planar rectangle itself. Gluing
with

80.1.3 The renormalization condition and the definition of βk
At level k, put n = 2k and define, on the reference box,
χk(β) :=− log w(2n, 2n)w(n,n) w(2n,n)2 . (80.2)
This is the physical Creutz ratio [90] of the loops with sides ℓ×ℓ, 2ℓ×ℓ and 2ℓ× 2ℓ. At k = 0
these are the lattice 1 × 1, 2 × 1 and 2 × 2 loops. The perimeter and the four right-angle corners
cancel identically.
Theorem 80.3 (The trajectory is well defined). For every c∗> 0 and k≥ 0, χk is real-analytic
on (0,∞),
χk(β) =−4k log(β/4) +O(β) (β↓ 0), χk(β)→ 0 (β→∞).
HenceZk :={β > 0 :χk(β) =c∗} is nonempty and compact, and
βk := minZk
is well defined.

Proof. All three loop expectations are strictly positive (Lemma 80.1) and are ratios of entire
functions of β, so χk is real-analytic. The exponent in Lemma 80.2(a) is 4n2 + n2 − 2 · 2n2 = n2.
Lemma 80.2(b) gives χk → 0. The intermediate value theorem gives a root. Zk is closed in
(0,∞), bounded away from 0 because χk →∞, and bounded because χk → 0<c∗.
Definition 80.4 (Reference-loop trajectory). The trajectory is the tuple
ak =ℓ2−k, βk = min{β > 0 :χk(β) =c∗},
box: reference torus (Z/M2kZ)4 (side L =Mℓ) and enclosing tori M′≥M even,
boundary conditions: periodic for all links, renormalization condition: χk(βk) =c∗.

Then ˆFk(C) =c∗A(C)/ℓ2 exactly on the three reference loops at every k.

Remark 80.6 (What is not known about the trajectory). (i) Uniqueness. Monotonicity of χk
in β is not known: Griffiths-type inequalities are not available for SU(2). The minimal-root
rule removes the ambiguity, but it is a convention.
(ii) Escape to weak coupling. We cannot prove βk →∞. If supkβk = B <∞, the lattice Creutz
ratio at size 2k would stay equal to c∗ at couplings in (0,B]. Excluding this requires a lower
bound on large lattice Creutz ratios at fixed coupling, which is a confinement statement in
its own right. If the strong-coupling cluster expansion is granted, βk eventually leaves the
strong-coupling region. Nothing proved here controls it afterwards.
(iii) The ultraviolet budget presupposes asymptotic freedom along the trajectory. The budget
ηk ≤Cg4 k with g2 k = 4/βk ≤ 1/(α + γk) requires βk ≥ 4(α + γk). This is a nonperturbative
statement about Definition 80.4 and is not established. Perturbatively, the identification is
∆(1/g2) = 2b0 log 2 per halving of a, with b0 = 11/(24π2). This gives ∆β→ 8b0 log 2 =
0.2575 ... and γ = 0.0644; three-loop data are in [85]. It identifies the expected ultraviolet
scaling and plays no role in any proof.

80.3 Exact blocking and the defect Dk
Identify the coarse torus Λk with the even sites of Λk+1. For a coarse link e, let Ve = Ue,1Ue,2,

Proof. (a) Sβk ◦B is constant on each fibre. (b) A fine plaquette lies in a coarse plaquette exactly

Remark 80.12 (Why this is not yet a controlled expansion). The representation (a) is exact, but
it does not provide an interaction range bounded independently of the box for SB k+1. The first
midpoint integration already produces − logJ(β˜r) of twelve-staple sums (Proposition 80.10).
Iterating can produce interactions on larger connected sets; their decay must be controlled
separately. A convergent polymer expansion of − log E[e−~Dk |B] can be sought in a sufficiently
small-coupling domain. The definition of the trajectory does not prove either that it stays in
such a domain or that it escapes to weak coupling (Remark 80.6). On the weak-coupling side,
Bałaban’s renormalization-group programme provides localized effective-action and coupling-
renormalization estimates in the small-field regime of four-dimensional lattice gauge theory
[13, 86]. It uses its own averaging blocking and gauge fixing, and it does not address the
large-loop ratio required in the scale comparison. Its conclusions are not assumed to control the
loop ratios below. Replacing Dk by a shift of one plaquette coupling is therefore an uncontrolled
approximation in four dimensions. The next proposition shows exactly what such a replacement
does in the one case where everything is computable.

80.5.3 Testing proposed simplifications against the ratio
(T1) Small-βr expansion of the one-link action. Not uniform along the trajectory: at z = 15 the
quartic truncation is off by 114 (the one-link formula).
(T2) Large-βr (saddle) expansion. Not uniform: r = 0 is attained. Discarding the small-r region
would require either its probability to be small relative to e−F (C), or cancellation between
the two terms of Γs. Neither is available.
(T3) Replacing Dk by a one-coupling shift. In two dimensions this is exact for fun-
damental loops (Proposition 80.13). In four dimensions the replacement error
δD = ∑ X δΦX contributes ∑ X[ν(WCδΦX)/ν(WC) −ν(δΦX)], and the only general bound
is (1 +ν(|WC|)/ν(WC)) ∑ X ∥δΦX∥∞, proportional to the volume.
(T4) Bounding Γs by the size of the defect. For smooth fields, ∑ p⊂cell(1 − 1 2 TrUp) at spacing
ak+1 and ∑ P (1 − 1 2 TrVP ) at spacing ak agree to leading order, so the classical part of ~Dk
is (βk+1 −βk) times the fine action density. This is a heuristic statement. Relative to the
action, this is of order (βk+1 −βk)/βk+1 ≈ 2b0 log 2 g2 k. Since ∑ kg2 k diverges logarithmically
when g2 k ∼ 1/(α + γk), no bound proportional to the size of ~Dk can meet the budget
ηk ≤ Cg4 k. A proof of (A) must use the cancellation enforced by the renormalization
condition, which removes this leading term for the reference loops by construction.
(T5) Absolute instead of relative errors. Already refuted in Section 79.3. Lemma 80.16 quantifies
the loss as eF/4.

(β between the strong-coupling radius and the onset of asymptotic scaling), no rigorous technique

80.7 The starting bound
Strong-coupling input (SC). There are βsc ∈ (0,

the one external input of this section.

Scope of the starting estimate. The reference-loop trajectory uses the Wilson action itself,
and Proposition 80.5 places its first point in the stated strong-coupling region. Assumption (SC),
including its uniformity in β, is explicit. The resulting area bound concerns the infinite-volume
limit. Local convergence transfers a comparison for each fixed loop to sufficiently large boxes,
with a tolerance and a box size that may depend on that loop. It does not yield a positive
uniform half-box estimate when the loop grows with the box. Corollary 80.19(c) leaves its
half-box coefficient undetermined.
Choice of the reference Creutz ratio. The sufficient numerical choice c∗ > 21.97 fixes
a coarse reference scale through the stated finite-loop equation. If an independently justified
area-dominated regime gave χ(ℓ,ℓ) ≃σℓ2, it would suggest ℓ≃ 4.7 σ−1/2 at this threshold. That
interpretation is heuristic here. Neither departure from strong coupling nor the number of
blocking steps needed to reach a weak-coupling regime is proved by the matching construction.
Estimate (A′) remains unproved along the selected sequence, irrespective of which coupling
regime it visits.
80.8 Limits
What survives. If (A′) and (B′) were proved, Corollary 80.19(b) would hold at every level, for
the chosen infinite-volume limit. Both conclusions survive any further limit that exists. If, along
a subsequence, potential differences Vk(R)−Vk(R′) converge as k→∞, the limit obeys
V (R)−V (R′)≥σ∗(R−R′),
which is the requested V (R) ≥ σ∗R− 2B∗ with the additive reference fixed by V (R′). By
Theorem 80.18, the limit is also concave and nondecreasing, so V′(R) ≥ σ∗ wherever it is
differentiable.
What is not established.
(i) Existence of the continuum limit. A Cauchy bound |ˆFk+1(C) − ˆFk(C)|≤MC(k + 1)−1−δ is
not proved. Note that a Cauchy bound with loop-dependent MC would not imply (A′).
Confinement needs MC controlled by ηA(C), which is a statement of the same type as (A).
(ii) Infinite volume. A unique, subsequence-independent infinite-volume state at fixed k is not
established here outside the stated strong-coupling regime. Elsewhere compactness gives
subsequential local limits, which may depend on the subsequence.
(iii) Identification. Even if all limits existed, identifying them with a nontrivial continuum
Yang–Mills theory requires the axioms (reflection positivity survives; Euclidean invariance
and nontriviality do not follow from anything here).
(iv) Mass gap. An area law does not by itself give a spectral gap; this is a separate problem.

SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Endpoint of the construction. The finite-level matching, exact blocking representation and
lifted reflection-positive interpolation are explicit. They identify the normalized action insertion
whose control would propagate an area bound. The reduced estimate (A′), together with the
starting bound, is a sufficient criterion for a positive bare asymptotic area coefficient at every
level. It has not been established along the four-dimensional trajectory. Renormalized loop
convergence, physical spectral control and identification of a nontrivial continuum theory remain
additional tasks.

Part VIII
Numerical evidence and conclusions
81 Lattice blocking experiments and effective-action diagnostics
The retained simulation records contain two complementary experiments: matching blocked
Wilson observables across lattice sizes, and estimating coefficients of a finite effective-action
ansatz. Their role is to test possible coarse-graining constructions. Their fitted masses and action
coefficients are statistical estimates; they do not certify a uniform physical spectral bound.
81.1 Simulation and blocking definitions
The ensembles use the four-dimensional Wilson weight exp(β∑ p TrUp/2), with β = 4/g2 0. Links
are unit quaternions. The supplied simulation codes use heat-bath updates, with over-relaxation in
the larger runs [90, 91]. Lattice sizes extend to 324 for blocking and 223 ×40 for the scalar-channel
measurements.
For each coarse link, let W be its two-link straight transporter and let Q1,...,Q6 be the four-link
paths that move one fine step in a transverse direction, two steps in the coarse-link direction,
and back one transverse step. Define the normalized staple map
Bc(U)µ(X) = Wµ(X) +c∑6 k=1 Qk,µ(X) |Wµ(X) +c∑6 k=1 Qk,µ(X)|.
The paths have common endpoints, so the map is gauge covariant wherever the denominator is
nonzero. This is a Swendsen-type blocking construction [92]. The exceptional zero set is excluded
when constructing numerical configurations; no smooth positive blocked Gibbs density follows
merely from this definition.
For two-lattice matching, configurations on L4 and (L/2)4 are blocked until their final lattice
sizes agree. Matching one blocked plaquette defines an observable-dependent effective coupling
and a step ∆β. Agreement of this one observable does not prove equality of the blocked measures
or a universal renormalization trajectory. The more extensively thermalized 324/164 records at
β0 = 2.4 give ∆β = 0.2412(5) at matching depth one and 0.243(2) at depth two. The supplied
two-loop comparison is approximately 0.275. An initial 164/84 survey gave a depth-dependent
spread near 0.21; the larger-lattice values replace that survey as the more informative estimate.
Neither set controls the asymptotic weak-coupling trajectory.

81.3 Haar blocking: an exact distinction between smoothing and decimation
Lemma 81.3 (Straight decimation preserves product Haar). For independent Haar-distributed

Label the four coarse sides by their positive orientations: (0,eµ), (2eµ,eν), (2eν,eµ), (0,eν),
with the last two reversed in the plaquette. Each straight path has two edges; its six bent
alternatives have steps (±eρ,eµ,eµ,∓eρ) with ρ̸= µ, and likewise for a ν side. Every first-
order summand has the same fine-link incidence parity as its selected bent path, because the
projection term inserts two extra copies of the straight path. A second-order correction on
one side has the parity of that straight path and two selected bent paths. The 24 first-order
possibilities and 144 single-side second-order possibilities all have an odd fine-link incidence.
Of the 216 pairs of first-order corrections on distinct sides, only two have every incidence
even: the two opposite sides both bend towards the plaquette interior. These counts follow
by listing the stated steps; the exact integer enumeration and word reductions are supplied in
code/conditioning/block_path_certificate.py.
For either surviving pair, let Q1,Q3 be the inward bent paths and W2,W4 the unchanged sides.
Their product Q1W2Q∗ 3W∗ 4 reduces to the identity. The two replaced straight transporters W1,W3
are independent Haar variables independent of these four paths. The Haar second moment is
E[⟨W,Q⟩W ] = Q/4, so integrating each first-order correction Qi −⟨Wi,Qi⟩Wi replaces it by
3Qi/4. Each surviving pair contributes (3/4)2 = 9/16. The two contributions sum to 9/8. The
uniform Taylor remainder proves the asymptotic statement.
Observables of the blocked Haar field with disjoint fine-link dependency sets are exactly indepen-
dent, even though its plaquette mean is positive. A plaquette mean and a worst-case sufficient
influence criterion therefore measure different properties.

81.4 Measured action flow and the proposed coefficient envelope
At β0 = 2.4, the 324 hot-start records give blocked plaquettes 0.58507(11), 0.3859(4), 0.1420(12)

Wilson coefficient alone discards sizeable compensating interactions.

fitted single-plaquette weight freshly reproduces 0.137339 for the last coefficient. This supplies
numerical evidence against that particular coefficientwise envelope for this blocking and ansatz.
Because the full omitted-action residual is unknown, it is not an exact counterexample for the
complete effective action.
The parameter scan c = 1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8 changes these comparisons. For c≥ 2 the first-step fitted
plaquette ratios fall below one in the recorded runs, while the omitted-loop diagnostic remains

supports Theorem 81.4.
82 Numerical evidence and its relation to the spectral claims
The numerical material has three distinct roles. Published glueball measurements provide evidence
about physical excitations. Recorded flow measurements permit an exact arithmetic check of a
finite empirical covariance. The coupled-replica experiment concerns an update algorithm. None
of these roles is interchangeable with a lower bound on the full vacuum-complement spectrum.

labels 100,..., 3999.[97] We follow that rule, leaving N = 3900 records; the compact extraction
preserves all 3999 original records so the selection is auditable.

gauge-invariant observables at this lattice spacing. It supplies neither local conditional-block
angles nor a physical transfer-gap bound, and does not construct a continuum limit.
82.4 A reported winding-channel comparison
The finite-box certificate in Section 4 is accompanied in the supplied research record by a
preliminary Monte Carlo report at β = 177/500 on 13 ×Nt periodic lattices. That report
describes four hot/cold chains with 1,000,000 retained measurements at Nt = 16 and two chains
with 300,000 retained measurements at Nt = 24. These are reported measurement counts, not

independent-sample counts. The raw six-chain records and their analysis executable were not
included in the supplied archives. Accordingly, the following summary preserves the reported
comparison but is not a reproduced numerical result of this version and contributes no input to
the mathematical certificate.
The gauge-invariant observable is the spatial winding loop Wi(t) = 1 2 TrUi(t), with correlation
C(d) = 1 3Nt 3∑ i=1 ∑ t ⟨Wi(t)Wi(t +d)⟩.
On this spatial torus the loop is closed and center odd. The report fits A(e−xd + e−x(Nt−d)) at
d = 1, 2, 3, with blocked covariance and 1,000 block-bootstrap refits. Its quoted results are

Both quoted percentile intervals contain the independently certified infinite-time transfer interval
[2.27102703117506, 2.27225894375269]. This numerical containment can be checked directly;
validating the sampling errors, thermalization and fit procedure requires the missing original
records. A finite-Nt fit also has possible excited-state and thermal contributions. The channel is
center-charged electric flux and does not determine the infinite-volume scalar-glueball mass.
83 Coupled-replica Monte Carlo: an algorithmic comparison
Thissectionanalysesthecoupled-updateexperimentrecordedwiththeresearchdata. Itsevolution
parameter is the number of update sweeps, not physical Euclidean time. No synchronization
rate, coupling time, or failure to synchronize is substituted for a physical transfer-operator gap.
83.1 A coupling with the correct Wilson heat-bath marginals
The simulated measure is four-dimensional pure SU(2) Wilson theory,
dµ(U) ∝ exp
[

on periodic L4 lattices with L = 2, 3, 4. Every plaquette contains four distinct links at these
extents. The usual conditional action is therefore linear in a chosen link U:
dµ(U| other links) ∝ eβ ReTr(US)/2 dU, ∥S∥≤ 6,
where S is the sum of its six staples and the norm is the Euclidean norm of its quaternion
coordinates. The source uses U =q0I−iq·σ.
For replicas A and B, hold their respective staples SA,SB fixed during a link update. Generate a
common sequence of independent Haar matrices Qj and uniforms uj. Replica r∈{A,B} accepts
the first candidate satisfying
uj ≤ exp
{

[

2 ReTr(QjSr)−∥Sr∥
]}
.
If one replica accepts first, it retains that candidate while proposals continue for the other. Each
marginal is consequently ordinary rejection sampling from its own exact conditional distribution.
393
=== PAGE 394 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Unequal rejection counts do not change either marginal: each replica uses its first accepted
candidate in the common independent sequence. The next link starts with fresh randomness.
Links are updated in the fixed site-major, direction-minor order recorded in the source. The
product of these conditional kernels preserves the Wilson measure for each replica.
This coupling uses common coordinate frames for the two configurations. The joint coupling
rule is not invariant under independently changing the replicas’ gauge frames. A gauge-invariant
observable does not remove that dependence of the coupling itself. This distinction is relevant
when interpreting coalescence statistics. Coupling-scheme dependence of damage spreading is
established in other Markov-chain models [98].
83.2 An exact algorithmic coalescence bound
Proposition 83.1 (Finite-box algorithmic coalescence). For the ideal exact-arithmetic shared-
candidate coupling just defined, let E = 4L4 be the number of links and let τ be the first sweep at
which the two configurations agree on every link. For any initial pair, any finite β≥ 0 and any
integer n≥ 1,
Pr(τ >n)≤
(
1−e−12βE
)n
, Eτ≤e12βE.
At β = 0, the configurations agree after one full sweep. Equality is absorbing under this coupling.
Proof. For either replica and every Haar candidate, 1 2 ReTr(QSr) ≥−∥Sr∥ and ∥Sr∥≤ 6. Thus
its acceptance probability is at least e−12β. If the first uniform in a link update is at most
e−12β, both replicas accept the same first candidate. Conditional on the entire past, that event
has probability e−12β. Requiring it at every one of the E updates in a sweep has probability
at least e−12βE. Previously updated links are not updated again during that sweep, so this
event leaves every link equal at its end. Once all links agree, the staples and all subsequent
acceptance decisions agree, proving absorption. Iterating the conditional failure bound proves
the tail inequality, and summing the tail proves the expectation bound. At β = 0 every first
candidate is accepted.
This bound is very conservative and deteriorates exponentially with the number of links. It
proves eventual coalescence at every finite volume and coupling, so finite-horizon noncoalescence
cannot be a literal finite-box transition to infinite coupling time. The proposition concerns the
Monte Carlo coupling and gives no physical transfer-gap bound.
83.3 Frozen experiment and observables
A retained exploratory pilot established feasibility and selected a grid. Before production, the
full design, seeds, source hashes, endpoints, and statistical analysis were frozen in production_d
esign.json. Production comprised 1,512 independently seeded pairs:
• Main calculation: 32 hot/cold pairs at each of 10 couplings β = 0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.12,
0.14, 0.16, 0.18, 0.2, 0.354, on each of the three volumes, with a 512-sweep horizon (960
pairs).
• Small-perturbation calculation: 24 pairs at each of β = 0.05, 0.12, 0.16, 0.2, 0.354 on each
volume (360 pairs). One configuration was warmed for 512 ordinary heat-bath sweeps; its
copy was perturbed by an independent random-axis quaternion rotation of angle 0.02 on
every link. The initial mean link distance is approximately 1 − cos(0.02) = 2.0 × 10−4. The
warmup is a specified initialization, not a proof of exact equilibrium.
394
=== PAGE 395 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
• Higher-coupling diagnostics: eight pairs for each initialization, volume, and β = 0.7, 1.5, 2.5,
with a separately labeled 128-sweep horizon (144 pairs).
• Independent-noise controls: eight hot/cold pairs on 34 at each of β = 0, 0.05, 0.16, 0.354,
1.5, 2.5, with 128 sweeps (48 pairs).
Two discrepancies were measured after each sweep:
DU = 1 2E ∑ e |qA e −qB e |2, DP = [ 1 Np ∑ p (pA p −pB p )2 ]1/2 , pr p = 1 2 ReTrUr p, Np = 6L4.
DU compares the link coordinates in a common frame; DP is invariant under separate gauge
transformations of the two configurations. Coalescence means exact componentwise equality of
every link, with no distance tolerance. Shared pairs stopped at this absorbing state. Subsequent
damage is mathematically zero, but no additional simulated data rows were invented. Independent
controls ran their full horizon.
The calculation produced 309,623 actual recorded rows, including initial configurations. Rows
within a pair are correlated; independent pair seeds are the statistical units. The initial production
run took 94.5 seconds of wall time with two workers; the sum of individually recorded process
elapsed times was 181.4 seconds. The latter is not a CPU-time measurement.

83.5 Numerical validation and reproducibility
Validation covered the new coupling as well as its inherited geometry. The maximum observed
discrepancy between staple-predicted and full-action changes on L = 2, 3, 4 was 4.91 × 10−14.
Tests confirmed exact one-sweep coalescence at β = 0, and absorption of identical pairs across
the tested couplings through β = 2.5. Separate gauge transformations changed DP by at most
2.23 × 10−16 in the test. Four sets of 150,000 coupled conditional draws checked eight marginal
projected means against the exact Bessel expectation I2(κ)/I1(κ); all deviations were below
1.64 estimated standard errors. The maximum link norm-squared error over production was
8.89× 10−16.
The frozen source, design and all 1,512 trajectory/metadata pairs have been checked against their
recorded hashes. Twenty-eight affected trajectory files were recovered by rerunning their original
seeds with the unchanged source; each recovered trajectory matched its original completion
hash. No outcome was excluded. The final analysis uses the complete recorded data. The V5
check revalidates the complete data and recomputes the summary; it is not an independent
regeneration of every stochastic trajectory.
The source, fixed design, raw measurements, original run hashes, validation, recovery evidence
and analysis are supplied. These Monte Carlo results are finite-precision statistical measurements.
Their uncertainty statements have a different meaning from the deterministic error certificates
for the physical transfer operator.
84 Conclusions and the next mathematical target
The established endpoint is a collection of physical lattice results and controlled passage criteria.
The finite-box bounds concern the full gauge-invariant vacuum complement, and their represen-
tation tails are included. The strong-coupling theory has estimates that survive spatial growth
at fixed lattice coupling. At arbitrary fixed spatial cutoff and positive Hamiltonian coupling,
subsequential thermodynamic dynamics and nonzero local correlations are constructed. These
statements resolve different regulator-level questions and retain their distinct uniformities.
396
=== PAGE 397 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
The concentration and fidelity results explain why spatial refinement cannot be handled by an
unexamined fixed electric basis or a global comparison with Haar measure. The improved local
estimate supplies a volume-independent bound on a fixed conditional sector, but the retained
sector and its coupling to the discarded sector still matter. A complete lower bound for the
interacting vacuum complement must control them collectively. The finite-dimensional Schur
certificates show how this can be done at fixed parameters, including all omitted modes; they do
not provide a uniform complexity or gap estimate along cutoff removal.
The conditioning calculations have a separate conclusion. The stated finite functional is bounded
throughout the certified field domain, including its analytic remainders. The corresponding
extended physical coupling range is conditional on the imported block-comparison hypotheses.
Exact sensitivity and ceiling calculations also delimit that method. A successful interval compu-
tation cannot by itself validate a missing comparison between the functional and the physical
transfer spectrum.
The explicit reference-loop trajectory proves that the renormalization equation has a selected
solution at every finite level. Exact blocking preserves the expectations of aligned loops. The lifted
reflection-positive interpolation connects the two endpoint measures and makes their generally
nonzero normalized insertion explicit. The construction does not prove that its couplings escape
to the weak-coupling regime, that its renormalized observables converge, or that a positive
asymptotic area coefficient persists. The corrected scalar wall and heavy-matter results remain
useful comparisons within their own models.
The next substantial advance would establish three controls on one and the same sequence:
1. Renormalized gauge-invariant states and local observables with nonzero limiting norms and
compatible physical-time correlations as as → 0, together with the local field properties
required to identify the continuum theory.
2. A collective estimate on the actual interacting vacuum measure, or a stronger full spectral
inequality, whose physical lower bound stays above a fixed M > 0. The estimate must
include all sectors and all omitted representations relevant to the limiting physical space.
3. Uniformity as physical spatial volume grows, including control of vacuum subtraction,
density of the limiting probe family, and the passage from finite-volume correlations to the
infinite-volume theory.
The continuum transfer theorems prove what follows once these controls are available. They do
not establish the controls themselves. The published lattice spectrum gives substantial numerical
motivation, and the certified benchmarks supply concrete tests for proposed methods. The work
therefore ends with an explicit, reproducible boundary between the proved lattice theory and the
remaining continuum construction. It does not determine an exact continuum mass or claim
that boundary has been crossed.

Mathematical calculation appendices
A Exact calculation records and reproducible certificates
A.1 What the calculation records establish
The preceding arguments use inequalities quantified over all admissible volumes, separations,
or cutoff indices. This section records finite calculations of quantities whose mathematical
meaning has already been established analytically. Its purpose is to test normalization, verify
implementations, and make the worked examples reproducible. The calculations are not estimates
of an unknown four-dimensional mass gap.
Three objects must be distinguished throughout. The first is the four-dimensional Wilson
measure. The second is the exactly solvable one-plaquette integral for SU(2). The third is
a two-dimensional, free-boundary rectangular lattice whose gauge fixing makes its plaquette
variables independent. The last two objects supply the numerical tables in this section. Their
exact integrals are useful controls for calculations in the first model, but their laws cannot be
substituted for its interacting plaquette distribution.
For the fundamental representation of SU(2), write
w(U) = 1 2 TrU = cosθ, 0≤θ≤π.
The normalized Haar class measure is (2/π) sin2 θdθ. The one-plaquette partition function and
the normalized spin-j character expectation are
z(β) = 2I1(β) β , aj(β) = I2j+1(β) I1(β) , β > 0.
The exact-model section proves these formulas from Haar integration. The present section proves
an elementary enclosure algorithm for their values. It uses neither asymptotic expansions nor
floating-point special-function libraries in the certificate arithmetic.
The elementary character identity
χ1(U)
3 = 4w(U)2 − 1 3
gives the one-plaquette variance
v(β) = 1 + 3a1(β) 4 −a1/2(β)2.
On a planar rectangular lattice with free boundary, a fundamental Wilson loop enclosing A
plaquettes has expectation a1/2(β)A. The integer A is the number of plaquettes, not a four-
dimensional physical area in unspecified units.
A.2 A positive-series enclosure theorem
For an integer n≥ 0 and a positive rational number b, define
tk(n,b) = (b/2)2k+n k!(k +n)!, SK(n,b) = K∑ k=0 tk(n,b).
Every term and every partial sum is rational. The series for the modified Bessel function is
In(b) =
∞∑
k=0
tk(n,b).

=== PAGE 400 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
Only nonnegative terms occur. Consequently truncation gives a lower bound with no cancellation
error. A complete upper bound needs a bound on the infinite remainder.
Theorem A.1 (rational enclosure of a positive Bessel series). Put
rK = b2 4(K + 2)(K +n + 2).
Whenever rK < 1,
SK(n,b)≤In(b)≤SK(n,b) + tK+1(n,b) 1−rK . (A1)
For every b> 0 and every prescribed relative tolerance η > 0, some finite K satisfies rK < 1 and
tK+1(n,b)
1−rK
≤ηSK(n,b). (A2)
Proof. Direct division gives
tk+1
tk
= b2
4(k + 1)(k +n + 1).
For successive terms after tK+1, this ratio is at most rK. Therefore
∞∑
k=K+1
tk ≤tK+1
∞∑
ℓ=0
rℓ K = tK+1 1−rK .
This proves (A1), including the entire infinite tail. As K→∞, the ratios tend to zero. Beyond a
finite index they are at most 1/2, so the terms decrease geometrically and the displayed remainder
tends to zero. Meanwhile SK ≥t0 > 0. This proves the eventual relative inequality (A2). No
numerical convergence test is substituted for this argument. □
The generator chooses K adaptively for each pair (n,b) and requires η = 10−45. Its stopping
decision compares rational numbers exactly. The tolerance describes the Bessel-series enclosure;
subsequent ratios and variance expressions have their own propagated interval widths. Those
widths are retained explicitly rather than being assumed equal to 10−45.
The distinction between rK and tK+1/tK matters. The tail starts at tK+1, so its later ratios
begin with tK+2/tK+1. Using an earlier, larger ratio would remain valid once below one but
would be less efficient. Using a later, smaller ratio without accounting for the first omitted term
would not justify the same geometric bound.
For rational b, factorial denominators can be large, but that is a computational cost rather than
a mathematical uncertainty. Python’s integer and rational arithmetic retains the numerator and
denominator exactly. The mathematical proof of (A1) is independent of the language used to
implement those integer operations.

Let m−≤ a1/2 ≤ m+ and s−≤ a1 ≤ s+. The bounds used below satisfy 0 < m−≤ m+ < 1.

No independence between the uncertain ratios is assumed. In fact, they share the same denomi-

though ignoring that dependence may enlarge the interval. This conservative propagation is

For a nonnegative integer area A,

The records use A = 4 and A = 16. Very small positive values can have an outward-rounded

The exact rational endpoint remains positive in the machine-readable certificate.
The ratio In/I1 and the plaquette variance have different qualitative behavior. As b↓ 0, the
fundamental mean tends to zero, while the variance tends to 1/4. As b→∞, the mean tends
to one and the variance tends to zero. These statements follow from the exact integral and
its asymptotics, not from the finite parameter grid. The grid is a consistency check on those
independently derived limits.
A.4 Decimal output with a proved direction of rounding
For a rational number x = p/q, q > 0, define its d-place lower and upper decimal representatives
by
xd = 10−d
⌊
10dp/q ⌋ , xd = 10−d ⌈ 10dp/q ⌉ .
Then xd ≤x≤xd. The implementation evaluates the two integer divisions directly. It does not
convert the rational number to a binary float and then attempt to infer which way that float
rounded.
Proposition A.2 (displayed enclosures). If L≤x≤U, then
Ld ≤x≤Ud.
The width introduced by decimal display is less than 2 × 10−d in addition to the rational interval
width.
Proof. The enclosing inequalities follow by transitivity. Each endpoint moves outward by an
amount in [0, 10−d). Adding the two changes proves the width statement. □
The CSV file displays 14 decimal places. The manuscript tables use fewer places to remain
readable. All full rational numerators and denominators are supplied separately. A reader can
reproduce the decimal tables from those fractions without evaluating a Bessel function.

A.6 Certifying the sharpened comparison threshold
The locality section improves the coarse influence coefficient β to tanhβ on the ordinary hyper-
cubic lattice. In four dimensions its sufficient contraction condition is
18 tanhβ < 1, equivalently β < arctanh(1/18).
The threshold is a sufficient condition for this comparison proof. It is not a determination of a
phase transition or a physical critical coupling.
404
=== PAGE 405 ===
SU(2) Yang–Mills: spectral bounds and continuum criteria V5
For 0<x< 1,
arctanhx =
∞∑
k=0
x2k+1
2k + 1.
This identity follows by integrating the geometric series for (1 −x2)−1 on a compact subinterval
of (−1, 1), where uniform convergence justifies termwise integration. Positivity provides a
particularly simple exact certificate.
Proposition A.3 (threshold enclosure). Put
TK(x) =
K∑
k=0
x2k+1
2k + 1.
Then
TK(x)≤ arctanhx≤TK(x) + x2K+3 (2K + 3)(1−x2). (A6)
Proof. In every omitted term, the denominator is at least 2K + 3. Hence
∞∑
k=K+1
x2k+1

Summing the geometric series proves (A6). □
The certificate uses x = 1/18 and K = 18. It also proves directly that the improved threshold
exceeds 1/18, because all terms after the first are positive. The improvement is a refinement of
the displayed sufficient estimate.
A.7 An analytic scaling control with no sampled-field interpretation
One figure plots the explicit comparison functions
Bp(a) =a−pe−1/a, p∈{0, 2, 4}.
Their logarithms are −p loga− 1/a. The graph is not evidence for a limit: the limit follows
immediately from the following elementary lemma.
Lemma A.4 (exponentials dominate polynomial normalization). For every c> 0 and
real p,N,
lim
a↓0
a−p−Ne−c/a = 0.
Proof. Set x = c/a. Up to a fixed positive constant, the expression is xp+Ne−x. Choose a
nonnegative integer k > max{p + N, 0}. The exponential series gives ex/2 ≥ (x/2)k/k! for x> 0.
Consequently
xp+Ne−x ≤ 2kk!xp+N−ke−x/2 −→ 0.
The final factors are bounded and converge to zero; in particular, p +N−k< 0. □
This elementary result enters the fixed strong-coupling obstruction because the interaction-graph
distance grows at least proportionally to physical separation divided by a. The theorem concerns
observables obeying its support-size and norm hypotheses. A graph of Bp cannot replace those
hypotheses or establish that arbitrary renormalized field observables satisfy them.
The exact records contain 33 Bessel enclosures and 66 derived intervals on the stated eleven-
coupling grid, together with the comparison-threshold interval. All are quantities of the specified
solvable calibration models. The accompanying rational data permit direct checking of the tail
and interval inequalities above.

A.8 How the calculations constrain a proposed proof
A proposed argument must preserve normalization across its stages. If a character expansion
uses TrU while a comparison estimate uses N−1 ReTrU, then the coupling parameter changes
by a factor of N. The series calculations make such errors visible. At small β, the fundamental
one-plaquette mean begins at β/4 in the convention used here; this coefficient is an exact local
check.
A proposed argument must also preserve the model’s dependence structure. The planar expecta-
tion aA 1/2 uses independent plaquette variables after a legitimate two-dimensional gauge change.
The one-cube calculation in the exact-model section gives a direct obstruction to extending that
independence into higher dimensions. Replacing a four-dimensional loop expectation by the
planar formula would remove the very curvature constraints that need analysis.
Finally, a proposed argument must preserve the units of its rate. A number obtained from
− loga1/2(β) is a dimensionless decay parameter for a specified solvable observable. Calling it a
four-dimensional particle mass requires a physical time variable, a transfer semigroup, a nonzero
state, and the correct factor of the lattice spacing. The spectral and reconstruction sections state
those requirements as mathematical assumptions and prove the deductions from them.
These controls are useful because they have exact answers. They permit a candidate calculation
to fail quickly and specifically: a wrong small-coupling coefficient is a normalization error; an
unjustified product of plaquette means is a dependence error; a missing factor of 1/a is a units
error. Passing these checks does not prove the remaining continuum estimate, but failing one
identifies a repairable mathematical defect before it propagates through the manuscript.
B The 96 plaquette classes of the perfect forest
For each parity class x mod 2 (first column) the second column gives eµ(x) from (10.3). The
remaining columns give, for the plaquette P (x; a,b), the unique link of F∗ it contains. The symbol
◦k is the link leaving the base corner x in direction k. The symbol ij is the link leaving the
corner x + ei in direction j. Each entry can be checked by looking up µ at the indicated corner.
